twofa_webauthn_platform_desc: This uses your screen lock method. The same biometrics (fingerprint, face scan) or PIN you already use to unlock your phone or computer to verify it's really you. It works because even if someone learns your password, they can't unlock your screen from far away. They would need to be holding your phone or sitting at your computer.
twofa_webauthn_crossplatform_desc: This uses a small physical gadget (often a USB stick, a key fob, or a tap card) to verify it's really you. When you log in, you plug it into your computer or hold it against your phone. It works because even if someone learns your password, they don't have this physical thing. It stays with you, like a house key on your keyring.
twofa_totp_desc: A separate app on your phone generates a new 6-digit code every 30 seconds. Common apps include Google Authenticator and Authy. Works even without an internet connection.
twofa_email_desc: We send a 6-digit code to your email each time you log in. Convenient, but only as secure as your email account. Anyone who can read your email can receive these codes.
twofa_sms_desc: We send a 6-digit code to your phone number via text message. This is the weakest option because phone numbers can be stolen through a technique called SIM-swapping. Use only if no other option is available for you.
twofa_push_desc: A notification pops up on your phone asking you to approve the login. You just tap "Yes, that's me" to get in. It works because someone would need access to your phone to tap that button. Requires the app to be installed and an internet connection on your phone.
exposure_hint_add_volunteer: This person will be able to read decrypted client data for any ticket they are assigned to. That data covers names, phone numbers, messages, and case notes. They can also export or copy it outside of CARE-Y. Only add people you trust with your clients' safety.
exposure_hint_remove_volunteer: This volunteer can no longer access new tickets. They have already seen decrypted content for tickets they were previously assigned to. That access cannot be undone.

onboarding_briefing_intro: CARE-Y encrypts everything in the volunteer's browser before it reaches the server. The server stores only scrambled data it cannot read. Decryption requires the volunteer's password plus verification from two separate servers in different countries. No single server holds enough information to decrypt anything.
onboarding_briefing_diagram_alt: Simplified diagram showing how CARE-Y derives encryption keys from passwords using two verification servers
onboarding_briefing_diagram_caption: How your password becomes encryption keys
onboarding_briefing_diagram_zoom: Pinch to zoom, tap background to close

onboarding_briefing_scenario_seizure_tit: Someone seizes or breaks into the CARE-Y server
onboarding_briefing_scenario_seizure_bod: An attacker with full access to the server's database gets encrypted data they cannot read. Client tickets, messages, case notes, and volunteer details remain locked. Decryption requires the volunteer's password plus both verification servers in two different countries. A seizure in one country is not enough.
onboarding_briefing_scenario_oprf_title: Someone compromises one of the two verification servers
onboarding_briefing_scenario_oprf_body: An attacker gets one half of the verification process, which is useless on its own. The other half is on a server in a different country under different legal jurisdiction. Even with one half, they cannot derive any volunteer's decryption keys. The verification shares are refreshed regularly.
onboarding_briefing_scenario_device_body: While that volunteer is logged in, the attacker can see everything the volunteer can see. This is the one scenario CARE-Y cannot fully prevent. You can limit the damage by assigning volunteers only to needed tickets, requiring hardware security keys, and training volunteers to recognize compromised devices.
onboarding_briefing_scenario_insider_bod: A volunteer can read any ticket they are assigned to. Once they have seen decrypted data, no technical control can undo that. Limit damage by assigning the minimum tickets needed, monitoring audit logs, and removing access promptly when a volunteer leaves.
onboarding_briefing_scenario_telephony_t: The telephony provider is compromised or subpoenaed
onboarding_briefing_scenario_telephony_b: The phone provider can hear calls and read SMS messages. They keep records of who your org called, when, and for how long. Sensitive conversations should happen through the encrypted web chat, not phone calls or text messages.
onboarding_briefing_scenario_network_bod: Someone monitoring internet traffic can see that a person is connecting to your server and determine their location by IP address. They cannot read what is being sent, but knowing someone connects to your service at all can be dangerous. A VPN hides this connection from your local network and internet provider by routing traffic through a separate server. For stronger protection, Tor hides the connection from everyone. Even your VPN provider cannot see where the traffic goes. Your org can recommend or require either option depending on the threat level.
onboarding_briefing_choices_heading: Your Setup Choices and Their Security Impact
onboarding_briefing_choices_intro: The decisions you make during setup affect the security of every volunteer and client in your org.
onboarding_briefing_choice_telephony_pro: Phone calls and text messages being recorded or listened to by a third party.
onboarding_briefing_choice_telephony_why: If someone gains access to your phone provider's records, they could see who called whom, when, and for how long. A managed provider holds these records. A self-hosted setup keeps them on your own servers instead.
onboarding_briefing_choice_telephony_tra: Self-hosted gives you more control, but calls to regular phone numbers still pass through a carrier. The encrypted web chat in CARE-Y is always more private than any phone call.
onboarding_briefing_choice_2fa_protects: Stolen passwords being used to access volunteer accounts.
onboarding_briefing_choice_2fa_why: A password alone can be guessed, leaked, or stolen through a fake login page. Two factor authentication adds a second check that makes stolen passwords useless on their own.
onboarding_briefing_choice_2fa_tradeoff: An authenticator app is easy to set up but can still be tricked by a convincing fake login page. A hardware security key (like a YubiKey) checks the website address automatically and cannot be fooled. Hardware keys cost money and volunteers need to carry them.
onboarding_briefing_choice_tor_protects: Someone finding out that your volunteers or clients are using this service.
onboarding_briefing_choice_tor_why: Without Tor, your internet provider (and anyone who can access their records) can see that someone visited your CARE-Y site. Every connection includes an IP address, which reveals the user's physical location. They cannot read the encrypted content, but the connection itself reveals involvement and whereabouts.
onboarding_briefing_choice_tor_tradeoff: With Tor enabled, users who connect through Tor Browser hide their connection completely. The downside is that Tor is noticeably slower, which can frustrate volunteers during busy shifts.
onboarding_briefing_choice_vpn_protects: Your internet provider or local network operator seeing that volunteers connect to this service, and learning their physical location from their IP address.
onboarding_briefing_choice_vpn_why: Every time a volunteer opens CARE-Y, their internet provider logs a connection to your server. If someone obtains those logs, they learn that this person is involved with your organization. A VPN routes all internet traffic through a separate server, so the internet provider only sees a connection to the VPN, not to your CARE-Y site. The VPN provider can still see where the traffic goes, so choose a trustworthy provider that does not keep logs.
onboarding_briefing_choice_vpn_tradeoff: A VPN is faster and simpler than Tor, making it a good everyday option. Volunteers can install a VPN app on their phone or computer in minutes. The tradeoff is that you are trusting the VPN provider not to log or share your traffic. For the highest protection, Tor hides your connection from everyone. Even the VPN provider cannot see your destination, but Tor is slower. Many organizations recommend a VPN for daily use and Tor for the most sensitive situations.

demo_narrative_search_overlay_body:
Global search opens as an overlay and shows recent searches and recently viewed cases and articles before the user enters a search term. Results appear after the user types at least two characters. [[#privacy #client-data #search]]
**Recent searches.** The list holds ten terms at most, in memory only. The terms are gone when the user signs out, reloads the page, or closes the browser. No search term is written to the device or sent to the server. A browser handed to someone else carries no record of what was searched for. [[#privacy #client-data]]
**Recently viewed cases and articles.** The server stores one envelope per account, sealed to that account's own public key. Only that user's browser can open it. The envelope holds the identifiers of up to twenty cases and articles and the times they were opened. It holds no titles. The server cannot read which case any identifier inside it belongs to, and no other user can open the envelope. [How encryption works](#deep-dive/how-encryption-works) covers the key it is sealed to. [[#encryption #server-holds]]
**What falls out of the list?** The overlay looks each identifier up against the same records it searches for a query. A case or article the account no longer has access to does not appear. A password change replaces the keys the envelope was sealed to and makes it unopenable. The app treats an unopenable envelope as empty history and overwrites it on the next view, so a password change silently clears the recently viewed list. [Password and key re-wrap](#settings/password) covers that rotation. [[#failure-states #keys]]
**How are results ordered?** Results are grouped by kind of record. The group matching the surface the search was opened from appears first, so the same query returns a different order from the ticket list than from the library. Each group reports how many records it searched against the total, so the user can tell when an answer covers only what is already unlocked on the device. [What global search covers](#search/entities) covers the kinds. [[#client-data #metadata]]
**The provider registry and the two lists.** The provider registry is `packages/client/src/lib/search/registry.svelte.ts`. The session term list is `recents.svelte.ts`. The recently viewed envelope is `recent-views.ts` against `user_recent_views` from `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`. That table stores one row per account with no server-side timestamp. [[#server-holds #client-data]]
demo_narrative_search_how_body:
No search term ever leaves the device. The browser matches the query against text it has already decrypted, which is why a query about case content can run at all when the server cannot read any of it. [[#privacy #server-holds #search]]
**The initial search.** The query runs against whatever the current session has already loaded and decrypted. Cases match from the existing cache with no server request. Articles and accounts each fetch their full set once, the first time the group is needed, and then search that set in memory on every later query. Each group reports how many records it searched against how many exist, so the user can see when the answer covers only part of the set. [[#client-data #metadata]]
**The deeper search and when it starts.** The deeper search pages in every record of that kind the account has access to, decrypts each one in the browser, and matches there. It also starts on its own when the initial search finds no result at all, as long as at least some records were available to search. The user can start it manually at any time. Changing the query abandons a running deeper search and discards its results. [[#failure-states #client-data]]
**What does the server receive during a deeper search?** Two kinds of request, neither carrying a word of the query. A paging request fetches records by cursor and page size. A content request carries a page number and a page size. The server answers both with ciphertext it cannot read. [[#trust-boundary #server-holds]]
**What can the server infer?** That a deeper search happened, when it happened, and how many records were paged in. The server does not receive what was typed, which records ultimately matched, or whether anything matched at all. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers what else the server can infer from traffic. [[#metadata #trust-boundary]]
**What does the server restrict?** Both requests return only records in the queues the user has access to. A deeper search cannot widen what the user can see. When the user has access to no queue, the result is empty rather than an error. [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers that boundary. [[#permissions #server-holds]]
**Why does client-side search work at this scale?** Paging an organization's full case set into the browser is practical at 200 to 2,000 cases and is the cost of the server not being able to index encrypted text. [[#failure-states #encryption]]
**The full-search functions and the registry.** Each provider's `fullSearch` function lives under `packages/client/src/lib/search/providers/`. The registry in `registry.svelte.ts` coordinates each run with a generation counter and an abort signal so an abandoned run cannot report over a live one. The server side is `contentSearch` in `packages/server/src/tickets/search.ts`. [[#client-data #server-holds]]
demo_narrative_search_entities_body:
One query runs against cases, knowledge base articles and, for a user holding the Manage users permission, other users. While a case is open the query also runs against that case's conversation. [[#client-data #permissions #search]]
**What does a case match on?** The title, the description, the client's alias, the queue the case sits in and the name of whoever holds it, all decrypted in the browser before the match runs. A deeper pass adds the text of the messages and notes on the case. Queue and assignee names are decrypted once each rather than once per case, so widening the match to those fields costs no extra decryption. [[#encryption #client-data]]
**What does an article match on?** The title and the excerpt already loaded for the library. A deeper pass adds the full body. [[#client-data]]
**What does an account match on?** The display name, decrypted in the browser. This group is present only for a user holding the Manage users permission, so the same query returns a group for one user and no group for another. [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers that grant. [[#permissions #privacy]]
**What does the open case add?** Its messages and notes become a fourth group, matched against the text already decrypted for the thread. [In thread search](#ticket-detail/deep-search) covers what that search reaches and what it skips. [[#client-data]]
**What does matching tolerate, and what can it not reach?** A query typed without accents finds the accented original, and a small mistyping in a word still matches. [Searching this page](#tickets/page-search) covers the exact tolerance. A case whose title has not decrypted is skipped until it has. A case the user holds no key for cannot match on its title or its client's alias, but can still match on its queue or assignee name because those are decrypted from the organization key. [[#failure-states #keys]]
**The provider modules and the shared matcher.** Each kind is a module under `packages/client/src/lib/search/providers/`, registered into the shared registry as the surface that owns it mounts, which is why the set of groups changes with the surface. The matcher shared by all of them is `fuzzy.ts` over `normalize.ts` in `packages/client/src/lib/search/`. [[#client-data]]

demo_narrative_topic_sort_body:
The ticket list can be sorted by creation date, priority, last activity, queue, follow-up count, client, title, assignee, and status. Which side performs the sort depends on whether the server can read the field's values or only the browser can. [[#metadata #trust-boundary]]
**Server-paged order.** Creation date, priority, last activity, queue, and follow-up count are plaintext columns, so the server sorts and pages results with creation time and ticket ID as tiebreakers. A sort request tells the server which field and direction the user selected, the same way a filter request does. [Filters](#tickets/filters) covers what else a list request carries. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
**Sorting after decrypt.** Client, title, and assignee are encrypted under the organization key or the ticket key. The New-versus-Active status distinction is derived from a ticket's follow-up count in the browser; the server only stores open and closed. The browser orders these fields over decrypted values after the rows arrive. A row still waiting for its decrypt sorts to the front rather than dropping out of the list. [[#encryption #client-data]]
**Partial-list sorting.** Sorting by a browser-side field while pages remain unfetched orders only the rows already loaded. The list states this and offers to fetch the rest before sorting again. Switching to a server-sorted field hands the entire sort back to the server. [[#failure-states]]
**New replies first.** New-replies-first puts tickets carrying replies the user has not read ahead of the rest, within whatever sort is otherwise active. Read state is encrypted per account, so the server cannot sort by it or detect that the option is on. [Unread badges](#tickets/unread-badges) covers how a reply counts as unread. [[#privacy #client-data]]
**Server query, browser comparator, and field-set gate.** The server clauses are the `ORDER BY` and keyset blocks of `list` in `packages/server/src/tickets/ticket-service.ts`. The browser comparator is `sortTickets` in `packages/client/src/lib/tickets/sort-tickets.ts`, which mirrors the server's tiebreakers so a partly-server, partly-browser list does not contradict itself. The field set that forces the browser path is `CLIENT_ONLY_SORT_FIELDS` in `packages/client/src/routes/(app)/tickets/+page.svelte`. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_topic_filters_body:
The ticket list can be filtered by status, queue, priority, assignee, creation date range, unread only, and needs attention only. Several dimensions can be active at once, and a badge counts how many are active. Clearing all filters resets every dimension but leaves the sort alone. [[#metadata]]
**The four statuses.** The status filter offers New, Active, On Hold, and Closed. The server stores only open and closed, plus an on-hold flag. The four partition every ticket. New and Active are both open tickets that are not on hold. The server computes whether anyone has responded to a ticket. A response is a volunteer reply (internal notes do not count) or an answered call. The client's own opening message does not count. The browser reads that field and shows New when nobody has responded, Active when someone has. Selecting New together with Active is one server query for open, non-held tickets. When exactly one of the two is selected, the browser narrows the result further. On Hold maps to an open ticket with the on-hold flag set. Closing a ticket clears the hold, so no ticket carries both statuses at once. Selecting New together with On Hold returns both open non-held tickets without a response and held tickets. Closed maps to the closed status. [[#server-holds #client-data]]
**Filter option counts.** Each filter option shows a count computed in the browser over an index of all ticket metadata the user can see. Each count honours every other active filter but not its own, so choosing one option does not zero its siblings. Counts are bare while the index loads and read "N+" while the index is incomplete. The queue filter's counts come from the same index. [[#client-data #metadata]]
**Which side evaluates what?** The server evaluates status, queue, priority, assignee, and creation date range, all of which are plaintext columns on the ticket row. The browser evaluates unread and needs attention, and separates New from Active. Before any filter runs, the server restricts the query to the queues the account has access to. A filter can only narrow what the account already has permission to see, and queue membership is what grants that access. [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers where access comes from. The server returns 50 tickets per page. The default sort is most recent activity first. [Sorting](#tickets/sort) covers the sort options. [[#metadata #trust-boundary #permissions]]
**What does a filter request reveal?** A filter the server evaluates is a filter the server can read. The request states which queue, which priority, which assignee, and which date window the user is browsing, and when. Keeping unread in the browser hides how much of a ticket the user has read. It does not hide that the user opened the ticket. A read-cursor row exists for every ticket a user has opened, and only the position inside it is encrypted. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers that row and the others like it. [[#server-holds #privacy #metadata]]
**How does the browser decide unread?** A ticket is unread when its read cursor decrypts to a real position and someone other than the signed-in user has added activity since. A ticket nobody has opened has no cursor row and is not unread; its New mark already says so. The server excludes the user's own replies from both read-state sources, so a user's own reply is not unread to that user. Read cursors are encrypted per account. Decryption happens in the crypto worker, and the decrypted state lives only in the browser until the user signs out or the tab closes. When the idle timer zeroes the keys, that state is cleared and the unread filter is unavailable until the next sign-in. The browser never sends anything derived from read state to the server. [[#client-data #encryption #privacy #keys]]
**How does the browser decide needs attention?** The ticket must be open, not on hold, and marked urgent or high priority. It then qualifies if it is unassigned, or if it is assigned to the signed-in account and unread. The dashboard bucket of the same name reads this same rule rather than a second copy, so the two surfaces cannot disagree. [[#metadata]]
**Unread beyond the loaded page.** The list holds one page at a time, so an unread filter reading only loaded rows would miss unread tickets on later pages. A separate sweep enumerates the account's cursor rows across every open ticket the account has access to, paging until exhausted. It reports which unloaded tickets are unread, not how many replies each holds. Those tickets are fetched and merged in only after they pass the same filters the loaded rows passed. [[#client-data #failure-states]]
**What survives a reload?** Filter selections live in memory and reset with the tab. A saved filter reapplies a combination in one step, and also carries the sort. [Saved filters](#tickets/saved-filters) covers that surface. [[#client-data]]
**The filter store and query path.** The store holding the dimensions and mapping them to server parameters is `packages/client/src/lib/stores/filters.svelte.ts`. The browser-side narrowing runs in `packages/client/src/routes/(app)/tickets/+page.svelte` over `packages/client/src/lib/tickets/create-list-read-state.svelte.ts`. The facet count computation is `computeFacets` in `packages/client/src/lib/tickets/facet-filters.ts`. The pill definitions and count formatting are in `packages/client/src/lib/tickets/ticket-filter-pills.ts`. The needs-attention rule is `isNeedsAttention` in `packages/client/src/lib/components/dashboard/filters.ts`. The server clauses are in `packages/server/src/tickets/ticket-service.ts`. [[#trust-boundary]]
demo_narrative_topic_saved_filters_body:
A saved filter keeps a combination of active filters under a name so the same combination can be applied again in one step. Every saved filter has a required name, a color, and an icon. The saved filters appear as chips, and selecting a chip applies that combination. A link can carry a saved filter's identifier so opening the link applies the filter. [Filters](#tickets/filters) covers what a filter combination can select. [[#client-data]]
**Private and shared.** A new saved filter is private. It is saved in the user's own encrypted preference store on the server, sealed to the user's own key. No colleague can read it. The filter follows the user to any device they sign in on. Sharing writes it to a separate row on the server, encrypted with the organization key. Every user with the View cases permission lists the organization's shared filters alongside the private ones as one list. A shared filter carries a share icon. Unsharing deletes the shared row and moves the filter back to the user's private preference store with a new identifier. [[#privacy #server-holds]]
**What does the server hold?** The server stores the name and the filter state encrypted with the organization key. It stores the color, the icon, the account that owns it, the organization key generation it was sealed under, and the time it was created in plaintext. The server cannot open either encrypted field. A database dump shows how many shared filters an organization keeps and which account owns each one. It does not show what any filter is called or which queue, priority, assignee, or date window it selects. [How encryption works](#deep-dive/how-encryption-works) covers the organization key and its rotation. [[#encryption #server-holds #metadata]]
**Key rotation.** Both encrypted columns are enrolled in the organization key rotation. A shared filter the browser cannot decrypt during a rotation in flight is left out of the list rather than shown broken. A chip whose name has not decrypted yet shows a placeholder. [[#encryption #keys]]
**Who can do what?** Listing the organization's shared filters requires the View cases permission, the same permission the ticket list requires. Sharing, unsharing, and deleting a shared filter are limited to the account that owns it. The server refuses all three from any other account. The list offers those three actions only on a filter the user owns. [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers where permissions come from. [[#permissions]]
**What does the device hold?** The device holds no private filter data. Private filters live in the encrypted preference store on the server and are decrypted in the browser only while the user is signed in. Logout and the idle timer clear the decrypted copy from memory. An unopenable or malformed preference document falls back to an empty filter list. [[#privacy #client-data]]
**The filter store and the ownership check.** `packages/client/src/lib/stores/saved-filters.svelte.ts` keeps the private and shared sets and presents them as one list. The list and its actions are `packages/client/src/lib/components/filters/SavedFilterList.svelte`; the create sheet is `packages/client/src/lib/components/filters/CreateSavedFilter.svelte`. The server route is `packages/server/src/routes/saved-filters.ts` over `packages/server/src/tickets/saved-filter-service.ts`, where the ownership check lives. The table is `saved_filters` in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_topic_view_modes_body:
The ticket list's "View as" switcher offers Table, Compact rows, Cards, Grid, and Kanban board. The overview page keeps its own view-mode preference, covered in [The view switcher](#dashboard/view-switcher). [[#client-data]]
**Preview loading and server visibility.** Every mode decrypts ticket titles in the browser. Table and Compact rows request no message previews. Cards, Grid, and Kanban board load each ticket's most recent messages as its card scrolls into view and decrypt them in the browser. To request previews, the browser must tell the server which tickets it is asking about, so the server can see which tickets a given browser requested previews for. The decryption step itself is covered in [Ticket decryption](#tickets/decryption). [[#metadata #server-holds]]
**Mode layouts.**
- Table shows one ticket per row with labeled columns for Status, Priority, Client, Title, Queue, Assignee, Activity, and Follow-ups. Narrower screens drop Queue, Assignee, Activity, and Follow-ups as width shrinks. Table fits the most tickets on screen at once with the most detail per ticket.
- Compact rows shows one ticket per line with no message preview, so more tickets fit on screen than the card modes.
- Cards shows one full-width card per ticket with the ticket's most recent messages.
- Grid arranges the same cards in multiple columns, at least two.
- Kanban board arranges cards in the Grid style in columns by workflow stage and adds actions for moving tickets through those stages; [Kanban board](#tickets/kanban-board) covers stages, auto-move, and configuration. [[#client-data]]
**Mode persistence and list rendering.** `packages/client/src/lib/stores/view-mode.svelte.ts` holds the ticket list mode under the localStorage key `care-y-view-mode`, using the load-validate-write primitive in `persisted-state.svelte.ts`. Rendering splits by mode. Table windows its rows by dividing scroll position by a uniform row pitch in `packages/client/src/lib/components/tickets/ticket-table-window.ts` and starts virtualizing at 200 rows in `TicketTable.svelte`. The other modes render through `VirtualList.svelte`, which measures each card, starts virtualizing at 500 items once at least 20 rows have been measured, and lays Grid out at no fewer than two columns. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_topic_kanban_board_body:
The Kanban board is one of the ticket list's view modes, selected from the "View as" switcher. It arranges tickets as cards in the Grid card style in columns by workflow stage. It adds actions for moving tickets through stages. [View modes](#tickets/view-modes) covers the other modes. [[#client-data]]
**Stages.** The default stages are Unassigned, Assigned, Reached Out, Meeting Scheduled, Interviewed, Request Submitted, Request Fulfilled, Continue Support, and Closed. Organizations can add, rename, reorder, and remove stages. Each stage is mapped to a trigger event chosen from a catalog. [[#metadata]]
**Auto-move.** An auto-move engine runs in the browser after the tickets are decrypted. It walks each ticket's event history and places the ticket in the highest stage whose trigger event has occurred. Auto-move only moves tickets forward. If an event is undone (for example an assignment is removed), the ticket stays in its current stage until someone moves it manually. [[#client-data]]
**Manual moves and locking.** Volunteers can move a ticket to any stage in either direction. On desktop and tablet that is drag and drop; on mobile it is a "Move to..." action on the ticket. Managers can lock a ticket to its current stage, which stops auto-move for that ticket and persists until a manager unlocks it. [[#failure-states]]
**Visibility and filtering.** Volunteers see their assigned tickets on the board. Managers see all tickets. Column headers show the stage label and a ticket count. The board shares the ticket list's filter controls, and filtering runs in the browser after decryption. [[#privacy #server-holds]]
**Layout.** Desktop and tablet show a horizontal board whose columns scroll vertically when a column holds more tickets than fit. Mobile has a tab layout and a swimlane layout. The tab layout shows a scrollable row of stage tabs with count badges and the selected stage's tickets below. The swimlane layout shows one collapsible section per stage, and the browser saves the user's layout choice. [[#client-data]]
**Privacy and encryption.** A ticket's stage and its lock flag are encrypted with that ticket's own key, the same key that protects its content. [Ticket decryption](#tickets/decryption) covers that key. The board's stage configuration (the stage labels and the trigger mapping) is encrypted under the organization key. The server stores no readable stage, lock, or configuration data, so it cannot learn where a ticket sits in the workflow. A stage such as Request Submitted would otherwise tell an attacker that a government filing is in progress for that case. [How encryption works](#deep-dive/how-encryption-works) covers the key hierarchy. [[#encryption #keys]]
**Status.** A coming-soon placeholder is shown while this feature is in development. A saved Kanban board view preference loads back unchanged when the feature ships. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_topic_select_mode_body:
Select mode lets the user pick several tickets so one action applies to all of them. The Select control beside the filters turns select mode on. A long press on a row also enters select mode and selects that row. [[#client-data]]
**What does each action write?** The bulk actions are assigning a ticket to an account, putting a ticket on hold, changing priority, and moving a ticket to another queue. Each action writes a plaintext column on the ticket row, so ticket content stays encrypted. A database dump shows a group of tickets that changed the same way at the same moment. Each action also writes a system event into that ticket's timeline. A priority or queue change that would leave the value unchanged writes nothing. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) sets out which columns each action writes. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
**Per-ticket outcomes.** A bulk action applies through a single request. Each ticket in the set receives its own outcome, so a refusal on one ticket does not prevent the others from completing. The selection clears when the run finishes. [[#failure-states]]
**Who can use bulk actions?** Assigning requires the Assign cases permission. Putting on hold, changing priority, and moving between queues require the Change case status permission. The bulk actions are hidden when the user lacks the required permission. The server refuses, ticket by ticket, any action whose permission the account lacks and any ticket outside the queues the account can access. [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers where permissions come from. [[#permissions]]
**Selection state and the bulk runner.** The mode is `createMultiSelect` in `packages/client/src/lib/composables/ticket-list/create-multi-select.svelte.ts`, which holds the selected ticket IDs and nothing else. The bulk runner is `batchMutate` in `packages/client/src/lib/composables/ticket-list/create-bulk-actions.svelte.ts`. Both belong to the tickets list only, and the overview's rows carry single-ticket actions instead, covered in [Quick actions](#tickets/quick-actions). [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_topic_quick_actions_body:
Quick actions are the common operations on a ticket, run without opening it. Rows in the ticket list carry them as a swipe gesture and cards carry them as buttons. [[#client-data]]
**Swipe gestures.** Pulling a row to the right offers reply and call. Pulling left offers assign and hold. Which action a released pull runs depends on how far it went. A pull can also be stopped short to leave that direction's buttons open for a tap. Only one row holds an open tray at a time; any new interaction on another row dismisses it. A long press selects the row for a bulk action instead. [Bulk selection](#tickets/select-mode) covers that path. [[#client-data]]
**Card actions.** Cards carry reply, call, hold or release from hold, and either take when nobody is assigned or assign when somebody is. [[#client-data]]
**Who can do what?** Hold goes through the ticket update mutation, gated on permission to change case status. Assign is gated on permission to assign cases. Take and release are gated on permission to claim cases. On top of every gate, the account must be the ticket's assignee, a watcher on it, or a member of its queue; anything else is refused as a permission error. [[#permissions]]
**What does each action write?** Holding writes the hold flag and assigning or taking writes the assignee, both plaintext columns on the ticket row. Each of the three writes a system event into the ticket's timeline. A reply opens a reply sheet over the list, and the message is sealed in the browser before it is sent. [Sending a reply](#ticket-detail/reply) covers what a reply carries. [[#encryption #permissions]]
**What happens when the server refuses?** The list changes immediately when an action runs. If the server refuses, the change reverts and an error message appears; the message does not name the missing permission. [[#failure-states]]
**The swipe component and action composables.** `SwipeableCard.svelte` in `packages/client/src/lib/components/tickets/` owns the release bands and the one-open-tray rule. Each action is a composable in `packages/client/src/lib/composables/ticket-list/`, shared with the overview's rows. The reply flow is `create-reply-flow.svelte.ts`, which opens a `ReplySheet` rather than the ticket detail's inline compose bar. [My tickets](#dashboard/my-tickets) covers those rows. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_topic_unread_badges_body:
Each ticket row shows how many replies the signed-in user has not read. [[#client-data #encryption]]
**Where does the count come from?** Each account keeps one encrypted read cursor per ticket, recording the last position read. The server returns that ciphertext with recent reply times for the current page. Reply times exclude system events and the user's own replies. The browser decrypts the cursor and counts the times after it. The server sends at most twenty reply times per ticket, so a ticket with more unread replies than that reads "20+". [Filters](#tickets/filters) covers the unread rule and the sweep beyond the loaded page. [[#client-data #encryption #privacy #server-holds]]
**What does the cursor row reveal?** The row is created the first time a user opens a ticket, filled with random bytes sized to match a real encrypted cursor. A row of random bytes is indistinguishable from one holding a real position, by content or by size. The server can tell which tickets a user has opened. It cannot tell which the user has read. Closing a ticket deletes its cursor rows. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers that row beside the others. [[#server-holds #privacy #metadata #trust-boundary]]
**When is the count absent?** The count needs the cursor decrypted, so no count appears while decrypts are in flight, after the idle timer zeroes the keys, or on a ticket whose key the account never received. None of those three means the ticket is read. An absent badge is not a zero. [Ticket decryption](#tickets/decryption) covers the missing-key case. [[#failure-states #keys]]
**The cursor lifecycle and read-state sources.** Both sources (window query for loaded rows and sweep for the rest) are in `packages/client/src/lib/tickets/create-list-read-state.svelte.ts`. The cap is `READ_STATE_TIMESTAMPS_PER_TICKET` in `packages/shared/src/schemas/limits.ts`. Random-byte fill and deletion on close are in `packages/server/src/tickets/read-cursor-service.ts`. The table is `ticket_read_cursors` in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`. [Needs attention](#dashboard/needs-attention) covers the overview bucket reading this state. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_topic_decryption_body:
The title, the description, and the messages are encrypted in the browser before they reach the server. [[#encryption #keys]]
**What does each field hold?** The title is the ticket's short name, shown in the ticket list. The description is the case write-up. The messages are the entries in the ticket's [unified case thread](#ticket-detail/conversation), where volunteers and the client communicate and where internal notes are recorded. [[#client-data #privacy]]
**Where does the content come from?** When a volunteer creates a ticket, they type the title and description in the new-ticket form, and the browser encrypts both before they leave the device. When a web intake form is submitted, the submitter's browser composes the title as "Web intake" plus the client's name if the form has a name field. It generates the description from the form answers and encrypts both fields before anything leaves the device. When an inbound phone call creates a ticket, the server generates the title "Call from" plus the client's internal ID, which is not a name; real names live encrypted. When an inbound SMS creates a ticket, the server generates the title "Inbound SMS". For those telephony tickets, the server holds the generated text in memory briefly, encrypts it to a fresh ticket key, zeroes the buffer, and stores only ciphertext. This is the one path where plaintext exists server-side, and only in memory, never on disk. Messages accumulate as the client and volunteers communicate. [Creating a new ticket](#tickets/new-ticket) covers how each creation channel populates the form. [[#encryption]]
**Who holds a ticket's key?** Every ticket has its own encryption key. A user who holds a copy of that key can unlock and read the ticket in their browser. A sealed copy is stored for each permitted account, one row per ticket, account, and key generation. A ticket created from a web intake form starts with an interim copy sealed to the organization key, and the browser unseals via that copy until per-account copies are created. A telephony ticket starts with copies sealed directly to each intake-queue member who has a public key. If no queue member has a public key at the time the ticket is created, no copy exists and nobody can read the ticket. [How encryption works](#deep-dive/how-encryption-works) covers the key hierarchy that these copies derive from. [[#keys #encryption]]
**Waiting for key sharing.** After an account joins a queue, tickets that were created before that account joined show their plaintext fields.
- Queue
- Priority
- Status
- Assignee
- Timestamps
The title is not shown because no copy of those tickets' keys has been wrapped for that account yet. The server cannot share the keys because it holds only sealed copies it cannot open. Only a signed-in browser that already holds a ticket's key can make a copy for another account. A teammate who already holds those keys shares them automatically on their next sign-in. That teammate's browser wraps a copy of each missing key for the new member's account, paced against idle time so it does not interrupt their work. The sweep is resumable; closing the browser mid-way loses no progress, and the next sign-in picks up where it stopped. After the account receives a key for a ticket, the browser can decrypt and display its title. [[#failure-states #keys]]
**Message previews.** Some view modes show a preview of a ticket's latest messages on the card. The preview content arrives encrypted. The browser fetches it in batches as cards scroll into view. The browser decrypts previews with the same ticket key that unlocks the title. A message can carry its own sealed copy of a temporary key for content written before per-account copies existed. The crypto worker unseals that key and re-encrypts the message under the ticket's key in the background. Preview data registers in the same cache registry as the other decrypted content, so it is wiped with everything else. [[#encryption]]
**Session cache.** A decrypted title stays in a browser-side cache for the rest of the session, so re-rendering the list does not re-decrypt. Every cache holding decrypted content auto-registers in a single cache registry. All registered caches are wiped together when the idle timer zeroes keys and when the page closes, and nothing derived from a decrypt is ever sent back to the server. [[#client-data #privacy]]
**Decrypt cache and backfill sweep.** `TicketDecryptCache` in `packages/client/src/lib/crypto/ticket-decrypt-cache.ts` sends each decrypt to the crypto worker and caches the result, and the base class auto-registers with the cache registry in `packages/client/src/lib/crypto/cache-registry.ts`. Wrap rows: `ticket_key_wraps` in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`. Intake title composition: `packages/shared/src/schemas/intake-ticket-composition.ts`. Telephony ticket creation: `packages/server/src/tickets/server-ticket-create.ts`. Re-wrap sweep: `packages/client/src/lib/crypto/wrap-backfill-sweep.svelte.ts` against `packages/server/src/tickets/wrap-backfill-service.ts`. Preview loader: `packages/client/src/lib/tickets/preview-loader.svelte.ts`. Preview decrypt: `packages/client/src/lib/crypto/follow-up-decrypt-cache.ts`. [Creating a new ticket](#tickets/new-ticket) covers which accounts receive a wrap when a ticket is first created. [[#encryption]]
demo_narrative_topic_new_ticket_body:
Creating a ticket seals its title and description in the browser under a ticket key minted there. The server files the ciphertext and never holds the key. [[#encryption #keys]]
**What does the form ask for?** A title, a queue and a client are required. The description is optional. The priority starts at normal. [[#client-data]]
**One ticket per client at a time.** A client has at most one open ticket. A creation for a client that already has one is refused and the form sends the reader to the existing ticket. That check runs when a looked-up phone number resolves to a client during selection and again before anything is encrypted. A closed ticket is reopened under its existing identifier, keeping its key generation and re-wrapping the ticket key for the destination queue. A new client gets a fresh identifier. The identifier is bound into the encryption as associated data. Content sealed against the wrong identifier would not decrypt. [Closing and reopening](#ticket-detail/close-reopen) covers the reopened path. [[#failure-states #keys]]
**Who can read it afterwards?** The ticket key is wrapped for the creator and for each active member of the destination queue. The creator is added as a watcher. A member who has not finished setting up their account has no public key yet, so nothing is wrapped for that member. A wrap set with no recipients is refused. A member who joins the queue later holds no wrap and receives one through the backfill a teammate's browser runs. [Ticket decryption](#tickets/decryption) covers both paths. [[#keys #permissions]]
**Permission gates.** Creating a ticket requires permission to open cases. The lookup that resolves the target ticket requires permission to view cases. The server refuses a queue that is absent or inactive, and a client record that is absent or already merged into another. [[#permissions]]
**What does the new row hold in plaintext?** The priority, the status, the key generation and the creation time are stored as readable plaintext. The queue and the client are stored as opaque references. A dump can tell that two tickets sit in the same queue or concern the same client, but cannot tell which queue or which client. The title and the description are ciphertext columns. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) sets out the full row. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
**The form and the creation service.** The form is `NewTicketForm.svelte` in `packages/client/src/lib/components/tickets/`. It fetches the destination queue's member keys and asks the crypto worker for one sealed copy of the ticket key per recipient. The server side is `create` in `packages/server/src/tickets/ticket-service.ts`. The row and its wraps are written in one transaction. [[#encryption]]
demo_narrative_topic_split_view_body:
A wide window shows the ticket list and an open ticket side by side. Choosing a ticket in the list replaces the open ticket in the second pane. The list keeps its scroll position and its loaded pages. [[#client-data]]
**Each ticket as its own page in a narrow window.** A narrow window opens each ticket as its own page. Narrowing the window with a ticket open navigates to that ticket's page rather than closing it. [[#client-data]]
**What does the address hold?** Opening a ticket in the pane pushes a history entry whose state carries the ticket's ID, but the address bar stays unchanged. The pane offers expanding the ticket to its own page. That action puts the ticket's ID in the address, which is what makes the page linkable. [[#privacy #metadata]]
**What does the pane ask the server?** The pane fetches one ticket exactly as its own page does. Reading ten tickets in the pane produces the same ten reads as opening them one page at a time. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
**The layout and its handoff.** `+layout.svelte` in `packages/client/src/routes/(app)/tickets/` chooses between the two arrangements. `layout-mode.svelte.ts` in `packages/client/src/lib/stores/` holds the width test. `split-handoff.svelte.ts` preserves the open ticket across a width change. [The case header](#ticket-detail/case-header) covers what the open pane renders. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_topic_list_stats_body:
The ticket list shows counts across the queues the account can access, plus a count of tickets carrying replies the user has not read. The status counts are New, Active, and On hold. [[#metadata]]
**Status counts.** Each status count covers open tickets in the accessible queues:
- New: open tickets that are not on hold and have no volunteer reply or answered call yet. Internal notes and the client's opening message do not count.
- Active: open tickets that are not on hold and have at least one volunteer reply or answered call.
- On hold: open tickets carrying the hold flag.
One query computes them from plaintext columns. An account that belongs to no queue gets zeros rather than an error. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
**Unread count.** The unread count is computed in the browser, not by the server. A sweep decrypts the account's read-cursor record for each open ticket it can access. The count appears only once all cursors have been decrypted, so it is absent for the first moments of a load rather than starting at zero. The server cannot produce this count because it cannot read a cursor. When the new-replies-first [sort](#tickets/sort) is on and the sweep finds no unread ticket, a line says nothing is unread across the queues the account can access. [Unread badges](#tickets/unread-badges) covers what makes a ticket unread. [[#encryption #client-data]]
**Counts query, unread sweep, and line condition.** `counts` in `packages/server/src/tickets/ticket-service.ts` sums one case expression per bucket in a single pass; `hasResponse` in `packages/server/src/tickets/has-response.ts` provides the EXISTS subquery that separates New from Active. The unread sweep is `readStateSweep` in the same service, consumed by `packages/client/src/lib/tickets/create-list-read-state.svelte.ts`. The caught-up line's condition is `showCaughtUpLine` in `packages/client/src/lib/tickets/ticket-list-utils.ts`. [[#metadata]]
demo_narrative_topic_list_search_body:
A search control in the ticket list header opens a search bar below the filters. The search bar matches a term against the decrypted fields of each loaded ticket and steps through the matches one at a time. The term is never sent to the server. [[#client-data #privacy #search]]
**What does the search match?** A term is matched against the title, the description, the client alias, the queue name, and the assignee name of each loaded row. Matching ignores accents and letter case. One inserted character, one substituted character, one transposed pair, or one deleted character per term is tolerated. Results are ordered by match quality, best first. A row whose title has not finished decrypting is left out until it has. The queue name and assignee name are decrypted once per queue and once per account, not once per ticket. [[#encryption #client-data]]
**Narrowed list and match stepping.** The list shows only the matches, best first, in place of whatever sort was active, once the term reaches two characters. A term under two characters does not reduce the list. Matching runs over the tickets the active filters have already selected and skips any ticket the filters exclude. [Filters](#tickets/filters) covers what each filter selects. The unread filter and the unread sort apply after the matching and narrow the matches further. The previous and next buttons scroll each match to the center of the list. Scrolling the list by hand moves the position readout to the nearest match. The view mode can be changed during a search, and the current match is scrolled back into view. [[#client-data]]
**The deeper search.** The deeper search loads the rest of the list, 100 tickets per request, and matches the same fields over all of them. For tickets that still do not match, it requests their encrypted message content in batches of 50. Each batch is decrypted in the browser and matched the same way. Tickets matched on message content are added alongside the field matches. The deeper search starts on its own when the loaded rows produce no match, the term is at least two characters, and the first page has finished loading. The button in the search bar starts it at any time. [[#encryption #client-data]]
**When does the deeper search stop?** The search bar reports progress while the deeper search runs and shows a completed marker when it finishes. If a request for a page of tickets or a batch of message content fails, the run stops there rather than continuing over a partial set. Changing the term or closing the search bar resets the run and discards the decrypted message content it gathered. A stopped run does not restart on its own. [[#failure-states]]
**Arriving from global search.** The global search's "Show all" link loads the tickets page with the term already in the search bar and starts the deeper search without the user pressing anything. The term is carried without entering the URL or browser history. [Search](#search/how-it-works) covers the shared search surface. [[#search]]
**What does the server see?** The server never receives the term and never receives the matches. Serving the list is the paging it would serve anyway. During the deeper search the server additionally serves encrypted message content requested by ticket ID. The deeper search carries the active filter parameters, so the server returns only tickets matching both the filters and the queues the account has access to. The request for message content requires the View cases permission, and the server restricts it to the queues the account can access, ticket by ticket, independently of which IDs were asked for. A database dump or request log shows that one user read much of their accessible queues at one moment, not which words they were looking for. Encryption is the reason the search works this way. The server cannot match encrypted content, so matching happens in the browser after decryption. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers the general model. [[#server-holds #metadata #trust-boundary]]
**Search bar state, deeper search run, and shared matching.** The search bar's state and match stepping are in `packages/client/src/lib/search/search-overlay.svelte.ts`. The deeper search run is `packages/client/src/lib/search/deep-search.svelte.ts`. The matching and message-content fetching shared with the global search are in `packages/client/src/lib/search/providers/tickets.ts`. The typo-tolerant matcher is `packages/client/src/lib/search/fuzzy.ts`. The functions `matchTitles`, `mergeSearchMatches`, and `applySearchOrder` in `packages/client/src/lib/tickets/ticket-list-utils.ts` match the fields, merge message-content matches, and reduce the list to matches. The server side is `contentSearch` in `packages/server/src/tickets/search.ts`. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_topic_case_header_body:
The case header reports the ticket's title, the priority, whether the ticket is closed, the description, the queue, who holds the ticket and how long ago it was opened. The header names the signed-in user when the ticket is assigned to them, and reads unassigned when nobody holds it. [The full case record](#ticket-detail/case-panel) covers the fields the header does not carry. [[#client-data]]
**What does the browser open here?** The title and the description are sealed with the ticket's own key. The queue name and the assignee's display name are encrypted with the organization key. Priority, status and the opened time are plaintext columns. A database dump shows the ticket's priority, whether it is still open and when it arrived. It does not show any of the words in the ticket. [How encryption works](#deep-dive/how-encryption-works) covers the two key tiers. [[#encryption #server-holds #metadata]]
**What happens when the title cannot be opened?** A user in the queue who never received a wrapped copy of the ticket key still gets the row. The title carries a failure message in its place. The queue, priority, status and opened time read normally. [Ticket decryption](#tickets/decryption) covers how the key reaches an account. [[#keys #failure-states]]
**The header component and its queries.** `packages/client/src/lib/components/tickets/CaseHeader.svelte` reads `tickets.get` under `ticketKeys.detail(ticketId)`, the same query key the thread uses, which keeps the header and the thread in sync. The ticket payload carries only the encrypted queue name. The queue color and icon come from the shared queue list instead. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_topic_conversation_body:
The unified case thread gathers everything said on a ticket into one sequence. It holds what the client sent, what the organization sent back, the notes written about it, and the events the ticket recorded. [[#client-data]]
**One sequence, several channels.** Text messages, replies typed into the application, emails, and voicemails are separate kinds of follow-up in the same thread. Whether the client or a user wrote a follow-up decides which side it sits on. The type is a plaintext column, so the server knows a ticket received four texts and sent one email at given times, but holds the words of none of them. [The telephony relay](#deep-dive/the-telephony-relay) covers what the carrier saw of a text before it arrived. [[#metadata #server-holds #telephony]]
**How are follow-ups sealed?** Each follow-up is sealed with the ticket key and bound to its own position in the sequence. A ciphertext moved to another follow-up or another ticket fails to open. Replies a client sends from their portal arrive under a one-off key that the ticket key absorbs on first reading. [How encryption works](#deep-dive/how-encryption-works) covers the slot binding. [The portal channel lifecycle](#deep-dive/portal-channel-lifecycle) covers the one-off key convergence. [[#encryption #keys]]
**Paging through a long thread.** The thread opens on the most recent fifty follow-ups. Older pages of fifty load as reading moves back, and the reading position stays steady as each page arrives. When unread follow-ups are older than the first page, pages load until the last read point is in view. A refresh of the newest page merges follow-ups individually rather than replacing the page, so an older page already loaded is not split at its boundary. [Date separators](#ticket-detail/date-separators) covers the day boundaries. [System events](#ticket-detail/system-events) covers the recorded events. [[#failure-states]]
**The paginator and the follow-up row.** `packages/client/src/lib/tickets/chat-paginator.svelte.ts` is the shared paging implementation behind both this thread and the client portal thread. Both call sites pass a page size of fifty. The row is `followups` in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`, with `encrypted_content` as `bytea` beside plaintext `source`, `type`, and `created_at`. [[#client-data #server-holds]]
demo_narrative_topic_thread_filters_body:
Filters narrow the ticket's case thread by entry kind, by author, and by a date range, and all three combine to select a smaller set. [[#client-data]]
**What does the server answer from?** The kind, the author, the source, and the timestamp of every entry are stored unencrypted. The server evaluates a filter request as a database query against those fields and never sees decrypted text. The server learns which author was requested, on which ticket, between which dates. The words in those entries stay sealed. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) lists the columns a query can reach. [[#metadata #server-holds #trust-boundary]]
**Note type narrowing in the browser.** A particular note type is narrowed in the browser after the response arrives, because the request groups all internal notes into one class. Before responding, the server removes note types the user's role may not view. A filter cannot surface a note the role could not otherwise read. [Note types](#admin-org/note-types) covers the view restriction. [[#permissions #privacy]]
**Gap indicators.** A filtered request returns up to two hundred entries. Each entry carries its position in the full unfiltered thread and the total unfiltered count. Where entries were skipped between two neighbours, the count of skipped entries is reported in line. Clearing the filters restores the paged thread already held, with no new request. [Conversation thread](#ticket-detail/conversation) covers that paging. [[#failure-states]]
**The filter composable and the type expansion.** `create-detail-filters.svelte.ts` in `packages/client/src/lib/composables/ticket-detail/` owns the selections and their labels. `TicketDetail.svelte` maps the grouped choices onto concrete entry types before the request, expanding assignment, status, priority, queue and hold into the event types each one covers. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_topic_compose_actions_bod:
The compose menu offers a reply on the client's encrypted channel, a text, an email, a file, a preset reply, or an internal note. [[#client-data]]
**Which options does the menu offer?** The menu offers an option only when the channel is available:
- A reply requires that the client has a portal channel and that the organization has secure links switched on.
- A text requires that the ticket has a phone number on file and that the SMS channel is on.
- An email requires that the ticket has an email address on file and that the email channel is on.
- Files, preset replies, and notes are always offered.
The server checks every send against the permission for that channel. A hidden option is not what prevents an unauthorized request. [Channel policy](#admin-comms/channel-policy) covers the switches, and [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers the grants. [[#permissions #portal #telephony]]
**Channel exposure.** A reply stays sealed for the client's own browser. A text reaches a phone company in a form it can read. An email is readable by every mail server between the sender and the recipient. The compose bar warns once per session when the user chooses a text or a call. [Sending a reply](#ticket-detail/reply) covers what each channel seals, and [Channel warnings](#ticket-detail/exposure-hints) covers when the warning appears. [[#encryption #telephony #privacy]]
**Preset replies.** A preset reply is organization text sealed with the organization key. The browser decrypts it. The compose bar places the text into the draft, and the user can edit it before sending. Each preset reply belongs to one queue or to the whole organization. [[#encryption #client-data]]
**File picker limits.** The picker offers the same content types the upload endpoint accepts. The browser does not encrypt or upload a file the endpoint would refuse. [File attachments](#ticket-detail/files) covers the size caps and the encryption envelope. [[#failure-states]]
**The compose component and its callers.** `ComposeActions.svelte` renders the menu and hosts the preset-reply and note sheets. Callers decide which options to pass: `TicketDetailOrchestrator.svelte` for the ticket detail page, `ReplySheet.svelte` for the quick reply from a list. Preset replies come from the `preset_replies` table in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts` through `packages/server/src/tickets/preset-service.ts`. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_topic_reply_body:
A reply is encrypted in the browser under the ticket key before it leaves the device, and the server stores the result without holding a key that can open it. How much of the path stays encrypted depends on the channel. A reply to an encrypted portal channel is sealed for the client's own browser, while a text message leaves the encrypted path when it reaches the telephony provider. [[#encryption #telephony]]
**What two copies does a reply produce?** Sending writes the message twice, under different keys. [[#encryption #portal]]
- The organization's copy is encrypted under the ticket's symmetric key and stored as a follow-up on the ticket, readable by every account the ticket key is wrapped for. [[#encryption #client-data]]
- The client's copy is sealed to the public key of their active portal channel and stored beside that channel, readable only in the client's browser. [[#portal #encryption]]
When the client has no encrypted channel open, the second copy is not written and the reply reaches them over the channel they came in on. [How encryption works](#deep-dive/how-encryption-works) covers the key hierarchy behind both copies. [[#encryption #portal]]
**Sending a text.** The browser posts the ticket identifier and the message to a relay endpoint. The server resolves and decrypts the client's phone number itself rather than accepting one from the browser, which keeps the number out of the request. The server hands both to the telephony provider and then zeroes every buffer that touched plaintext in a `finally` block.
- The raw request body
- The ticket identifier
- The message
- The phone number [[#telephony #server-holds #encryption]]
- The endpoint logs no request body and returns no content in an error response.
- The message is capped at 1600 characters, and both the browser and the server count the same unit.
- The provider interface accepts strings rather than buffers, so two immutable copies of the number and the message exist for the length of one outbound HTTP call and persist until garbage collection. This residual risk is recorded in the code beside the line that creates it.
- A text is refused when the organization has switched the SMS channel off.
[The telephony relay](#deep-dive/the-telephony-relay) covers what the carrier and the provider see after the message leaves. [[#telephony #server-holds #encryption]]
**What happens when the relay succeeds but the thread write fails?** The relay runs before the follow-up write. A message can reach the client and then fail to be recorded. The composer keeps the encrypted copy it already built and retries the follow-up write without re-posting the relay. [[#failure-states #telephony]]
**What does the server store from a reply?** The follow-up row's content is ciphertext. Its ticket identifier, its source, its type, its private flag, the user who wrote it, the users mentioned in it, and its creation time are plaintext columns. A database dump shows that a particular user sent a text on a particular ticket at a particular time, and shows neither the text nor whom the ticket concerns. The content is sealed with an authenticated stream cipher, so ciphertext length follows message length and separates a one-word reply from a long one. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) lists the plaintext columns elsewhere in the schema. [[#metadata #server-holds #client-data]]
**Drafts.** Unsent compose text is held in memory and cleared on sign-out and on idle timeout. Closing the tab also discards it. [[#client-data #privacy]]
**What gates each channel?** Each relay endpoint requires its own permission, so an organization can staff text, email, and calls separately. The text relay requires the Send client SMS permission, the email relay requires the Send client email permission, and the call relay requires the Call clients permission. The server checks the permission on every request rather than relying on the compose bar that hides the option. [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers moving those between roles. [[#permissions #telephony]]
**The send composables and relay handlers.** The compose surfaces are `ReplySheet.svelte` and `TicketCompose.svelte` under `packages/client/src/lib/components/tickets/`. The send paths are `create-send-message.svelte.ts`, `create-sms-send.svelte.ts`, and the shared `relay-then-record.ts` under `packages/client/src/lib/composables/ticket-detail/`. The relay handlers are in `packages/server/src/routes/relay.ts` with shared body parsing and authentication in `relay-utils.ts`. The follow-up row is written through `packages/server/src/tickets/followup-service.ts`, and its schema is the `followups` table in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`. [[#client-data #server-holds]]
demo_narrative_topic_notes_body:
An internal note records what the organization wants to remember about a ticket. Nothing from a note reaches the client. The note is encrypted with the ticket key, the same key that protects the messages around it. [[#client-data #encryption]]
**What does the server hold?** The note's content is ciphertext. The note's type, author, creation time, mentioned accounts, and private flag are stored in plaintext. A database dump shows that a user wrote a note of a given type on a ticket at a given hour and mentioned two people in it, but nothing of what the note says. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) lists those columns beside the rest of the schema. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
**Note types and visibility.** Each note carries a type. A type carries a minimum role for writing and a minimum role for seeing. The server removes the notes that the requesting user's role cannot see before building the response. A note below the user's threshold never leaves the server. An author always sees their own. A type's name, icon, and description are encrypted with the organization key, and the roles it restricts on are plaintext. The server enforces the rule without reading the type's name. [Note types](#admin-org/note-types) covers creating and editing them. [[#permissions #privacy #encryption]]
**Escalation targets.** A type can name who to notify when someone writes a note of that type. Those targets are encrypted with the server's operational key, not the organization key, because the server sends the notification without anyone signed in. Mentioning a user in a note pings them once rather than subscribing them to the ticket. [[#trust-boundary #server-holds]]
**Reactions, edits, and deletions.** The reactions are acknowledge, approve, disagree, flag, and complete. Each reaction is a plaintext row naming the account, the note, and the time. The user can edit their own notes and delete their own. An administrator can delete another user's note but cannot edit it. Deleting a note overwrites the content and keeps the row as a tombstone. [[#permissions #retention #metadata]]
**The compose surface and role filter.** The compose surface is `InternalNoteSheet.svelte`. The role filter is in `listFollowUps` in `packages/server/src/tickets/followup-service.ts`. Types and their role columns come from the `note_types` table in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`. Reactions are `followup_reactions` in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`, and mention validation is `packages/server/src/tickets/mentions.ts`. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_topic_case_fold_body:
Folding a ticket hides the description, the queue, who holds the ticket, and how long ago it was opened. The title, the priority, and whether the ticket is closed stay. The fold control is available in the split pane and on the standalone ticket page, but not in the full-page desktop layout. [[#client-data #ticket-detail]]
**Where does the fold live?** One entry in a reactive map held in the tab's memory, keyed by ticket identifier. The fold choice stays in memory only and leaves no trace on the device or the network. The server cannot learn which tickets the user folds or how long any ticket stays open, and a later reader of the device cannot either. A reload creates the map fresh, so every ticket opens with its fields showing. Folding one ticket leaves the others unchanged for the rest of the session. [[#privacy #server-holds]]
**The fold store and drag handling.** `packages/client/src/lib/tickets/case-fold-store.svelte.ts` holds the map; unfolding deletes the entry rather than storing false. Drag and keyboard handling is in `packages/client/src/lib/shell/use-fold-drag.svelte.ts`. [The case header](#ticket-detail/case-header) covers the fields themselves. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_topic_date_separators_bod:
A date separator marks each change of day in the thread, and a separate line marks where reading stopped last time. One component draws both lines on both threads, the ticket thread and the client's portal thread. A client and a user reading the same conversation see the day boundaries in the same places. [[#client-data]]
**How does the browser decide the day boundary?** Two follow-ups fall on different days when their timestamps fall on different calendar dates in the device's time zone. The browser computes this from the timestamps it already holds, with no server input. A user on a device set to a different time zone sees different day boundaries. [[#failure-states #privacy]]
**Where does the unread line come from?** The line is read from an encrypted read cursor per account per ticket, sealed with the ticket key. The read cursor records the last position read. Writing a read cursor tells the server that the user opened the ticket, which is why the ticket list never writes one. [Unread badges](#tickets/unread-badges) covers the read cursor's encryption, its indistinguishability from a first-open decoy, and the sweep that turns cursors into counts. [[#encryption #server-holds #metadata]]
**Debounce and deletion.** The read cursor is held in memory for a few seconds and written once, rather than after every follow-up the user scrolls past. Closing a ticket deletes every account's read cursor for it. Reopening does not restore them, so a closed ticket carries no record of who read how far. [Closing and reopening](#ticket-detail/close-reopen) covers what else a close removes. [[#retention #privacy]]
**The separator and cursor services.** `formatDateSeparator` and `needsDateSeparator` in `packages/client/src/lib/utils/time.ts` decide when a break is needed and format its label. `DateSeparator.svelte` draws the break on both threads. The cursor is handled by `create-read-cursor.svelte.ts` in `packages/client/src/lib/composables/ticket-detail/` against `packages/server/src/tickets/read-cursor-service.ts`. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_topic_system_events_body:
Assignments, status changes, priority moves, queue moves, holds, and merges each appear in the conversation thread as a follow-up. The record of what was done to a ticket sits in the same sequence as the messages on it. The server writes these follow-ups. No key the server holds can read or seal ticket content, so each follow-up is a type and a few parameters in plaintext with no sealed content. A database dump shows that an account was assigned a ticket on a given morning, that its priority changed from normal to urgent an hour later, and which queue it moved to. The words of the ticket stay closed. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers the rest of what a dump reaches. [[#client-data #server-holds #metadata #encryption]]
**How does the browser resolve the names?** The parameters store accounts and queues by identifier. The browser decrypts each identifier against organization-key ciphertext it already holds. The readable name exists only where the organization key is present. An identifier the browser cannot decrypt reads as an unnamed account or queue, not as a failure. [[#failure-states #client-data]]
**Grouping consecutive follow-ups.** Consecutive follow-ups of the same type within ten minutes of each other collapse into one line that shows how many were grouped. Only hold placed, hold removed, status opened, and status closed are eligible. A priority or queue change carries before-and-after values that cannot be summed, so each one stays separate. [[#client-data]]
**What writes each follow-up?** Each follow-up is written by the operation that records it, not by the component that draws it. An assignment produces the same follow-up whether it comes from the ticket list, the panel, or an automatic rule. Who may perform each operation is a separate permission. [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers those grants. [[#permissions]]
**The label map and the event column.** `system-event-label.ts` maps each type to its sentence and `SystemEvent.svelte` draws it. The parameters live in the `event_params` column on `followups` in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`. Hold, priority, queue, and status writes are in `ticket-service.ts`; assignment writes are in `assignment.ts`; merge writes are in `merge-service.ts`; the shared reopen path is in `ticket-reopen.ts`. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_topic_voicemails_body:
A voicemail left on the organization's line becomes a follow-up on the client's ticket, with audio the browser can play and the server cannot read. [[#telephony #encryption]]
**What happens to the audio before it is stored?** The server fetches the recording from the provider. It encrypts the recording with the ticket key, writes the ciphertext to blob storage, and asks the provider to delete the recording and the call log entry it belongs to. The audio exists in plaintext only during that single handler invocation, in buffers the code zeroes afterward. [Call log](#ticket-detail/call-log) covers the provider cleanup that follows, and [The telephony relay](#deep-dive/the-telephony-relay) covers the rules that endpoint works under. [[#server-holds #telephony #retention]]
**What happens when a recording cannot be matched?** A voicemail that cannot be matched to a client or a queue is encrypted with the organization key and held in quarantine for an administrator to route manually. The system does not store it unencrypted and does not discard it. [Voicemail quarantine](#admin-comms/quarantine) covers what an administrator can do with one. [[#failure-states #encryption]]
**Playback and metadata.** Fetching the ciphertext requires the Download case media permission. The endpoint hands back ciphertext and decrypts nothing itself. The browser decodes the audio on the device. The decrypted sound exists only in that tab and is dropped when the user closes the follow-up. The recording's size, duration, and timestamps are stored in plaintext, so a database dump shows that a ticket received a ninety-second voicemail on a given evening. [[#permissions #privacy #metadata]]
**How is a recording bound to its ticket?** A recording is encrypted directly with the ticket key, or encrypted with a separate key that the ticket key unwraps.
