Terminology and note type names are sealed to the organization key. Note type escalation targets are encrypted under the server's operational key because the server sends those notifications itself. [General info](#admin-org/general) covers the four plaintext columns in detail. [[#encryption #server-holds]]
**Which permission gates each destination?** General, Branding and Terminology share the Manage org identity permission. Retention, Follow-Up Types, Intake Forms and Keys each carry a separate permission. A user needs the Manage keys permission to reach the Keys destination, and that permission is one of three locked to the administrator role. Intake Forms is the one destination in this group that a default manager account holds, through the Manage intake forms permission. [Permission matrix](#admin-people/role-permissions) covers which grants an organization can reassign. [[#permissions #keys]]
demo_narrative_admin_hub_analytics_body:
The analytics group collects the reporting and logging destinations under separate permission gates. [[#permissions #metadata]]
- The Impact, Operations, and Research dashboards and [Call history](#admin-logs/calls) require the View reports permission.
- [Audit log](#admin-logs/audit) requires the View audit log permission, so an organization can grant charting and call records without exposing who performed which action.
**What do the dashboards read?** Server-side charts aggregate plaintext metadata.
- Ticket counts
- Timestamps
- Queue assignments
- Priority levels
- Resolution times
Volunteer names and queue names are organization-key ciphertext that the browser decrypts for chart labels. A separate set of charts decrypts ticket content in the browser to extract topic keywords and conversation patterns, and sends nothing decrypted to the server. Those charts can analyze only tickets the viewer holds keys for, so two users with access to different queues see different figures. [[#server-holds #encryption]]
**Dashboard configuration.** Each organization has three dashboard tabs whose names, chart selections, and display order are encrypted with the organization key and stored as a single blob in the organization record. The server holds the ciphertext and cannot read which charts an organization has chosen or what it has named its tabs. Every user with the View reports permission sees the same three dashboards. [[#encryption #privacy]]
demo_section_schedule_desc: The schedule page manages recurring shifts, coverage assignments, and a calendar that reads by day, week, or month. Shift data is encrypted at rest. Automatic ticket assignment uses shift coverage to route a new case to someone whose hours overlap. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers what the server holds.
demo_narrative_schedule_body:
The schedule page defines recurring shifts with start and end times and assigns volunteers to cover them. A calendar shows coverage by day, week, or month. Each shift reads as complete, partial, or absent. Automatic ticket assignment routes a new case to the on-shift volunteer holding the fewest open cases. [[#schedule #metadata]]
**What does the server store?** [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers what the server holds. [[#server-holds #encryption]]
**How does availability matching work?** An intake form can include an availability field that asks a client when they are reachable. The system compares that answer against shift coverage and assigns the case to a volunteer whose hours overlap. A client's availability is sensitive on its own, because when and where someone can talk is a pattern about that person. The comparison runs in the browser or transiently on the server, and the client's answer stays out of plaintext storage. [Submission](#client-intake/submit) covers what an intake form collects. [[#privacy #encryption]]
**Who can edit a schedule?** Creating and assigning shifts requires a separate permission at the manager tier. Viewing shift assignments requires the View own shifts permission. [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers how permission grants work. [[#permissions]]
**The shift provider and assignment path.** The `ShiftProvider` interface in `packages/server/src/tickets/shift-provider.ts` returns the on-shift volunteers for a given queue. The caller is `packages/server/src/tickets/assignment.ts`, which picks the candidate with the fewest open cases and falls back to the next future shift when nobody is currently on. [[#server-holds #schedule]]
demo_section_settings_desc: The settings section covers what the user controls about their own account and device. Display names and language preferences are sealed to the organization key in the browser before storage. Usernames pass through the server only at creation or change and are stored as keyed hashes. A password change re-derives the account's encryption keys and re-wraps every case key the account holds. Appearance is kept on the device alone, with no copy on the server. Two-factor enrollment metadata and notification preferences are stored in plaintext. [How encryption works](#deep-dive/how-encryption-works) covers the organization key, and [How keys are derived](#deep-dive/how-keys-are-derived) covers what a password change re-derives.
demo_section_client_intake_desc: The intake form is where someone without an account asks for help. A built-in default ships with every organization, and custom forms can replace it with different fields and destination queues. Field labels, messages and banner images are readable by anyone who opens the form's public address. The answers a visitor types are encrypted in the browser under a per-case key the server cannot derive. [How encryption works](#deep-dive/how-encryption-works) covers the two key trees, and [How the visitor is protected](#client-intake/how-protected) covers what the server is left with after a submission.
demo_section_client_privacy_desc: The privacy notice is a static page of fixed text shared by every organization, with the organization's name and its own retention setting filled in per deployment. It states what data is collected, how long it is kept, and what rights the visitor has. The page holds no key material and performs no encryption. Every client page links to it from the drawer.
demo_section_client_portal_desc: The secure portal gives a client a private page to read and reply to messages from the organization. A user in the organization creates the link and hands it over by copy or by text. The credential that opens the page stays in the URL fragment, after the `#`, which browsers never include in server requests. Messages on the channel are encrypted with a key derived from that credential, and the server stores ciphertext it cannot open. The client can add a passphrase to guard the link. The client can also move to an account with a username and password without asking the organization. [The portal channel lifecycle](#deep-dive/portal-channel-lifecycle) covers how a channel is created, how it expires, and what each tier protects.
demo_section_client_account_desc: A client account lets the client return to the same conversation with a username and password instead of a link. The password runs through the same key derivation pipeline that members of the organization sign in through. The server stores ciphertext it cannot open. There is no password reset. A user holding the Reset client login permission can delete the account so a new way back in can be set up, at the cost of the client's copies of the conversation. [How keys are derived](#deep-dive/how-keys-are-derived) covers the derivation, and [The portal channel lifecycle](#deep-dive/portal-channel-lifecycle) covers how the account channel fits the broader channel model.
demo_section_client_share_desc: A share link delivers one encrypted message to a reader who has no account in the system. The decryption key sits in the URL fragment, which browsers never include in server requests. The link stops working after one read or after 72 hours, whichever comes first. When the link travels by text message, the carrier and the telephony provider see the full address, key included. [How encryption works](#deep-dive/how-encryption-works) covers the sealing model, and [Single use access](#client-share/one-time) covers what happens after the first read.
demo_section_deepdive_desc: The deep dives cover what CARE-Y is, encryption, key derivation, the organization key lifecycle, the trust boundary, deployment, verifying the code, what the network sees, what stays on the device, the permission system, the telephony relay, the portal channel lifecycle and data retention. Feature entries throughout the handbook link here for mechanism details they reference but do not repeat.
demo_narrative_settings_identity_body:
The user has a display name visible on their work and a username used to sign in. The display name is encrypted in the browser before it reaches the server. The username passes through the server in plaintext at account creation and again at a username change. A username change requires the current password, and a display name change does not. [[#privacy #server-holds]]
**How is the display name protected?** The browser seals the display name to the organization's public key. The server stores the resulting ciphertext and cannot read it. Every surface that shows a display name decrypts it in the browser. A user with the Manage users permission can update another account's display name through the same seal, from their own browser. [How encryption works](#deep-dive/how-encryption-works) covers the organization key. [[#encryption #server-holds]]
**Why does the username reach the server in plaintext?** Sign-in requires the server to match a username against a keyed hash it computed earlier. The server computes that hash, stores it for future lookups, and seals a separate copy with the organization key so browsers can decrypt it. No plaintext column is kept. The hash is salted with the organization's identifier, so one username shared by two organizations yields two distinct hashes. [Username and password](#login/credentials) covers the sign-in side and the fake-salt defense. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
**What can someone learn from the stored hash?** The hash uses HMAC-SHA256 keyed with a value derived from the server's operational key. Someone holding both the database and that key can test a guessed username and confirm whether it belongs to an account. The hash cannot be reversed into a username. Without the operational key, a database dump alone is not enough to test guesses. A username based on a legal name or email address is confirmable with the key; one unrelated to any person is not. [[#metadata #privacy]]
**What does a failed username change say?** A taken username gets the same generic failure wording as other failures, so an attempt does not reveal whether a name is taken. A wrong current password gets its own message. The administrator path (Manage users) names the conflict for the administrator. An administrator cannot change their own username through the administrator path and must use the self-service path, which requires the current password. [[#failure-states #permissions]]
**The profile mutations and their columns.** Both changes are mutations in `packages/server/src/routes/profile.ts` over `updateDisplayName` and `updateUsername` in `packages/server/src/auth/service.ts`. The columns are `users.encrypted_display_name`, `users.encrypted_identifier` and `users.identifier_hash` from `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`, and the keyed hash is `hashIdentifier` in `packages/server/src/crypto/field-encryptor.ts`. [[#server-holds]]
demo_section_library_desc: The library holds articles written and organized by the organization for its own reference. Article titles, excerpts and bodies are encrypted with the organization key in the browser before storage. The server keeps each article's category, the author's account identifier, vote tallies, rating and timestamps in plaintext. The author's display name is encrypted separately. Reading requires the View knowledge base permission. [How encryption works](#deep-dive/how-encryption-works) covers the organization key.
demo_narrative_library_browse_body:
Any user holding the View knowledge base permission can read every article the organization keeps, with no per-article access restriction. An article has no draft state; saving it makes it visible to every user with that permission. The list loads fifty articles at a time, newest first, and scrolling fetches the next fifty. [[#permissions #client-data]]
**What does each row carry?** Title and excerpt are organization-key ciphertext that the browser decrypts. Category, the author's internal account identifier, vote tallies, rating and timestamps are plaintext the server can read. The author's display name is encrypted separately. [Knowledge base](#dashboard/kb) covers that row column by column. [[#encryption #server-holds]]
**How does category filtering work?** The listing endpoint accepts a list of categories and filters on the server in a single expression that serves both the page and the total. The count beside the list reflects the server total for the active filters. Per-category article counts come from the server and appear in the manage-categories sheet. [[#metadata #failure-states]]
**The listing query and its paging.** `listItems` in `packages/server/src/routes/kb.ts` calls `list` in `packages/server/src/kb/service.ts`, which pages by keyset on the sort field and the identifier rather than by offset. Timestamps are truncated to milliseconds so a page boundary cannot repeat a row. The schema caps a single request at one hundred rows, and this surface requests fifty. [List tools](#library/tools) covers the sort and filter dimensions the query accepts. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_library_detail_body:
The browser fetches the article's encrypted body from the server, decrypts it with the organization key, and strips anything that could run as code before rendering the result. The title and metadata come from the list cache and are readable before the body arrives. [[#encryption #client-data]]
**How does the author name arrive?** The browser decrypts the author's display name from its own cache of organization-key names rather than receiving it with the article. When the browser does not hold the author's name, it fetches it from the server. An author that cannot be resolved produces a label identifying the author as unknown rather than a missing line. [Browsing articles](#library/browse) covers which fields on the row are plaintext and which are sealed. [[#encryption #failure-states]]
**How are images in the body fetched?** Each image reference in the document uses a custom URI scheme that maps to an attachment identifier. The browser downloads the ciphertext from the organization's blob storage and decrypts it as the article renders. An image that fails to decrypt is replaced with its alt text or a fallback message. All image data comes from the organization's own blob storage and no external source. [File attachments](#library/attachments) covers the blob route and the checks it runs. [[#server-holds #failure-states]]
**What does an open record?** Opening an article adds its identifier and a timestamp to the user's recently viewed list. [Opening global search](#search/overlay) covers how that list is stored, sealed, and cleared on a password change. [[#privacy]]
**What happens when the article cannot be read?** A body that fails to decrypt reports the failure in place of the article content. A deleted article returns a not-found error from the server, and the query surfaces that error instead of rendering an empty page. [[#failure-states]]
**The detail query and the render pipeline.** `ArticleDetailView.svelte` in `packages/client/src/lib/components/library/` calls `getItem` from `packages/server/src/routes/kb.ts`, which returns `encrypted_body`. The decrypted bytes are ProseMirror JSON serialized through `DOMSerializer`, then sanitized by DOMPurify with a strict tag and attribute allowlist in `renderArticleBody` in `packages/client/src/lib/utils/render-article.ts`. Legacy plain-text articles are wrapped in paragraphs and sanitized through the same allowlist. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_library_attachments_body:
Articles accept file attachments that the browser encrypts with the organization key before upload. Accepted types are images (JPEG, PNG, GIF, WebP), PDFs and Word documents, each up to ten megabytes. Uploading requires the Edit knowledge base permission; downloading requires the View knowledge base permission. [[#encryption #permissions]]
**What does the server hold for each file?** The file bytes and the filename are each sealed as organization-key ciphertext and stored separately. The declared content type, the byte count, the upload timestamp and a storage key remain in plaintext. A seized database reveals how many files an article carries, each file's approximate kind and size, but no filename and nothing from inside the file. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers the plaintext columns across the schema. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
**What can the server check?** The server validates the declared content type against its allowlist, the byte count against its ten-megabyte limit, and that the declared size matches the bytes received. It cannot inspect the file itself, because what arrives is ciphertext with no file signature. A file whose declared type passes the allowlist but does not match its actual content becomes an image the reader's browser cannot render. The server accepts at most five uploads per minute per account. [Article editor](#library/editor) covers the consequences when a first save exceeds that limit. [[#failure-states]]
**Downloads.** The server responds with raw bytes, sets `Cache-Control: private, no-store`, and decrypts nothing. The browser decrypts the file on the device; the plaintext never leaves that device. [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers where the download permission comes from. [[#encryption]]
**The upload route and the attachment service.** `uploadAttachment` in `packages/server/src/routes/kb.ts` writes through `BlobStore` under the `kb-attachment` category and records the row via `packages/server/src/kb/kb-media-service.ts`. When the row insert fails, the route deletes the blob it wrote. Downloads run through `createBlobDownloadHandler` in `packages/server/src/routes/blob-download.ts`. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_settings_password_body:
A password change rebuilds the encryption keys from the new password and re-wraps every sealed copy those keys protect. The browser derives both the old and new key sets, re-wraps each sealed copy for the new keys, and sends a single request carrying the results. The server stores none of the private keys and cannot open anything it receives. [[#keys #encryption]]
**What gets re-wrapped?** Every ticket key the user can read, and the user's copy of the organization key. Each ticket keeps its own key, and only the sealed copy for this user changes. A user holding a thousand tickets re-wraps a thousand small keys, not a thousand tickets of ciphertext. The browser processes ticket keys in batches of forty. [How keys are derived](#deep-dive/how-keys-are-derived) covers where both key sets come from. [[#keys #encryption]]
**What does the server receive?** A new salt, a new public key, and the re-wrapped sealed copies. The server confirms that the current password matches its stored hash and stores a hash of the new one, replaces the salt and public key, and writes the new sealed copies. It receives no private key and nothing it can unwrap. [Username and password](#login/credentials) covers what the server holds of a password. [[#server-holds #keys]]
**Other sessions.** The same transaction that stores the new hash deletes every other session on the account. A session opened on another device stops working at the moment of the change. The browser that performed the change re-derives its keys from the new password and continues without a second sign-in. [[#failure-states #privacy]]
**When is a change refused?** The server allows five requests per minute per account and IP address. A wrong current password, a new password equal to the current one, or a missing verified second factor when one is enrolled each reject the request before any state changes. The new hash, the cleared forced-change flag, the deleted other sessions and the re-wrapped keys all commit in one transaction. If the re-wrapped keys no longer cover the user's current key wraps, the transaction rolls back and the old password and keys keep working. [[#failure-states #keys]]
**The orchestrator and the rotation service.** The browser sequence is `changePassword` in `packages/client/src/lib/settings/password-change.ts`, which spawns a second short-lived crypto worker for the new keys and processes ticket keys in batches of forty. The server side is `profile.changePassword` in `packages/server/src/routes/profile.ts`, which calls `changePasswordWithRotation` in `packages/server/src/auth/password-change-service.ts` over `packages/server/src/crypto/key-rotation.ts`, whose `rotation_lock` column prevents new ticket key wraps from being sealed to a public key the account is about to discard. [[#keys #server-holds]]
demo_narrative_settings_twofa_body:
The user enrolls and removes second-factor methods from settings. An account can hold several active methods at once, and each one works independently. [Two factor authentication](#login/two-factor) covers what a sign-in does with them and how the methods compare in strength. [[#privacy #permissions]]
**How is each method proved at enrollment?** [Passkeys and security keys](#login/passkey) and [Authenticator app codes](#login/totp) are verified on the spot, from the device or from a code the app generates. [Email codes](#login/email) and [Text message codes](#login/sms) deliver a verification code and keep the method inactive until the user confirms it. [Push approval](#login/push) sends a test notification to confirm the device can receive it. [[#failure-states]]
**Resend cooldowns.** The server enforces sixty seconds between email codes and ninety seconds between text message codes. The browser counts down from the same values, so the wait the user sees and the wait the server applies cannot drift apart. [[#failure-states #telephony]]
**Who can remove a method?** Removal requires the user to have already verified a second factor in the current session. The server refuses to remove the last active method. [[#permissions #failure-states]]
**Backup code lifecycle.** [Backup codes](#login/backup-codes) are generated as a set of eight after the first method is enrolled. Generating a new set deletes the previous one, so codes recorded earlier stop working at that moment. [[#failure-states]]
**What does a database copy show?** The method names on each account and whether each is active are stored without encryption. The count of unused backup codes is also unencrypted. A copy of the database reveals which types of second factor each account uses and how many backup codes remain. Method secrets (TOTP keys, passkey credentials) are stored in encrypted columns, and backup codes are stored only as hashes. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers the rest of the unencrypted schema. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
**Does removing email as a second factor change where notifications go?** Email second-factor codes and notifications use the same address. Email enrollment says the address also receives notifications. Removing the email method clears that address unless the user chooses to keep it for notifications. Settings has a place to view, change and clear the notification address on its own. [Notification preferences](#settings/notifications) covers the notification address. [[#server-holds #privacy]]
**The enrollment service and cooldown constants.** Enrollment, verification, and removal live in the `enroll` and `methods` routers in `packages/server/src/routes/two-factor.ts`, backed by `packages/server/src/auth/two-factor-service.ts`. The cooldown constants are in `packages/shared/src/schemas/auth.ts`. [Notification preferences](#settings/notifications) covers the notification address. [[#server-holds]]
demo_narrative_settings_appearance_body:
The color scheme can be dark, light, or follow the device. The choice is stored in the browser's local storage on that device and never sent to the server. A browser with no stored preference starts dark. [[#client-data #privacy]]
**What does "follow the device" store?** The browser keeps the word "system" rather than the scheme it resolved to. When the device's own setting changes, the app re-resolves without a new choice from the user. [[#client-data]]
**Interface language.** The interface language is stored on the account, not in the browser, so it travels with the user across devices. A color scheme belongs to the single browser that chose it. [Language selection](#settings/language) covers what the server holds of that choice. [[#encryption #server-holds]]
**Platform styling.** The iOS or Material styling is detected from the browser's user agent on every load. No request goes to the server. No setting exists to change it. [On the device](#deep-dive/on-the-device) covers the full set of values each page leaves in browser storage. [[#client-data]]
**The theme store and scheme toggle.** `packages/client/src/lib/stores/theme.svelte.ts` holds the color scheme under `care-y-color-scheme` in local storage. `toggleSchemeWithPalette` in `packages/client/src/lib/branding/scheme-toggle.ts` flips the scheme and re-derives the palette from the organization's brand colors for the new scheme. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_settings_security_body:
The security briefing is part of onboarding and can be reopened from settings at any time. Reopening it does not write the seen flag. The flag is set only on the onboarding path, so the server cannot tell whether a user has revisited it. [[#privacy #server-holds]]
**What does the briefing cover?** The briefing explains how encryption works and includes a diagram of the key hierarchy. It names each category of data the system holds, the access rules that govern it, and what a seizure of that store would expose. It then walks through threat scenarios and answers each one with the specific data the adversary obtains and the data that remains encrypted or inaccessible. It closes with operational choices that carry lasting tradeoffs, such as telephony provider selection and two-factor authentication policy. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers each data category in more detail. [[#trust-boundary #server-holds]]
**What do the threat scenarios address?** The scenarios cover server seizure, compromise of one of the two key-derivation servers, a compromised device, an insider with administrative access, a compromised or subpoenaed telephony provider, and network surveillance. [Deployment](#deep-dive/deployment) covers where those servers run and who operates them. [[#trust-boundary #failure-states]]
**Lasting tradeoffs.** No mechanism exists to reset a forgotten password. Text messages travel outside the encrypted channel. An organization that has removed every user who held the organization key loses all data that key protected. [The organization key lifecycle](#deep-dive/organization-key-lifecycle) covers that last scenario. [[#keys #failure-states]]
**The briefing component and the seen flag.** The content is `SecurityBriefing.svelte` in `packages/client/src/lib/components/onboarding/`. Settings reopens it through `SecurityBriefingPopup.svelte` in `packages/client/src/lib/components/settings/`. The seen flag is `users.has_seen_briefing` from `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`, written by `profile.markBriefingSeen`. [[#server-holds]]
demo_narrative_settings_notifications_bo:
Each event type has a separate switch for push, email and text message, and the user controls which channels carry which events. The in-app feed delivers all events whether or not any switch is on, and a user who has turned off the three switchable channels still sees events when the app is open. An account with no stored preferences has all switches on. [[#privacy #client-data]]
**What does a queue or ticket override do?** A queue override applies to events in that queue and takes priority over the global switch. A per-ticket override takes priority over both. Setting a ticket override requires the user to hold that ticket's key, and the server refuses a ticket the user cannot read and a ticket that does not exist with the same response, so the refusal reveals nothing about whether the ticket exists. [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers where that access comes from. [[#permissions #metadata]]
**When does a preference not hold?** When the user enabled text messages for an event but has no verified number, the event is skipped for that channel rather than rerouted to email. [[#failure-states #telephony]]
**What does a notification email contain?** An email names the event type and links to the sign-in page. It carries no ticket title, no client alias and no message text. The mail provider learns the address and the time. [What the network sees](#deep-dive/what-the-network-sees) covers what other observers learn from notifications. [[#server-holds #privacy]]
**Where does the notification address come from?** The notification address is visible and manageable from the notification settings. The user can view, change or clear it at any time. [Two factor enrollment](#settings/two-factor) covers how the email second-factor method shares the notification address. [[#server-holds #privacy]]
**What does a database copy show about notification settings?** Each preference row stores the user's ID, the scope, the event type, the channel and whether it is on or off. A database copy shows which queues a user set overrides for and which events a user silenced, which maps what the user watches. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers the rest of the unencrypted schema. [[#metadata #server-holds]]
**The preference cascade and email column.** Cascade resolution and the reset path are in `packages/server/src/notifications/preferences.ts`, the table is `notification_preferences` in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`, and the fan-out that reads the allow lists is `packages/server/src/notifications/service.ts`. Preferences are resolved when a notification is queued, not when it is sent, so a retried delivery uses the original recipient set. Email is sent to `users.encrypted_notification_addr`. [[#server-holds]]
demo_narrative_settings_consultant_phone:
The user registers a personal phone number for receiving forwarded calls. A verification code sent to that number must be confirmed before the server will connect any call to it. [[#telephony #privacy]]
**How does the number reach the server?** The number passes through the server once, during verification. From that single pass the server stores a sealed copy encrypted to the organization's public key, a keyed hash for later comparison, and a copy encrypted under the server's own key only when the user opted into SMS notification pings. Any browser holding the organization key can open the sealed copy, but the API returns it only to the user who registered the number. The server-key copy exists so the server can send SMS pings without a browser present. [The telephony relay](#deep-dive/the-telephony-relay) covers how the server handles the number while it holds it. [[#trust-boundary #telephony]]
**Verification code and rate limits.** The code is six digits and expires after fifteen minutes. A third wrong attempt clears the code and requires a fresh send. A fresh send is refused within sixty seconds of the previous one and after five sends in an hour. Submitting a different number resets the verified state. An unproved number cannot inherit standing from a proved one. [[#failure-states]]
**What is each stored form for?** The keyed hash lets the server confirm that the number submitted with a call request matches the number that was verified, without the server holding the number in readable form. A compromised session that submits a different number fails the hash check and cannot redirect a client's call. Without pings, the server holds a number it cannot read and a hash it can only compare. [[#server-holds #telephony]]
**What changes when pings are switched off?** Switching pings off deletes the server-key copy along with the opt-in flag. Switching pings on afterward is refused because the server no longer has the number to re-encrypt, and the number must be verified again. Removing the registration deletes the sealed copy, the hash, the server-key copy, and the verified state together. [[#failure-states #server-holds]]
**What does the telephony provider learn?** Bridged calls and SMS pings both hand the number to the telephony provider, which sits outside the encryption boundary. The provider and the carrier learn which numbers spoke and when. [[#telephony #trust-boundary]]
**The verification handler and the columns.** The single phone write path is `/relay/consultant-verify` in `packages/server/src/routes/relay.ts`, calling `prepareVerification` in `packages/server/src/telephony/consultant-service.ts`. The handler reads the number as a `Buffer`, derives all three stored forms, sends the verification SMS, and zeroes every buffer that touched the number in a `finally` block. The columns `encrypted_phone`, `ops_phone_hash`, `ops_encrypted_phone`, and the rate-limit counters are on `consultants` in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`. The hash uses the `consultant-phone-index` HKDF label, separate from the client phone label. [[#server-holds #telephony]]
demo_narrative_admin_people_body:
The roster shows every account belonging to the organization, whether active or deactivated. Each account shows its role, key status and queue memberships. [[#permissions #privacy]]
**Who can do what on the roster?** Viewing the roster, deactivating an account and managing invitations all require the Manage users permission. Role assignment requires the Manage roles permission. An account cannot change its own role, and the server refuses to demote the last active administrator. Direct account creation requires the Manage users permission; picking a non-default role during that creation requires the Manage roles permission as well. Sending an invitation at a non-default role also requires the Manage roles permission. [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers where those grants come from. [[#permissions]]
**Invitation path.** The invite link contains a random token that expires after seventy-two hours. The invitation records the role the future account will hold, and the invited person picks their own password. Keys are derived on that person's device; the administrator never touches key material for the new account. [How keys are derived](#deep-dive/how-keys-are-derived) covers what a password produces. [[#keys #privacy]]
**Direct creation path.** The administrator provides a username and a temporary password at least sixteen characters long. The administrator's browser derives keys for that account and wraps the organization key on its behalf. The first sign-in forces a password change and re-derives the account's keys, so the administrator's knowledge of the temporary password gives no lasting access. [[#keys #privacy]]
**What does the server store for an invitation?** The token is kept as a SHA-256 hash. Role, inviting account, creation timestamp and expiry sit in plaintext columns. Revoking stamps the row with a revocation time instead of removing it, and accepting stamps it as consumed while keeping the row intact. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
**What does deactivation destroy?** The operation removes the account's ticket key wraps, its wrapped organization key and its stored key record in a single transaction. From that moment the user cannot decrypt anything. The server blocks the request when the account is the sole key holder for one or more cases and reports how many are affected. Overriding the guard makes those cases permanently unreadable. Reactivation brings the account back without restoring any deleted key material. [The organization key lifecycle](#deep-dive/organization-key-lifecycle) covers what deactivation and rotation do to the organization key itself. `revokeVolunteerKeys` in `packages/server/src/crypto/offboarding.ts` handles the deletion. [[#keys #failure-states]]
demo_narrative_admin_roster_tools_body:
Filtering, sorting and searching the roster all run in the browser after the full list has loaded, so none of them send search terms or filter selections to the server. [[#privacy #client-data]]
**What does each filter select?** The filters narrow by role, account status, key state and queue membership. A row must satisfy every active filter. The key state filter uses two flags from the roster query and reads as Ready, Hasn't signed in yet or Needs a key share. The queue filter matches against every queue assignment in the organization, not only the queues the reader belongs to; loading the assignments requires the Manage queue membership permission. [Encryption keys and escrow](#admin-org/keys) covers what the two flags mean. [[#permissions #keys]]
**What does search match?** The browser compares a normalized term against display names it has already decrypted, starting at two characters. The term stays on the device. An account whose display name fails to decrypt is excluded from search results and sorted last by name, so a key problem looks like a missing row rather than an error. [[#privacy #failure-states]]
**Bulk deactivation.** Bulk deactivation confirms the count and the consequence before proceeding. The bulk path sends no force flag, so an account that is the sole key holder for a case stays active. Each account in the selection is attempted, and the result reports which accounts were refused. Deactivating a single account opens a confirmation first and offers to force past the sole-key-holder refusal. [User roster](#admin-people/people) covers what deactivation does to an account's keys. [[#failure-states #keys]]
**The filter and sort utilities.** `filterUsers` and `sortUsers` in `packages/client/src/lib/admin/users-section-utils.ts` accept a decryption callback rather than pre-decrypted values, which keeps the comparison on the device while the roster query returns ciphertext. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_admin_roles_body:
Each role has a reference page that lists the capabilities a manager or a volunteer can expect, in fixed wording that the organization's permission changes do not rewrite. [[#permissions]]
**What does the manager page report?** The page lists every active queue and the open case count of each one, whether or not the user belongs to that queue. A separate section lists the user's own queue memberships without counts. Queue names arrive as organization-key ciphertext, and a name the browser cannot decrypt is replaced with a placeholder. Opening the manager page requires the Manage users permission. [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers how that gate is applied. [[#metadata #encryption #permissions]]
**What does the volunteer page report?** The page lists only the queues the user belongs to, with no case counts. A name that fails to decrypt is replaced the same way. Any signed-in user can open the volunteer page, and the page reports only that user's own data. [[#encryption #permissions #privacy]]
**Where can the text fall out of step with the grant?** The capability lines are fixed strings shipped with the application, while the permission set behind each role is editable through the matrix. An organization that has changed a role's grants still sees the original description. [Permission matrix](#admin-people/role-permissions) covers what an organization can change. [[#permissions]]
**The page components and the queries.** The manager page is `packages/client/src/routes/(app)/admin/manager/+page.svelte`, calling `listQueues` for all active queues and `myQueues` for the reader's own. The volunteer page is `packages/client/src/routes/(app)/admin/volunteer/+page.svelte`, calling `myQueues` only. Both endpoints sit in `packages/server/src/routes/tickets.ts`. [[#permissions]]
demo_narrative_admin_role_permissions_bo:
The matrix lists every permission against each of the three roles, grouped by the area of work each permission governs. An organization can move most permissions between roles to match the way it divides responsibility. [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers how each effective set is computed and cached. [[#permissions]]
**What does a cell change write?** Changing a cell writes one override row for that role and permission. Returning a cell to its shipped default deletes the row, so the table holds only the differences the organization chose. The server drops the cached permission sets on the same request, and the new set takes effect for every account holding that role from the next request onward. [[#permissions]]
**Locked permissions.** Manage keys, Manage roles and Manage infrastructure are fixed to the administrator role. The server rejects the write when a locked permission is toggled toward another role. When permissions are read, the server adds all three back to the administrator and strips them from every other role, so an override row placed on another role by a direct database insert produces no effect. [[#permissions #keys]]
**View intake responses and key distribution.** View intake responses controls who receives a decryption key wrap when an intake form is submitted. Revoking the permission stops new wraps from that point forward and does not revoke wraps already issued. [[#keys #permissions]]
**Queue membership as an access grant.** Manage queue membership controls who may add an account to a queue. Being a member of a queue grants read access to every ticket it holds. [Queue management](#admin-people/queues) covers what adding and removing a member does to ticket access. [[#permissions]]
**View own shifts.** View own shifts governs who can see their own shift schedule and coverage assignments. [Shift scheduling](#schedule/intro) covers the full scope of the scheduling surface. [[#permissions]]
**Resetting and access to the matrix.** A reset deletes every override row after a confirmation and restores all three roles to their shipped defaults in one step. Reading the matrix and editing it both require the Manage roles permission, so a user who manages the roster through Manage users alone cannot see what the roles are permitted to do. [[#permissions]]
**The override table and the permission enum.** Override rows live in `role_permission_overrides`, one sparse row per role and permission. The `Permission` enum in `packages/shared/src/roles.ts` is append-only after deployment because renaming a member orphans every row that names it. Lock enforcement and the merge function are in `packages/server/src/auth/roles.ts`. [[#permissions]]
demo_narrative_admin_queues_body:
Queues are governed by three independent permissions. The Manage queues permission controls creation, reordering and deletion. The Manage queue membership permission controls who belongs to each queue. The Manage queue notifications permission controls who receives alerts when a queue's tickets change. [[#permissions]]
**What does creating a queue encrypt?** The browser encrypts the queue's name, color and icon under the organization key before sending the request. The server stores only the ciphertext, appends a sort position after the current highest, and records the organization key generation in force at the time. [Queue overview](#dashboard/queues) covers the plaintext columns each queue keeps. [[#encryption]]
**Reordering and deletion.** Reordering renumbers every queue's position inside one transaction, in two passes, because no two queues may share a position. Deleting a queue is refused while it is the last one remaining. Deleting a queue that holds tickets is refused until another queue is named to receive them. Once a destination is named, the tickets move, and the membership and watcher rows for the deleted queue are removed with it. [[#metadata #failure-states]]
**Membership and access.** Adding an account to a queue grants it access to every ticket in that queue. Removing the account deletes its assignment row and revokes access on the next request. [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers how access is checked. [[#permissions #keys]]
**How does a new member receive keys?** Membership grants access but issues no keys. A browser that already holds ticket keys detects members in its queues who are missing wraps, mints one wrap per ticket against that member's public key, and submits them. The sweep runs after sign-in. Until a teammate's browser completes it, the new member can reach each ticket's plaintext fields but cannot decrypt its title or content. [[#keys #encryption]]
**Intake form routing.** A submitted intake form goes to the queue the form names. When the form names none, the ticket goes to the organization's fallback intake queue. Setting that fallback requires the Manage channel routing permission. The fallback queue identifier is stored as plaintext on the organization's configuration row. [Intake forms list](#admin-org/intake-forms) covers per-form destination settings. [[#metadata #permissions]]
demo_narrative_admin_clients_body:
The client list holds every client record the organization has created, paginated twenty-five at a time, with a ticket count beside each record. The alias is organization-key ciphertext that only a browser with that key can read. The phone number and the email address are encrypted with the server's operational key. The server holds that key, so the running server can read both values back at any time. That is what allows it to dial the number and send the mail. The encryption protects contact values in a database dump or backup taken without the key. It does not protect them from the server itself. [[#client-data #encryption]]
**What does the server return without View client PII?** The server decrypts each contact value, builds a masked form, and zeroes the buffer before the response leaves. A phone number becomes the last four digits behind three asterisks; an email address becomes its first character and domain. A user with the View client PII permission receives the full formatted value instead. The masked form is built server-side and the full value never reaches a browser that lacks the permission. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers why contact values sit on a different key from ticket content. [[#privacy #server-holds]]
**Who can change a client record?** Viewing the list requires the View clients permission. Renaming a record requires the Edit client alias permission. Changing a phone number or email address requires the Edit client contact permission, or the user must be assigned to a ticket belonging to that client. [Contact correction](#ticket-detail/correction-status) covers the flow that carries a correction from the client into the record. Deleting a client permanently removes the client row, its tickets, portal channels, and attached files, and writes an audit row carrying counts. Deletion requires the Delete clients permission. [Audit log](#admin-logs/audit) covers what an audit row holds. [[#permissions #client-data]]
**How does exact search work?** The browser hashes the search term with the organization key and sends the hash to the server, which matches it against a stored alias hash on each record. The server compares hashes without learning the term. Alias hashes are backfilled proactively so that every record is searchable. Anything shorter than an exact alias match filters the records already loaded in the browser. [[#privacy #metadata]]
**Merged records.** A client record merged into another drops out of the list. It keeps its own row and its own tickets. [Merging clients](#admin-people/client-merge) covers what a merge changes. [[#client-data]]
**The client route and its service.** `packages/server/src/routes/clients.ts` defines the tRPC router. `packages/server/src/clients/client-service.ts` holds listing, alias editing, phone replacement, and duplicate detection. Masking runs in `phoneForViewer` and `emailForViewer` in `packages/server/src/utils/sql.ts`. Deletion delegates to `purgeClient` in `packages/server/src/jobs/pii-retention.ts`, which cascades through tickets, merge events, portal channels, and orphaned phone and email rows inside a transaction. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_admin_client_merge_body:
Merging two client records sets one as the survivor and writes a pointer from the other into it. Neither record is rewritten. The merged-away record keeps its own cases and its own row, so the survivor's case count stays separate and both histories remain distinct. [[#client-data]]
**What does the merge close and revoke?** The merge closes the merged-away record's open case and writes a system note on it. A case whose ticket depends on an open ticket elsewhere blocks the merge rather than closing with unresolved work. When both records have an active portal channel, one channel is kept and the other is revoked. The revoked channel's content is kept until the merge is locked. When only the merged-away record has a channel, that channel is moved to the survivor. [[#client-data #portal]]
**What does undo restore?** The browser seals a snapshot of the merged-away record with the organization key before sending the merge request. Undo removes the pointer and flags the event as reversed. Before the merge is locked, undo reinstates a revoked channel and its content and points a moved channel back to its original record. Locking prevents undo. An unlock control lifts the lock, after which undo is offered again. [[#encryption #failure-states]]
**What does the server hold in plaintext?** The merge event row stores both clients' identifiers, the timestamp, whether the event is reversed, and whether undo is locked. The snapshot sits beside them as organization-key ciphertext. The audit log gains a row for the merge, for an undo, and for a lock change. The merge row carries both clients' identifiers and no names. The undo and lock-change rows carry the merge event's identifier and no names. [Audit log](#admin-logs/audit) covers what an audit row holds. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
**What does the Merge clients permission cover?** Merging, undoing, and locking all require the Merge clients permission, which is separate from View clients. The user can read the client list without being able to consolidate it. [Possible duplicates](#dashboard/merge-candidates) covers the scan that proposes pairs. [[#permissions]]
**The merge transaction and channel helpers.** `createMergeService` in `packages/server/src/tickets/merge-service.ts` runs the merge, the undo, and the lock toggle. Channel collisions are resolved by `reconcileChannels` in the same file, which delegates to `purgeAndRevokeChannel` in `packages/server/src/portal/channel-service.ts` for the destructive path and to `repointChannel` for the move path. The dependency check is `allResolved` in `packages/server/src/tickets/dependency-service.ts`. [[#client-data]]
demo_narrative_admin_general_body:
General information holds the organization's name, its country code, its default language and the address the client-facing quick exit navigates to, and all are stored without encryption. [[#server-holds]]
**What does each field control?** The name is visible before anyone signs in, which is why it stays in the clear. The country code fills in the international prefix when a phone number is entered without one during sign-in code enrollment. The default language sets the language the server uses when it composes text on its own, such as the footer on a reply-by-email message and the notice a client receives through the portal. The exit address is the destination a client-facing page navigates to when the quick exit fires. [Quick exit](#client-portal/quick-exit) covers what leaving does to the session. [[#portal #telephony]]
**Why is the exit address validated twice?** A stored address must be an absolute https URL with a real hostname. A looser check would allow schemes that execute script rather than load a page, and the exit URL is the navigation a person triggers when leaving fast. The same validation runs again at read time, so a value saved before the rule existed or written through a path that bypassed it resolves to the built-in default instead of being served as stored. [[#failure-states #portal]]
**What does a database dump reveal?** A dump shows the organization's name, its country code, its default language and its exit address. The name already appears on unauthenticated pages, so the country, the language and the exit address are what the dump adds. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers what else the server holds in the clear. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
**Who can edit general information?** Editing requires the Manage org identity permission, which belongs to the Admin role by default. An organization can move it to another role. [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers how grants move between roles. [[#permissions]]
**The name column and branding.** The organization name on this page and the display name under branding are the same column, `org_config.name`. A change here is the change branding shows. [Branding](#admin-org/branding) covers the rest of that row. [[#server-holds]]
**The config service and exit URL validation.** `getOrgGeneral` and `updateOrgGeneral` in `packages/server/src/org/org-config-service.ts` read and write the four columns behind permission-gated procedures in `packages/server/src/routes/org.ts`. The exit URL rule is `safeExitUrlSchema` in `packages/shared/src/schemas/org.ts`, and the read-back check is `readSafeExitUrl` in `packages/server/src/branding/branding-service.ts`. [[#server-holds]]
demo_narrative_admin_branding_body:
Branding holds the organization's logo, its two brand colors, the welcome text a visitor reads on the intake form, and the support label a client sees on portal messages. All fields are stored without encryption, because the pages that use them are reached before anyone signs in. [[#server-holds #portal]]
**Why is none of it encrypted?** The organization's subdomain arrives in the clear on every request, and the server resolves it by comparing a plaintext slug. A database dump already lists every organization on the server regardless of what these columns hold. The logo is served by an unauthenticated route to pages a visitor reaches without an account. A previous design encrypted these columns under a key whose public half sat in the same row, which protected neither of those two facts and placed decryption inside a web process that otherwise holds no key material. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers what else a dump reveals. [[#encryption #server-holds]]
**How is a logo sanitized?** The browser redraws every accepted upload (PNG, JPEG, or SVG) to a resized PNG, so no markup or script travels inside the image. The server validates the file type and enforces its own 2 MB ceiling before storing the result. App icons for the installed app and the home screen are generated in a separate step after the save, and a failure there raises its own notice while the saved logo stands. [[#failure-states]]
**How are colors kept readable?** The app stores a brand color as chosen and derives two working colors from it, a text color and a fill color. Each working color has its lightness adjusted until it clears the WCAG AA contrast ratio of 4.5:1 against the worst surface it can land on, separately for light mode and dark mode. A chosen shade that falls close to the red reserved for urgency or the ochre reserved for care draws a notice offering a shifted alternative, and saving the original is allowed. [[#failure-states]]
**Editing branding.** Editing branding requires the Manage org identity permission, the same grant that covers [General info](#admin-org/general). [[#permissions]]
**The branding columns and the icon route.** The plaintext columns are on `org_config` in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`, with no encrypted counterpart. `encrypted_terminology`, the org public key, and the icon blob keys are separate columns on the same row. Reads and writes go through `packages/server/src/branding/branding-service.ts`. Icons are served without authentication by `packages/server/src/routes/branding-icons.ts`, which uses the blob key as the ETag. The rasterizer in `packages/client/src/lib/branding/rasterize.ts` scales to a 512-pixel maximum before upload. The contrast derivation and proximity check are in `packages/client/src/lib/branding/konsta-palette.ts`, and the server-side validation (magic bytes and size cap) is in `validateMagicBytes` from `packages/server/src/telephony/attachment-validator.ts`. [[#server-holds]]
demo_narrative_admin_terminology_body:
The terminology editor lets an organization rename the words the interface uses for its people and work. Each group is configured separately for English and Spanish, and both language sets are saved together. The groups that carry a singular and a plural are:
- Team member role
- Senior team member role
- Person helped
- Work item
- Work group
The reference library group carries one word. The browser encrypts the groups under the organization key and stores them as a single ciphertext blob the server writes without reading, because what an organization calls the people it serves reveals what the organization does. [[#privacy #encryption]]
**Why does the handbook use "ticket", "queue" and "volunteer"?** The handbook uses the shipped defaults rather than any one organization's terminology, because it documents CARE-Y itself. When an organization sees its own words in the app, that text comes from this configuration. [[#admin-org]]
**Auto-pluralization and reset.** Typing a singular fills the plural automatically until the user edits the plural by hand. The editor detects a hand-edited plural by comparing it against the rule's output. Reset restores the defaults for the language being edited and leaves the other language unchanged. Saving applies the new words across the interface without a reload. [[#client-data]]
**What does the server hold?** The groups are one encrypted value the server cannot read. The support label that a visitor sees on the portal is stored in the clear on the same row, because a visitor reaches it before authenticating and cannot hold a key. [How encryption works](#deep-dive/how-encryption-works) covers the organization key. [[#encryption #server-holds]]
**Who can edit terminology?** Editing terminology requires the Manage org identity permission, the same grant that covers [General info](#admin-org/general) and [Branding](#admin-org/branding). [[#permissions]]
**The terminology column and the write path.** The ciphertext is `org_config.encrypted_terminology`, a `bytea` column defined in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts` and written through the `saveBrandingField` procedure with JSON encrypted in the browser first. The reading side is `packages/client/src/lib/terminology/`. A Svelte context that feeds every screen reads the terminology on save. [[#encryption #client-data]]
demo_narrative_admin_note_types_body:
Each organization defines the categories that internal notes can carry, and each type has a name, an icon, and an optional description. The product also lists system types for events it records on its own, such as a status change, a call, or an assignment change. [[#client-data]]
**Per-type settings.** Each configurable type carries a notification switch for administrators, one for managers, and one for all accounts with ticket access. A switch can mark a note of that type as required before closing the ticket. Each type also sets a minimum role for reading notes filed under it and a minimum role for writing one, and the server enforces both. A type restricted to managers or administrators cannot be read or written by a lower role even through a direct request. [Internal notes](#ticket-detail/notes) covers how the user writes one. [[#permissions]]
**Starting types.** Comment, Resolution, Safety Concern, and Request ship as configurable types, not protected ones, so an organization can rename, reconfigure, or retire any of them. Comment is the default type for a new note. Resolution is marked as required before closing. Safety Concern and Request escalate to administrators and managers in addition to accounts with ticket access. Comment and Resolution notify only accounts with ticket access. [[#client-data]]
**What does the server store about a type?** The name, icon, and description are sealed with the organization key. The server holds the resulting bytes and has no key to open them. The notification targets are encrypted with the server's operational key and decrypted when a notification fires, because routing the notification is the server's job. The server can identify that a given category escalates without knowing that category's name. The minimum-role thresholds, the required-on-close flag, and the active flag are plaintext columns. A database dump reveals how many categories an organization runs, how each one gates access, and which ones escalate, without any of their names. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers what else a dump yields. [[#server-holds #encryption #metadata]]
**Deactivation.** Deactivating a type preserves every note already filed under it, and those notes remain filterable by category. The type set as the organization's default cannot be deactivated, which keeps at least one category available for writing. [[#failure-states]]
**Who can configure note types?** Configuring note types requires the Manage note types permission, which sits with Admin by default. [[#permissions]]
**The service and its two encryption layers.** `packages/server/src/tickets/note-type-service.ts` seals names and icons with the organization public key and encrypts notification targets with the operational secrets key. `DEFAULT_NOTE_TYPES` in the same file defines the starting types. The table, with its description column and two role-threshold columns, is `note_types` in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`. The default-type pointer is `org_config.default_note_type_id` in the same file. [[#server-holds #client-data]]
demo_narrative_admin_intake_forms_body:
The intake forms list holds every form the organization has built. A single switch on this page turns web intake off for the whole organization. [[#portal]]
**Saving and publishing.** A form is created inactive and cannot receive submissions until the user activates it. Activation is a separate operation from saving, so editing a live form cannot take it off the public address by accident. Deactivating a form stops new submissions and leaves both the form and every answer already collected in place. [Field list](#admin-forms/builder) covers what a save writes. [[#failure-states #portal]]
**What answers the public address when no form is active?** When web intake is on and no custom form carries the default flag, a built-in two-field form (a name and a message) takes its place, answering in the language the visitor's browser requests. That built-in form has its own toggle, separate from the organization-wide switch. [The intake page](#client-intake/form) covers what the visitor is asked. [[#portal #client-data]]
**What does the server store in the clear?** A form's internal name, its slug, its active and default flags, and its destination queue are plaintext columns. Everything written into a form is public to anyone who opens the form's public page, and the builder warns the author of that. A database dump reveals the number of forms, their internal names, their public addresses, and the wording of their fields. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers the rest of that picture. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
**How are answers protected?** Answers carry a per-case key wrapped to individual accounts. A user who builds and publishes a form gains nothing toward reading the submissions it collects. [Response cards](#admin-responses/responses) covers reading the answers. [[#encryption #keys]]
**Duplicating and deleting.** Duplicating a form mints fresh field and option keys, appends a suffix to the name and clears the slug. The copy shares no key material with the original and cannot collide on a public address. Deleting a form is refused once any response exists, so removing the form cannot remove the answers it collected. [[#failure-states #encryption]]
**Who can manage forms and who can read answers?** Managing forms requires the Manage intake forms permission. Reading answers requires the View intake responses permission. Neither carries the other, so a user who publishes a form cannot read its submissions unless the organization also grants View intake responses. [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers moving either permission. [[#permissions]]
**The service and the audit trail.** `packages/server/src/portal/intake-form-service.ts` holds the whole-form save, the slug uniqueness check, the atomic default swap and the single writer of the active flag. `packages/server/src/routes/intake-forms.ts` gates every procedure on one of the two permissions. Saving, deleting, activating, deactivating, and both the web-intake and built-in-default toggles write audit entries. [[#server-holds #failure-states]]
demo_narrative_admin_keys_body:
Each account in an organization holds its own wrapped copy of one organization key. This page reports whether the user's account has that copy and offers escrow export and key rotation. [The organization key lifecycle](#deep-dive/organization-key-lifecycle) covers how the key is created, distributed and restored from escrow. [[#keys]]
**What happens without a wrapped copy?** A user whose account has enrolled keys but holds no wrapped copy of the organization key cannot decrypt queue names, note type names, custom terminology, or display names on the roster. Case content wrapped to that account individually remains readable. A wrapped copy arrives automatically. Any signed-in user holding the Manage keys permission polls every five minutes for enrolled accounts that lack one and wraps the key for each. A duplicate wrap from a second session is discarded silently. Until a session with that permission runs, the account stays in that state. [Roster tools](#admin-people/roster-tools) covers the filter that finds those accounts. [[#keys #failure-states]]
**Escrow export.** Export produces a single JSON file containing its format identifier, key derivation parameters, salt, nonce, and ciphertext, so the file can be parsed on an air-gapped machine without CARE-Y code. The passphrase must be at least 20 characters, and a strength estimate sized for offline attack rejects a weak one. The derivation is Argon2id at 256 MB and four passes, tuned for a workstation rather than a sign-in. The file's SHA-256 fingerprint is split into four-character groups so two copies can be compared visually. Both the passphrase bytes and the organization secret key are zeroed after the export finishes or fails. Possessing the file is equivalent to possessing the organization's data. Escrow restores key material, not database rows. Anything [the retention policy](#admin-org/retention) deleted is absent from an escrow recovery. [[#keys #encryption]]
**How does rotation work?** The browser generates a new Curve25519 keypair, seals the outgoing secret key under the incoming one as a generation record, wraps the new secret for each active account that holds a public key, and submits all wraps in a single request. The sealed chain keeps pre-rotation data readable. Each ciphertext row carries the generation it was sealed under, and decryption walks the chain backward to reach it. Inactive accounts and accounts that have never signed in receive no wrap. The people-identifying rows reseal to the new key immediately:
- Client records
- Account rows
- Sessions
- The blocklist
- Consultants
- The two tables of wrapped case keys
The remaining organization configuration converges afterward through a sweep that any later sign-in holding the Manage keys permission resumes where it left off. The browser then fetches and unwraps its own copy through the standard sign-in path instead of trusting the key it just generated. [How keys are derived](#deep-dive/how-keys-are-derived) covers where the organization key sits in the key hierarchy. [[#keys #encryption #failure-states]]
**Who can export and rotate?** Escrow export and key rotation both require the Manage keys permission, one of three grants locked to the administrator role regardless of role configuration. A database row granting it to another role produces no effect. [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers the other two locked grants. [[#permissions]]
**The generation table and the reseal service.** `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts` creates `org_key_generations`, one row per generation carrying the public key and the previous secret sealed under it. Every table holding organization-sealed ciphertext gains an `org_key_generation` stamp. Re-encryption runs through `packages/server/src/crypto/org-reseal-service.ts`, which cannot verify the plaintext it receives because the server holds no organization key. Its guarantee is structural. A row accepts an update only while its stamp is below the current generation, the stamp advances in the same update, and the browser declares any rows it could not decrypt rather than passing over them. [[#keys #server-holds]]
demo_narrative_admin_retention_body:
A new organization starts with automatic deletion off. The user turns it on by choosing a window between 1 and 3,650 days; 365 is filled in as a starting point. Closed cases, their messages, files, and caller personal information older than the window are hard-deleted permanently. Enabling the policy and changing the window both require confirmation, and the confirmation states that deleted data cannot be recovered, because the escrow file holds key material and not data rows. Disabling the policy also requires confirmation and returns the organization to keeping records until someone deletes them by hand. [[#retention]]
**Why one window?** The window is a single organization-wide setting, not a choice per queue or per case type. A per-queue window would be a decision someone has to get right on the day they create a queue. [[#retention #metadata]]
**What falls outside the window?** Independent schedules delete data on their own terms and are unaffected by this setting.
- Portal message copies on the client side
- One-time share links
- Logs held at the telephony provider
[Data retention](#deep-dive/data-retention) covers each of those lifetimes. Nothing outside the organization's own database is in scope, so a copy a client kept on a personal device, a message in someone else's mailbox, or a record a third party holds all survive the window. Deletion is permanent; no escrow ceremony and no backup restores a row the policy removed. [[#retention #failure-states]]
**What does the setting itself disclose?** The window is stored as a plaintext integer column alongside the encrypted columns in the organization configuration row. A database dump shows the organization's retention choice in the clear. After a sweep, the row counts and foreign key relationships that remain are still readable structurally, so the dump reveals the shape of the deleted work. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers what that shape gives away. [[#server-holds #metadata #retention]]
**Who can change the retention window?** Changing the window requires the Manage retention permission, which belongs to Admin by default and can be moved to another role. [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers how a permission moves and which three can never move. [[#permissions]]
**The retention column and its write path.** `RetentionSection.svelte` renders on the organization admin page and again inside the first-run setup flow with its save button supplied externally. The value is written through `setPiiRetentionDays` in `packages/server/src/auth/service.ts` behind a permission-gated procedure in `packages/server/src/routes/auth.ts`, and read back through `auth.hubRetention`. The column is `org_config.pii_retention_days` in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`. [[#retention #server-holds]]
demo_narrative_admin_telephony_provider_:
The provider connection gives an organization a path to the phone network under one of two arrangements. Self-managed telephony means the organization owns a provider account and gives CARE-Y the credentials for it. Managed telephony means the platform operator provisions numbers on the organization's behalf. [Deployment](#deep-dive/deployment) covers which deployment types offer each arrangement. Saving or changing either arrangement requires the Manage infrastructure permission. [[#telephony #permissions]]
**Why can the server read these credentials?** Provider credentials are encrypted under the server's operational key, not the organization's end-to-end key. The server holds that key, so the running server can read the credentials at any time. That is what allows it to place calls and send texts through the provider. The encryption protects the credentials in a database dump or backup taken without the key. It does not protect them from the server itself. [The telephony relay](#deep-dive/the-telephony-relay) covers what the provider learns during a call. [[#keys #trust-boundary]]
**What does the credential row hold?** One row per organization on the platform database. The provider name, the key version and the two timestamps are plaintext. The sealed configuration holds the account identifier, the authentication token and the provisioned phone numbers. A dump taken without the operational key gives the provider name and when the credentials last changed. [Encryption keys and escrow](#admin-org/keys) covers the key the rest of the product uses. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
**What does a save validate?** A save checks the credentials against the provider's expected format and makes an authenticated read-only request to the provider before storing them. Wrong credentials are refused at save time. A test action is available for later checks, and a provider failure surfaces in the admin hub. After saving, the read-back masks the account identifier and replaces the token with a fixed run of dots. The stored token is not sent back. [[#failure-states #encryption]]
**What does switching to managed do?** Switching to managed telephony deletes the credential row rather than leaving it unused. Any cached provider instance built from those credentials is invalidated on the same request. A call already in progress with the provider is unaffected, because the provider accepted the session before the row was deleted. [[#failure-states]]
**The config service and the provider factory.** `packages/server/src/telephony/config-service.ts` holds the encrypt, decrypt and upsert path. `packages/server/src/telephony/factory.ts` builds one provider instance per organization from the decrypted credentials and caches it. A save or a mode change invalidates the cached entry. A provider the server has no implementation for is refused at the factory before any call reaches the provider. [[#failure-states]]
demo_narrative_admin_phone_lines_body:
Phone lines are the numbers an organization's provider account holds. Each number carries a provider-assigned ID that the server uses to tell them apart. One line can be designated for outbound calls and texts to clients, and another for automated system messages. An organization with only one number needs no assignment, because both purposes fall through to that number automatically. [[#telephony]]
**How does the server pick a line?** A system message tries the system line first, then the outbound line, then the first provisioned number. An outbound call or text tries the outbound line first, then the first provisioned number. When no number is provisioned at all, the server refuses the request rather than placing a call on an unintended number. The client sees the organization's line as the caller ID, not the user's own number. The server resolves the client's number from the ticket itself. [The telephony relay](#deep-dive/the-telephony-relay) covers what happens once a call is placed. [[#privacy #failure-states]]
**What does the assignment store?** Two provider IDs in plaintext columns on the organization's config row. [Provider connection](#admin-comms/provider) covers that sealed configuration. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
**The purpose resolver and the exclusion rule.** `createPhoneResolver` in `packages/server/src/telephony/phone-resolver.ts` owns the fallback chain. The purpose SIDs are `phone_outbound_sid` and `phone_system_sid` on the tenant `org_config` row in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`. `lookupProvisionedPhones` in `config-service.ts` excludes any number that carries no provider ID rather than falling through to the first provisioned number while a deliberate assignment is on file. [Greetings](#admin-comms/greetings) covers those recordings. [[#failure-states]]
demo_narrative_admin_sms_templates_body:
An SMS template is the text of an automatic reply, written once per language an organization serves. An organization can write an auto-reply template and an error response template. [[#telephony]]
**Language fallback.** The server selects the template in the language stored for the sender's number, then the organization's default language. The reply leaves on the organization's own line, so a response from the sender reaches the same number. [[#failure-states]]
**Character limit.** Template text is capped at 1600 characters. The server rejects a save that exceeds the cap rather than truncating it. Providers split messages longer than 160 characters into multiple segments, and each segment is billed separately. [[#failure-states]]
**What does a database dump reveal?** The wording, the language and the template type are plaintext columns, with no client and no ticket attached. A dump gives the languages an organization serves and the exact text it sends to a stranger. The inbound message that triggered the reply is encrypted and stored as a follow-up under a per-ticket key. [[#server-holds #privacy]]
**The fallback function and the response table.** `selectAutoReply` in `packages/server/src/telephony/sms-auto-reply.ts` runs the language chain. `packages/server/src/telephony/inbound-sms.ts` sends the result after the inbound message has been encrypted and stored. The table is `sms_responses` in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`, unique on language and type. Editing a template requires the Write automatic replies permission. [[#permissions]]
demo_narrative_admin_blocklist_body:
