[How encryption works](#deep-dive/how-encryption-works) covers the organization key. [[#keys #permissions]]
**Who receives a copy of the ticket key?** Queue members and users holding the View intake responses permission receive a copy, provided they have set up their keys. A user who joins the queue or receives the permission afterward can still gain a copy. When another user who already holds the key opens the response viewer, that user's browser seals the missing copies. [Unreadable response](#admin-responses/key-not-held) covers what happens when no copy exists yet. [[#keys #permissions]]
**What does a database dump reveal?** The stored row holds ciphertext for the visitor's answers, a sealed alias that identifies the new client record without naming anyone, the destination queue, the priority and the write timestamps. A dump confirms that a submission arrived, which queue received it and at what priority. It cannot recover what was written. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers the other plaintext columns across the schema. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
**The sealing and conversion modules.** `encryptIntake` in `packages/client/src/routes/(client)/intake/intake-crypto.ts` seals the per-submission key to the organization's public key. The server writes that sealed copy to `intake_key_wraps`, defined in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`. `packages/server/src/portal/intake-conversion-service.ts` replaces the sealed copy with per-user wraps in a single transaction and removes the interim row. The backfill path for users added later is `backfillWraps` in `packages/server/src/portal/intake-response-service.ts`. [[#keys #server-holds]]
demo_narrative_client_intake_contact_bod:
The default form accepts a phone number, an email address, or a refusal as the visitor's contact preference. The answer is encrypted alongside the submission. A new client record carries only a generated alias, with nothing the server could use to match this person against other records. The submission stays unmatched until a user opens the case and writes a contact value onto it. [Possible duplicates](#dashboard/merge-candidates) covers the hashes that comparison needs. [[#client-data #privacy]]
**What does the account option open?** The visitor can set a username and password while filling out the form. The browser derives all keys before sending anything to the server. No password reset exists. A client who forgets the password loses their own copy of the conversation and the channel it traveled through. The organization's ticket stays, and a user holding the Reset client login permission can delete the old account so a new channel can be set up. When the visitor also refused to leave contact details, the organization has no way to reach them, so a forgotten password ends the exchange entirely. [Account sign in](#client-account/sign-in) covers what the client opens afterward. [[#keys #failure-states]]
**What does the link option open?** The alternative is a link that reopens the same conversation without an account. The key travels in the URL fragment after the `#`, a portion that browsers do not transmit. Holding the link is the entire access check. Losing the link has the same cost as forgetting a password. The organization can set up a new link if it has another way to reach the client. [The portal channel lifecycle](#deep-dive/portal-channel-lifecycle) covers what the channel is. [[#keys #portal]]
**Why only one of the two?** Expanding one option collapses the other. When a submission carries both, the account takes precedence. Each option creates a separate channel for the same conversation, and two channels would mean two sets of keys that can read it. [[#permissions #portal]]
**The contact assembly and the two channel paths.** `handleSubmit` in `IntakeFormBody.svelte` collects the contact answers. Labels resolve to the organization's base locale so that queue-facing text is uniform regardless of form language. `buildAccountPayload` and `buildContinuationPayload` in `intake-crypto.ts` prepare the two branches. On the server, `handleAccountStep` and `handleContinuationStep` in `packages/server/src/portal/intake-service.ts` write them inside the submission transaction. [[#portal #server-holds]]
demo_narrative_client_intake_fields_body:
Each organization can replace the built-in form with one carrying its own fields. The data field types are text, text area, dropdown, checkboxes, checkbox, date, and availability. Page break and text block shape the form without collecting an answer. Everything written into a form is public to anyone who opens the form's public page. The answers a visitor types are encrypted under a per-case key the server cannot derive. [[#portal #client-data]]
**Conditional fields.** A field can depend on an earlier answer. When its condition is not met, the field stays hidden and its value is excluded from the encrypted answers. The browser submits answers only for fields the visitor was shown. [[#client-data #privacy]]
**What does a field role store readably?** Most fields have no role and produce no server-readable metadata. A field assigned a routing, urgency, or escalation role changes that. For those fields, the browser looks up the visitor's selection in a mapping and sends the result (a queue ID, a priority level, or an alert level) without encryption. When each option maps to a different value, the stored result identifies which option the visitor picked. The answer text stays encrypted, but the mapping can narrow it to one possibility. [Field settings](#admin-forms/field-config) covers how a role is configured. [[#metadata #server-holds]]
**What does each field tell the visitor?** A field whose role produces server-readable metadata carries a notice stating that. A field whose role produces nothing readable carries a notice stating the answer is encrypted. A field with no role carries no notice. [[#privacy #metadata]]
**The field table and the key path.** Field definitions live in `intake_form_fields` (defined in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`), where `role` is a plaintext tag and `routing_queue_ids` is a plaintext allow-list. Answers are encrypted by `encryptIntake` in `packages/client/src/routes/(client)/intake/intake-crypto.ts`. The helpers for form field definitions and form metadata are in `packages/crypto/src/intake-form.ts`. Visibility evaluation and page slicing are in `packages/client/src/routes/(client)/intake/intake-form-logic.ts`. [[#server-holds #encryption]]
demo_narrative_client_intake_submit_body:
The browser encrypts every answer, composes the ticket title and body from them, and sends only ciphertext to the server. The server creates the ticket, assigns it to a queue, and notifies that queue's members. A failed submission creates nothing and notifies nobody. [[#encryption #server-holds]]
**Multi-page validation.** A form split into pages validates the current page before advancing and lists each problem with the question it belongs to. The visitor can advance past problems on any page except the last. On the last page, validation runs across all pages, lists each problem with its page number, and blocks submission until all are resolved. Pages whose fields depend on an earlier answer that was not given are skipped, and the progress count reflects only the pages that apply. [[#failure-states #client-data]]
**Rate limit.** The server limits submissions per network address per hour. The limit is configured per deployment. A refused visitor sees a message stating how long to wait and can retry without losing what was typed. An organization can also enable a proof-of-work puzzle that the browser solves before each submission. The puzzle is off unless a difficulty is configured. Shared-network visitors are not refused when a single device on the same address has already submitted. [[#failure-states #portal]]
**Where does a submission go?** The ticket goes to the queue named by a routing-role answer when the form has one, then falls back to the form's destination queue, then to the organization's intake queue. Intake cannot be enabled without a queue configured at one of those levels. A missing queue triggers a warning on the administration side. [Queue management](#admin-people/queues) covers queue membership and its effect on access. [[#permissions #metadata]]
**What does the visitor receive?** A successful submission returns a reference code. The code is the generated alias for the new client record, sealed as ciphertext. The form's own confirmation message appears when one is configured. [[#client-data #privacy]]
**The encryption and submission path.** `handleSubmit` in `packages/client/src/routes/(client)/intake/IntakeFormBody.svelte` calls `encryptIntake` and `resolveSubmitMetadata` in `intake-crypto.ts`. The server route is `submitIntake` in `packages/server/src/routes/client-portal.ts`, which checks the rate limit and the puzzle gate before reading any payload. The ticket insert, key wrap, form response, and notification intent run in one transaction in `createIntakeTicket` in `packages/server/src/portal/intake-service.ts`, so a rollback discards all four. [[#server-holds #failure-states]]
demo_narrative_client_intake_closed_body:
A form whose closing date has passed replaces its fields with the organization's closing message. When no closing message has been written, a built-in notice takes its place. The banner image remains, so a visitor arriving from a shared link reaches a recognizable page. [Form settings](#admin-forms/form-settings) covers where the date and the message are set. [[#portal #failure-states]]
**What does a late submission get?** The server compares the closing date against its own clock at submission time. A page left open past the closing date is refused on submit. The visitor's typed answers stay in the browser and are not lost. [[#failure-states #metadata]]
**The date column and its two checks.** `intake_forms.closes_at` stores the closing date, defined in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`. `resolvePublicForm` in `packages/server/src/portal/intake-form-service.ts` reports it as a flag the page reads. `createIntakeTicket` in `packages/server/src/portal/intake-service.ts` re-checks it and raises `IntakeFormClosedError`, which the route maps to the same shape as a disabled or missing form. [[#server-holds #failure-states]]
demo_narrative_client_privacy_notice_bod:
The privacy notice is a fixed page linked from the drawer on every client page. It states who collects a submission, what data is gathered, who can read it, how long it is kept, what rights the visitor holds, and what cookies the site uses. The organization's name and its own retention setting change between deployments. [[#privacy #client-data]]
**What does the notice promise about reading a submission?** The notice says that volunteers open submissions on their own devices, that the organization key gives access until someone first takes the case, and that afterward only the people working on it can read it. Before that first open, any member holding the organization key can unseal the submission, and the server restricts it to members of the destination queue. The intake form states the same claim. [How the visitor is protected](#client-intake/how-protected) covers the encryption behind that claim. [[#keys #privacy]]
**What does the notice say about retention?** Encrypted data is described as kept while the case is open plus any retention period the organization chooses. Automatic deletion is off until an administrator enables it, so closed cases are kept indefinitely by default. The notice states that default. [Data retention](#deep-dive/data-retention) covers the deletion order, and [Retention policy](#admin-org/retention) covers where the window is configured. [[#retention #server-holds]]
**What rights does the notice offer?** The notice lists the rights the organization can fulfil. The visitor is told to quote the reference code returned after submission. The organization stores a generated alias, not a searchable name, and without the code it has no way to locate the record. [Submission](#client-intake/submit) covers where the code originates. [[#client-data #metadata]]
**What does the notice say about cookies?** Only session and security cookies required for the form are set, and the notice confirms none of them track the visitor. Outside the form itself, the language picker stores a preference cookie and the color-scheme toggle persists its choice in local storage. [The intake page](#client-intake/form) covers what traces a visit leaves on the device. [[#privacy #client-data]]
**The page component and its substitutions.** The page is `packages/client/src/routes/(client)/intake/privacy/+page.svelte`, rendering the `intake_privacy_*` messages and embedding `intake_retention_disclosure` within the retention section. The server substitutes the organization's name into the page for each organization when it serves it, or the page reads it from the public branding response. Branding is stored as plaintext because it is not a secret. No key material is present on the page. A language switch re-renders the entire notice in the new language without reloading. [[#server-holds #privacy]]
demo_narrative_client_portal_thread_body:
The portal thread merges the client's messages, the organization's replies, voicemails, call log entries, files and contact corrections into one sequence ordered by date. The client can filter by type, by author and by date range. [[#portal #client-data]]
**How are messages encrypted?** Each message is encrypted to the channel's public key, and the matching private key is derived in a dedicated worker from the credential the link carries. Files carry a random key of their own sealed to the same channel key, and voicemail recordings open by the same path. The server stores call entries as plaintext metadata, so a database dump reveals that a call happened, when and how long it lasted. [The portal channel lifecycle](#deep-dive/portal-channel-lifecycle) covers the channel key. [[#encryption #keys #server-holds]]
**How does the credential stay private?** The credential sits in the part of the URL after the `#`, which browsers never send to a server. The page reads it once and removes it from the address bar, so it is absent from the browser's history and from any address the client copies. [Quick exit](#client-portal/quick-exit) covers what the page discards on exit. [[#privacy #keys]]
**What stays on the device?** Filters and in-thread search operate on text already decrypted in the tab. No search term or filter choice leaves the device. The thread loads fifty messages at a time and fetches the older page when the client reaches the oldest one loaded. [[#privacy #client-data]]
**How long do the client's copies last?** Every read stamps the channel as seen. The client's copies of messages, files and recordings expire after a period. The organization's record of the ticket is stored separately under the ticket key and follows its own schedule. [Data retention](#deep-dive/data-retention) covers that schedule. [[#retention #portal]]
**What happens when a read is refused?** The server rate-limits portal reads to sixty per address per hour by default. A refusal carries the number of seconds to wait, and the page retries automatically after that interval. The automatic retry matters because a client who mistakes a transient refusal for a dead link may discard a link that still works. [[#failure-states]]
**The thread component and the paging path.** `PortalThread.svelte` in `packages/client/src/lib/portal/` renders messages, date separators, images, voicemails, call entries and corrections using components from `packages/client/src/lib/components/tickets/`, shared with the organization's own conversation thread. Pages come from `portalMessagePage` in `packages/server/src/routes/client-portal.ts`, and the seen stamp and the expiry sweep are in `packages/server/src/portal/portal-message-service.ts`. [Conversation thread](#ticket-detail/conversation) covers the organization's end. [[#portal #client-data]]
demo_narrative_client_portal_passphrase_:
When a secure link carries a passphrase, the client enters it before any message is decrypted. A passphrase set up with the secure link is generated from a word list in the setting-up user's browser during that step and read to the client on the call. A client who received a link without a passphrase can add one from the portal. No copy is written to the server, to the ticket thread, or to any audit record. [[#portal #keys]]
**Why can a guess not be checked locally?** Each guess is a request to the server, not a computation the device can run on its own. The server rate-limits these requests and can refuse them. A proof-of-work puzzle may be required before a request is answered. The combined cost is deliberate. Revoking the channel stops all further guesses from being answered. [[#keys #encryption]]
**What does the server see during entry?** The server sees each attempt against a named channel, the timing of each attempt, and the network address it came from. It does not learn whether any attempt was correct. The browser checks the result locally against a small ciphertext sealed to the correct public key, and reports nothing back. [[#server-holds #privacy]]
**Normalization.** Capitalization, spacing, and accented characters typed different ways are all normalized before derivation. A passphrase spoken on a call and retyped with different casing or extra spaces still derives the same key. Only the words themselves and their order need to match. [[#failure-states #keys]]
**The derivation path and its components.** The browser stretches the normalized passphrase with Argon2id, concatenates the result with the seed from the link, and sends a blinded value for evaluation under a tag naming that organization and channel. Only the evaluated answer derives the channel keypair. The gate is `PortalPassphraseGate.svelte` in `packages/client/src/lib/portal/`. The concatenation and blinding input are built by `portalOprfInput` in `packages/crypto/src/portal.ts`, which calls a private `stretchPassphrase` function internally. The key-check ciphertext is returned in the bootstrap response from `packages/server/src/portal/portal-message-service.ts`. [How keys are derived](#deep-dive/how-keys-are-derived) covers the evaluation and the two holders that answer it. The passphrase words are drawn on the organization side, in the setup step of `SecureLinkSheet.svelte`. A client-added passphrase is set from `AddPassphraseForm.svelte` in `packages/client/src/lib/portal/`. [Secure link setup](#ticket-detail/secure-link) covers how a user creates the link and the passphrase. [[#keys #portal]]
demo_narrative_client_portal_composer_bo:
The client encrypts each reply in the browser before sending it. The server receives and stores ciphertext it cannot open. [[#portal #encryption]]
**Who can read a reply?** The browser makes a temporary key for the message and encrypts the text under it. It seals one copy of that key to the channel key, letting the client reread the message later, and seals a second copy to the organization's public key. Before the first member of the organization opens the reply, any member whose account holds the organization key can decrypt it. The server delivers the reply only to a user who is assigned to the ticket, watching it, or a member of its queue. The first user to open the reply re-encrypts the content under the ticket's key, and the server deletes the organization-key copy in that same write. After that point, only a user whose account holds a copy of the ticket's key can read it. [How encryption works](#deep-dive/how-encryption-works) covers the key hierarchy. [[#encryption #keys #server-holds]]
**What happens when the client sends a reply?** Sending a reply on a closed ticket reopens it. A stored reply always produces a notification to the organization. On failure the composer restores the text and reports the error for the client to retry. The composer does not indicate whether a stored reply has been read. [[#failure-states #portal]]
**Rate limits.** A conversation accepts thirty replies per hour. A reply from the organization resets that window, so an active two-sided exchange runs without interruption. A second, broader cap tallies writes per address per hour but exempts any channel where the organization has responded within the last hour. That cap bounds flooding without the server tracking which address corresponds to which conversation. A refusal states how long to wait. [[#failure-states #privacy]]
**When are replies turned off?** An organization that disables the secure link channel at the policy level keeps existing links readable but refuses new replies. The composer reports the channel is off rather than letting a send fail silently. [Channel policy](#admin-comms/channel-policy) covers the setting. [[#permissions #portal]]
**Unsent text.** A draft is held in tab memory, keyed to the channel. It persists across navigation within the session and disappears when the tab closes. Nothing unsent reaches the device's storage. [[#privacy #client-data]]
**The compose path and the wrap tables.** `PortalComposer.svelte` and the in-memory draft store `packages/client/src/lib/tickets/draft-store.svelte.ts` handle the browser side. Encryption runs in the portal worker under `packages/client/src/lib/workers/`. On the server, `clientReply` in `packages/server/src/portal/portal-message-service.ts` persists the follow-up row, the sealed organization-key wrap and the client's self-copy in a single transaction, and enqueues the notification in that same transaction so the two commit together. `packages/server/src/tickets/rewrap-service.ts` deletes the organization-key wrap after convergence. [[#portal #encryption]]
demo_narrative_client_quick_exit_body:
Every client-facing page has a quick exit control, from the intake form and the portal through the account page, the privacy notice, and a share link. The control is unlabeled, because the word "exit" visible on a shared device is itself a signal. Pressing the control or pressing Escape blanks the tab title, zeroes the key material the page holds, and sends the browser to an ordinary site the organization has chosen in its settings. When no safe URL is configured, a weather service is used. The replacement overwrites the current history entry, so the back button does not lead back to the page. On the account page the control also revokes the server-side session before navigating. Escape leaves the page even when a sheet or panel is open. [[#privacy #portal]]
**What does the control not clear?** Earlier browser history entries survive. Cache, stored form data, and the language cookie remain on the device. [On the device](#deep-dive/on-the-device) covers the full inventory of what each page leaves behind. A screenshot, a printout, or a saved copy of a message stays wherever the client put it. Monitoring software on the device records whatever the person sees well before the control fires. A client whose device is controlled by someone else is better served by a channel the organization can close from its side, which [The portal channel lifecycle](#deep-dive/portal-channel-lifecycle) covers, and by retention limits, which [Data retention](#deep-dive/data-retention) covers. [[#privacy #failure-states]]
**What does the server learn?** On the intake form, the portal, and a share link, no request reaches the server. An activation leaves no record on the organization's side. On the account page one request tells the server that a session ended and nothing about why. [[#server-holds #metadata #privacy]]
**What happens when the page closes without the control?** Closing the tab or navigating away zeroes the same key material but does not revoke the server session; that session lapses within twenty minutes of the last renewal. The account page also runs a 15-minute idle timer that counts human input alone. At the 10-minute mark it announces a warning to assistive technology. When the timer fires it revokes the session and returns the page to the sign-in form. Background refreshes and network requests do not extend it. [[#keys #failure-states]]
**The component and the safe URL.** `QuickExit.svelte` is mounted once by `ClientShell.svelte` in the navbar, so it stays present through every state a client page passes through. Each page supplies its own key-zeroing callback through the client shell context. The control delegates to that callback and zeroes no keys itself. The Escape keydown listener runs on the capture phase and cancels the event, so it fires ahead of the overlay stack that would otherwise close an open sheet. A `pagehide` listener zeroes the same key material as a fallback when the tab closes or the browser navigates away. On the account page the session revocation is sent as a `sendBeacon` call because the navigation that follows would cancel an ordinary request. The safe URL is resolved from the page value, the organization's branding configuration, a server-injected copy, or the default, in that priority. [[#client-data #keys]]
demo_narrative_client_portal_upgrade_bod:
A client on a secure link can strengthen protection without involving the organization, either by adding a passphrase or by creating an account. [[#portal #privacy]]
**Who is offered which path?** A bare link offers both options. A passphrase-protected link offers only account creation, and the client gains access to the contact details the organization has on file. Contact details are withheld from a bare link because a key derived from the URL alone would hand them to anyone who held the URL. A client already on an account has no further option. [The portal channel lifecycle](#deep-dive/portal-channel-lifecycle) covers the three tiers. [[#portal #permissions]]
**Adding a passphrase.** The browser suggests five random words from a published word list, and the client can replace them. On submission the browser derives a fresh channel key from the passphrase and re-seals every message the device can still open under that key. Messages the device cannot open, such as ones sealed to a previous key the session no longer holds, are left behind. Before submission, the form tells the client how many messages cannot be carried over, with a way to go back. After success, if any messages were left behind, a notice says so. The server accepts the change only when the re-sealed messages and the skipped messages together account for every message in the channel, so a message arriving mid-upgrade aborts the operation. The link address keeps working afterward but no longer opens the conversation without the passphrase. [[#keys #encryption #failure-states]]
**Creating an account.** The client picks a username (minimum three characters) and a password (minimum eight characters). The password goes through the same key derivation that staff sign-in uses. One operation revokes the previous channel, creates the account and a new channel, moves the re-sealed messages across, and deletes anything the device could not open, since those messages were already unreadable to the client. Before submission, the form tells the client how many messages will be deleted, with a way to go back. The secure link ceases to work at that point. [Account sign in](#client-account/sign-in) covers what the account provides afterward. [[#keys #portal]]
**What does the server store afterward?** The passphrase and the password both stay in the browser. The server records a public key, a login-token hash, and a key check value after either upgrade. Usernames are kept as keyed hashes, not as readable text. [How keys are derived](#deep-dive/how-keys-are-derived) covers the derivation protocol. [[#server-holds #keys #metadata]]
**The upgrade components and the coverage guard.** The chooser is `UpgradeChooser.svelte`, the two forms are `AddPassphraseForm.svelte` and `AccountCreateForm.svelte` in `packages/client/src/lib/portal/`, and the re-seal helpers are `add-passphrase-crypto.ts` and `account-crypto.ts` beside them. The word suggestion draws from the EFF large wordlist (7776 entries) using rejection sampling over a 13-bit range. The coverage guard is `hasExactMessageCoverage` in `packages/server/src/portal/message-coverage.ts`, called by `addPassphrase` in `channel-service.ts` and by `upgradeFromSecureLink` in `account-service.ts`. The skipped-message notice after either path is `portal_reseal_skipped_note`. [[#portal #encryption]]
demo_narrative_client_account_sign_in_bo:
The sign-in form asks for a username and a password. It appears on a first visit, after a reload, and after the idle timeout or a closed tab clears the keys, because the keys that open the client's messages come from the password and are not stored anywhere. [[#portal #keys]]
**What does the password produce?** The browser derives a keypair for reading the client's messages and a separate token for authenticating to the server. Both come from the password alone. The derived material stays on the device and is cleared when the page closes. [How keys are derived](#deep-dive/how-keys-are-derived) covers the derivation steps and the two servers that participate. [[#keys #encryption]]
**What does an unknown username get back?** An unknown username, a wrong password, and a nonexistent account all receive the same failure after the same amount of work. The server cannot be made to answer differently for a name that exists and one that does not. [[#server-holds #privacy]]
**How long does the session last?** The server-side session uses a short cookie with sliding renewal on human activity. The cookie that carries it cannot be read by scripts on the page. The server stores a fingerprint of the token, not the token itself. After fifteen minutes without input from the client, the idle timeout clears the keys in the browser and revokes the session. Closing the tab clears the keys but does not revoke the server session; that session lapses within twenty minutes of the last renewal. [Sign out](#client-account/sign-out) and [Quick exit](#client-portal/quick-exit) also end the session. [[#server-holds #keys #failure-states]]
**Rate limits.** Salt requests and sign-in attempts are each capped at ten per address per hour. [[#failure-states #server-holds]]
**The sign-in derivation and enumeration defense.** The browser runs Argon2id on the password, blinds the stretched result, sends the blinded value to two evaluation servers, and derives from their combined answer the keypair and authentication token. The password, the stretched output, and the derived keys stay inside a worker and are zeroed on page close. The server answers every salt request with both a real salt and a deterministic fake salt computed in parallel, and compares the presented token against a fixed dummy hash when no account row matches, so timing and work are constant regardless of whether the username exists. The session cookie is HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Path=/, carries no domain attribute, and is always Secure in production. The server stores a BLAKE2b hash of the session token rather than the token itself, and purges expired session rows on each successful sign-in. The form is `AccountLoginForm.svelte` in `packages/client/src/lib/portal/`. Key derivation runs in the portal worker through `account-crypto.ts` and `packages/crypto/src/client-account.ts`. The server side is `getSaltForUsername` and `login` in `packages/server/src/portal/account-service.ts`, against the `client_accounts` and `client_account_sessions` tables in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`. [[#keys #server-holds]]
demo_narrative_client_account_thread_bod:
An account gives the client a password-based way to reopen the same conversation on every visit. The encryption is the same as a secure link, and only the source of the private key differs, which the password supplies. [Message thread](#client-portal/thread) covers the timeline and [Reply composer](#client-portal/composer) covers the reply path. [[#portal #client-data #encryption]]
**What does an account not change?** The expiry schedule for the client's copies is the same whether access comes from an account or a link. [Message thread](#client-portal/thread) covers the expiry in full. [[#retention #portal]]
**What does the server store?** The server keeps a fingerprint of the username that cannot be read back, plus what it needs to check a sign-in. Neither the username nor the password is readable. The server can also see that an account exists for this client, when it was created, and when the client last visited. That metadata is how a server that cannot read the conversation knows a client returned. [The portal channel lifecycle](#deep-dive/portal-channel-lifecycle) covers the channel record. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
**Who can reset an account?** A user holding the Reset client login permission can reset a client's account. Resetting deletes the account and the client's message copies, revokes the channel, and returns the client to text and email. A client who has lost the password has no other route back into the conversation. [Portal access tier](#ticket-detail/portal-tier) covers the control. [[#permissions #failure-states]]
**The account tables and channel service.** The account record is a `client_accounts` row holding `username_hash`, `salt`, `public_key`, and `auth_hash`. The channel is a `portal_channels` row with a `kind` of `account` and plaintext columns for `created_at` and `last_seen_at`, so the messaging services operate on it without modification. The tables are in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts` and the service is `packages/server/src/portal/account-service.ts`. [[#portal #server-holds]]
demo_narrative_client_account_password_b:
The client's encryption keys derive from the password, so changing the password rebuilds the keys and re-encrypts the conversation. A minimum of eight characters is required. The change either completes entirely or has no effect; a failure partway through leaves the password and the conversation unchanged. [[#keys #portal]]
**Why does a password change re-encrypt messages?** Each message on the channel is sealed to a key pair derived from the password. The browser proves the current password, derives a fresh key pair, decrypts the messages it can open, and re-encrypts each one to the new key. Any message the device could not decrypt stays sealed to the old key and becomes permanently unreadable under the new one. Before submitting, the client is told how many earlier messages would be left out of the change, with a way to back out. [How keys are derived](#deep-dive/how-keys-are-derived) covers the derivation, which follows the same path as sign-in. [[#keys #encryption]]
**What happens when a message arrives mid-change?** The server checks that the re-encrypted messages and the declared-unreadable messages together account for every message on the channel. A message that arrived while the browser was working belongs to neither group, so the server refuses the change. [[#failure-states #encryption]]
**Other sessions.** The change signs out every other session on the account. A session open on another device stops working at that moment. The client's account ID does not change, because it identifies the client rather than the key. [[#server-holds #keys]]
**No password reset.** There is no way for the client to recover a forgotten password. A member of the organization holding the Reset client login permission can delete the account so a new way back in can be set up, at the cost of the client's message copies. [Durable thread](#client-account/thread) covers what the deletion removes. [[#failure-states #retention]]
**The form and its services.** The form is `AccountSettings.svelte`. The browser rebuilds registration material through `buildAccountRegistration` in `packages/client/src/lib/portal/account-crypto.ts`, and the server side is `changePassword` in `packages/server/src/portal/account-service.ts`. The server runs the credential update, the re-encrypted messages, and the session deletion in a single transaction, so a failure at any step rolls back the whole operation. A member of staff changing their own password follows a different service path on the same derivation shape, which [Password and key re-wrap](#settings/password) covers. [[#keys #server-holds]]
demo_narrative_client_account_settings_b:
The drawer entries for managing an account require a sign-in. Without signing in, the drawer shows no account actions; the organization header, the theme toggle and the privacy notice link still appear. [Change password](#client-account/change-password) and [Sign out](#client-account/sign-out) each cover one of the remaining entries. [[#portal #privacy]]
**How is contact information served?** The client's phone number and email address are fetched only when the client opens the contact card. The server reads both from columns encrypted under its operational key, seals them to the channel's public key, and sends the sealed result. Only the client's own device can open it. The operational key holds these values because the server needs to read a number to dial it and an address to send to it. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers where that exception sits and what it exposes. [[#trust-boundary #server-holds]]
**How does a correction work?** The client sends a correction as an encrypted message on the conversation, following the same encryption as any other reply. The organization reads the correction and applies it. Nothing the client submits writes to a stored number or address directly. [Contact correction](#ticket-detail/correction-status) covers what happens on the organization's side. [[#client-data #encryption]]
**The account page and the contact card.** The drawer actions are published through the client shell context in `packages/client/src/lib/client-shell/`. The contact card is `ContactInfoCard.svelte` and the correction form is `ContactCorrectionSheet.svelte` in `packages/client/src/lib/portal/`. The server builds the sealed payload in `getSealedContactInfo` in `packages/server/src/portal/contact-exposure-service.ts`. [[#portal #server-holds]]
demo_narrative_client_account_sign_out_b:
Signing out ends the server-side session, expires the cookie and zeroes the keys the tab holds. The page returns to the sign-in form. [[#portal #keys]]
**What separates sign-out from closing the tab?** Sign-out revokes the server session immediately. The idle timeout does the same. Closing the tab or navigating to another page zeroes the keys in the browser but does not revoke the server session; that session lapses within twenty minutes of the last renewal. Quick exit replaces the page with a safe destination and also revokes the session. [On the device](#deep-dive/on-the-device) covers what stays in the browser after the keys are gone. [Quick exit](#client-portal/quick-exit) covers the other path and what it does differently. [[#server-holds #failure-states]]
**What does sign-out not hide?** The tab title stays unchanged and the browser stays on the page. Sign-out does not conceal that the page was visited. A client who needs concealment has quick exit. [[#privacy]]
**The logout handler and the cookie.** The handler runs against `accountLogout` in `packages/server/src/routes/client-portal.ts`, which calls `logout` in `packages/server/src/portal/account-service.ts`. The server hashes the token from the cookie, deletes the matching session row, and returns an expired cookie. The deletion is idempotent and the server learns only that a session ended. [[#server-holds #metadata #portal]]
demo_narrative_client_share_view_body:
A share link delivers one encrypted message to a reader who has no account, no sign-in and nothing installed. The server hands over the scrambled message without being able to read it, and the reader's own device performs the decryption. [[#portal #encryption]]
**What does the server see of the address?** The share's identifier travels in the URL path. The key that decrypts the content sits after the `#` fragment mark, which browsers never include in a request. The page replaces the address bar entry with the path alone as soon as it loads, before fetching and decrypting, so the key is absent from the browser's history and from any address the reader copies or forwards even when opening fails. [How encryption works](#deep-dive/how-encryption-works) covers the sealing. [[#keys #server-holds]]
**Why does the key open only this message?** Each link gets its own key, generated fresh for that share alone. The key is unrelated to any credential the reader may hold for a portal or an account, and opening the link ties the request to no other conversation. [[#encryption #privacy]]
**What does a broken link report?** A link that arrives truncated or missing its fragment tells the reader to check that the complete link was opened. Text messages are the delivery channel for these links, and a message split across segments is the likeliest cause. [Single use access](#client-share/one-time) covers the remaining end states. [[#failure-states #telephony]]
**What survives after decryption?** The decrypted message sits in the page and cannot be wiped the way the key can. Quick exit leaves the page. A screenshot, a copy, or a printout remains wherever the reader placed it. [On the device](#deep-dive/on-the-device) covers what a share link leaves in the browser's history and storage. [Quick exit](#client-portal/quick-exit) covers what that control clears and what it does not. [[#failure-states #privacy]]
**Rate limit.** The server allows ten opens per address per minute, which blocks guessing link identifiers without getting in a reader's way. [[#failure-states]]
**The view page and the sealing pair.** The page is `packages/client/src/routes/(client)/share/[id]/+page.svelte`. `encryptShare` and `decryptShare` in `packages/client/src/lib/portal/share-crypto.ts` seal and unseal on the main thread, because no session or worker exists on this page. The share key is bound to the share's identifier in the authenticated data, which prevents replaying the ciphertext under a different identifier. The key is zeroed immediately after use. `openShare` in `packages/server/src/portal/share-service.ts` performs the server-side consume against the `share_links` row from `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`. [Share link](#ticket-detail/share-link) covers the sending end. [[#encryption #server-holds]]
demo_narrative_client_share_one_time_bod:
Each share link can be opened once. The first open gets the message and the server deletes it at that moment, so a second open gets an already-opened state instead of content. The link stops working seventy-two hours after it was made, and expired links are cleared daily. [Data retention](#deep-dive/data-retention) covers the sweep schedule and what clearing removes. [[#portal #encryption #retention]]
**What does the reader see when the content is gone?** A consumed link reports already opened, and the reader sees that the link was used. An expired link reports that the window closed. A link whose identifier matches no record reports not found, whether the record was cleared or the identifier never existed, so probing tells an observer nothing about which identifiers were real. [Shared content](#client-share/view) covers the incomplete-link state for a truncated or broken address. [[#failure-states #server-holds]]
**Who can spend the single read?** The page's own script spends the read after it loads. A fetcher that does not run scripts, such as a link preview bot or a messaging provider's URL scanner, loads the page without spending it. A scanner that opens pages in a full browser and runs scripts would spend it, and the reader who opens the link afterward sees the already-opened state. [[#trust-boundary #privacy]]
**What does interception before the first read mean?** A share link usually travels by text message, so it crosses the carrier and the messaging provider. An attacker who intercepts the full address before the reader opens it can spend the single read. The link is kept short-lived for that reason. [How the reader is protected](#client-share/exposure-hint) covers what the reader is told about that boundary. [[#trust-boundary #telephony]]
**What stays on the server after the read?** The record keeps the ticket, the times it was created, set to expire, and read. The message is gone. Authorship lives in a follow-up on the case thread, whose author is a plaintext column like every follow-up's author, and the follow-up records the share's identifier in plaintext. A seized database reveals when a share was created and opened, who created it and on which case, and nothing of what it contained. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
**The conditional update and the cleanup job.** `openShare` in `packages/server/src/portal/share-service.ts` runs a conditional update (`UPDATE ... WHERE read_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now()`) that gates the race. The first caller to match sets `read_at`, gets the ciphertext from the RETURNING clause, and a second statement nulls the ciphertext column inside the same transaction. Subsequent callers fail the `IS NULL` predicate and fall through to classification (opened, expired, not_found). `registerShareCleanupHandler` in the same file handles the daily expired-row delete across all tenant schemas. The row is `share_links`, defined in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`, and carries no `created_by` column. The expiry is written as `now() + make_interval(secs => ...)` so both the write and the enforcement use the database clock. [[#server-holds #retention]]
demo_narrative_client_share_exposure_bod:
The share page tells the reader that the link carried the decryption key, that the server cannot read the content, and that the link works only once. The notice appears when decrypted content loads. [[#privacy #portal]]
**What does the server see?** The server receives the share's ID and the address of the request. The key is in the URL fragment, which browsers never send to a server. The server hands back scrambled data it cannot read. Nothing in the request ties the reader to any other conversation with the organization. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
**What does the notice not cover?** When the link is sent by text message, the carrier and the telephony provider handling delivery can read the full address, decryption key included. Single use protects against interception after the reader has already opened the link. Interception before that first read still yields a working key. [The telephony relay](#deep-dive/the-telephony-relay) covers what those intermediaries retain. [[#telephony #trust-boundary]]
**The hint component.** `PortalHint.svelte` in `packages/client/src/lib/shell/` renders a notice on four client surfaces. The share page passes its own message and raises the hint on the transition to decrypted content. [[#portal #privacy]]
demo_narrative_deepdive_what_is_care_y_b:
CARE-Y is a call intake and case management system for mutual aid organizations whose clients would be in danger if their identity or their case became known. The people staffing the organization are exposed the same way. A seized server holds no case content. [[#overview #encryption]]
Organizations use it to take calls, texts and emails, keep a case record per client, route work through queues, look up resources in an internal library, and reach clients back on whichever channel is safe for them. The interface is a mobile-first web app that installs to a phone home screen or runs in a desktop browser. [[#overview]]
Client data is encrypted in the user's own browser before it reaches the server, and the server stores ciphertext it has no key for. That protection is a consequence of where the keys live rather than a policy the operator promises to honor. The user's password, stretched in the browser and hardened through a key derivation protocol, is what produces those keys. The server stores no private key and nothing that can reproduce those keys without the password. [How encryption works](#deep-dive/how-encryption-works) covers the full model, and [How keys are derived](#deep-dive/how-keys-are-derived) covers the derivation. [Verifying the code](#deep-dive/verifying-the-code) covers how the browser confirms the code it runs has not been changed. [[#overview #encryption #keys]]
Encryption cannot protect a device that is already compromised. A browser extension or malware that can read the screen can read decrypted case content. Some facts stay readable to the server because the server has to route work with them. A case exists, it was created at a time, it sits in a queue, it carries a priority, and someone is assigned to it. An attacker with the database learns the shape and rhythm of the organization's work without learning a single client's alias or a word of any message, and an attacker holding the secrets file as well reads the stored phone numbers and email addresses. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) names each of those facts. [[#overview #metadata #trust-boundary]]
Clients reach the organization through whichever channel fits their situation, and the channels differ in how much protection each can offer. A regular text message is readable by the phone carrier and by the telephony provider. [The portal channel lifecycle](#deep-dive/portal-channel-lifecycle) covers the tiers and what each one protects, and [The telephony relay](#deep-dive/the-telephony-relay) covers what happens to a text or a call on its way through. [[#overview #portal #telephony]]
**How do the tiers divide?** [[#encryption #keys #server-holds]]
- The PII tier covers cases, messages and case notes, protected by per-case symmetric keys that are wrapped to each authorized user's public key. A client's alias is sealed under the organization key, so any signed-in member of the organization can read it. [[#encryption #keys]]
- The non-PII tier covers shared organization material such as library articles, queue names, note types and configuration, protected by one organization keypair whose private half is wrapped to each user. [[#encryption #keys]]
- The operational tier covers what the server itself must act on without a person present, such as the phone number and email address it dials or writes to, telephony credentials and SMTP configuration, encrypted under a server-side key from the secrets file. [[#encryption #server-holds]]
- Organization branding (name, logo, colors) is stored and served as plaintext, because a client must recognize the organization before trusting it. [[#encryption #privacy]]
**Deployment shape.** One codebase serves a multi-tenant hosted deployment and a self-hosted single-tenant one. Each organization gets its own PostgreSQL schema, and cross-organization queries are structurally unavailable at the SQL layer because every query is scoped through a Kysely schema transformation rather than through a session variable. [Deployment](#deep-dive/deployment) covers where each evaluation share lives, who operates the servers, and what the self-hosted path requires. [[#overview #server-holds]]
**Licence and governance.** The source code is licensed AGPL-3.0-only. Anyone can read, run and modify it, and anyone running a modified version as a network service for others must publish their changes under the same licence. A separate trademark policy requires forks to choose a distinct name, remove CARE-Y branding from the interface, and state that the fork is not the official project. Factual attribution is permitted. An acceptable use policy prohibits surveillance, encryption sabotage, misrepresentation of security properties, facilitation of harm, data commercialization, and honeypot operation. The acceptable use policy is standalone and not part of the licence, and its enforcement is through community governance. [[#overview #privacy]]
**Contributor map.** The monorepo splits into five packages, and anyone adding a field to any of them decides which of the tiers above it belongs to before choosing a column type. [[#overview #client-data]]
- `packages/client` is the SvelteKit app for users, admins and the client-facing portal. [[#overview]]
- `packages/server` is the tRPC API with authentication, webhooks and relay endpoints. [[#overview]]
- `packages/crypto` is the isomorphic encryption library both sides share. [[#overview #encryption]]
- `packages/shared` holds types, Zod schemas and permission enums. [[#overview]]
- `packages/demo` is this handbook, running the real client and server against an in-browser PostgreSQL build. [[#overview]]
demo_narrative_deepdive_how_encryption_w:
A client's messages and the notes written about them are encrypted in the browser before they leave the device, and the server holds only the result. The server has no key that opens it, which is a different and stronger statement than a promise not to look. [Verifying the code](#deep-dive/verifying-the-code) covers how the browser confirms the code performing that encryption has not been tampered with. [[#encryption #client-data]]
Each kind of data has its own key and its own audience, and one kind is public on purpose. [[#encryption #keys #server-holds]]
- The case record, its messages and its notes are readable only by the users authorized on that case. A client's alias is sealed under the organization key, so any signed-in member of the organization can read it. A fresh intake submission or portal reply is sealed to the organization key until someone opens the case, so any signed-in user can unseal it during that window. [How the visitor is protected](#client-intake/how-protected) covers that conversion. [[#encryption #client-data]]
- Shared organization material such as library articles, queue names, note types and settings is readable by any signed-in user in the organization. [[#encryption #keys]]
- Operational configuration such as telephony credentials and mail server settings is readable by the server itself, along with the phone number and email address it needs to reach a client, because the server is what places a call at three in the morning with nobody watching. [[#encryption #server-holds]]
- Organization branding (name, logo, colors) is stored and served as plaintext, because a client must recognize the organization before trusting it. [[#encryption #privacy]]
An attacker who seizes the server and takes the whole database gets ciphertext for all three encrypted tiers, plus the telephony credentials from the operational tier, which grant phone system access and nothing about any client. Opening the case tier requires a user's password run through the key derivation protocol, and opening the organization tier requires the same password first. [How keys are derived](#deep-dive/how-keys-are-derived) covers why a password guess is expensive and why a single seized machine is not enough. [[#encryption #server-holds]]
Without breaking the encryption, an attacker does learn the shape of the work. Case rows carry a plaintext status, priority, queue reference, creation timestamp and assignment. A database dump shows that cases exist, how many, when each arrived, which queue took it, how urgent someone judged it, and that a particular account was assigned to it. It does not show the client's alias, the case summary or a single message. The client's phone number and email address sit in the operational tier, so a dump taken together with the server's secrets file yields those two. The design does not hide overall activity levels or when they occur. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) lists this exposure field by field. [[#metadata #trust-boundary #server-holds]]
Encryption also stops at the edges of the device. A user whose laptop is compromised, or whose browser runs a malicious extension, is showing decrypted case content to whatever is watching, and no server-side property can prevent that. A message that arrived as an ordinary text message was readable by the carrier and the telephony provider before CARE-Y ever encrypted it, which is why the case thread marks where a message came from. [[#failure-states #telephony]]
**Per-case keys and wrapping.** Each case gets its own 32-byte symmetric key, and case content is sealed with XChaCha20-Poly1305. The additional authenticated data binds each ciphertext to the case and to the storage slot it was encrypted for, so a ciphertext moved to a different slot or a different case fails authentication rather than decrypting into the wrong place. No copy of the case key exists in the clear. For each authorized user it is wrapped to that user's ristretto255 public key using ECIES, so the server can wrap a key for a user it cannot impersonate and cannot unwrap. A new case is wrapped for the creator and for each queue member whose public key is on file, and an empty wrap set is refused. Joining a queue backfills the wraps for that queue's existing cases through a resumable sweep, and deactivating the only account holding a case's wrap is refused unless an administrator forces it past a confirmation stating how many cases would become unreadable. On open, the browser worker computes the shared secret from the user's private scalar and the stored ephemeral point, unwraps the case key, and decrypts, with no server round trip in the decryption step. [[#encryption #keys]]
**The organization tier and the public tier.** Shared material uses one organization keypair. The private half is wrapped per user under a key derived from that user's master key, so every signed-in user can open library articles and queue names while the server, holding only the public half, can seal new values without reading any. User display names and login identifiers are stored as sealed boxes under the same organization public key, which is why an administrator's browser can list users by name and the server cannot. Organization branding sits outside both tiers, stored as plaintext by design. [The organization key lifecycle](#deep-dive/organization-key-lifecycle) covers creation, rotation, and what happens when no account holds a copy. [[#encryption #keys #privacy]]
**What does the password not unlock?** Deactivating a user deletes their per-case wrapped keys, so the user's derived private key has nothing left to unwrap even if they still know their password. Changing a password changes the derived private key, which is why a password change re-wraps every case key the user can read. That re-wrap is proportional to the number of cases they have access to. [Password and key re-wrap](#settings/password) covers the full sequence. [[#keys #failure-states]]
**Contributor boundaries.** The primitives live in `packages/crypto/src`, split by job. [[#encryption #client-data]]
- `content.ts` does slot-bound content encryption. [[#encryption]]
- `ecies.ts` and `keywrap.ts` do key wrapping. [[#encryption #keys]]
- `derive.ts` and `hkdf.ts` do derivation. [[#keys]]
- `mem.ts` zeroes buffers. [[#encryption]]
Column shape is the design decision that outlives the code. The `tickets` table holds `encrypted_title` and `encrypted_description` as bytea beside plaintext `status`, `priority`, `queue_id`, `assigned_to` and `created_at`, and `ticket_key_wraps` holds one row per user per case with the ephemeral point, nonce and wrapped key. Adding a field to a case means choosing between the encrypted payload and the plaintext metadata, and a field chosen as plaintext stays visible in every future database dump. [[#encryption #client-data #server-holds]]
demo_narrative_deepdive_how_keys_are_der:
Signing in proves who the user is and also rebuilds, in the browser, every key that opens that user's data, from the password alone. No copy of those keys is kept on the server, encrypted or otherwise, so there is no stored key for an attacker to take away and attack at leisure. [[#keys #encryption]]
The browser first grinds the password through Argon2id, a deliberately slow and memory-hungry function, which turns a fast guess into an expensive one. The result of that grinding is then blinded, a step that scrambles it into a value carrying no information about the password, and the blinded value goes to the application server, which has two independent key services answer it, each applying its own half of a secret neither of them ever hands to the other. The two answers come back combined into one, the browser unblinds it, and what comes out is the seed for every key the user needs. Neither service sees the password, the stretched password, or the final output, and neither one alone can produce the answer. [[#keys #privacy]]
The split changes what a stolen database and a stolen key service are each worth. [[#keys #server-holds]]
- An attacker who takes the database gets an Argon2id hash that allows offline password guessing at 64 MiB and 4 passes per guess. The hash confirms the password but cannot produce the derived keys, because deriving keys still requires going through the two services, which rate limit. [[#keys #server-holds]]
- An attacker who takes one service gets half of a secret that is useless without the other half. On the hosted deployment, the other half is in a different country under a different legal system. Both halves are re-randomized every twenty-four hours, so a half copied in one period cannot combine with its counterpart in the next. [[#keys #server-holds]]
The design does not remove the risk of a stolen password. Someone who learns a user's password, and who has also obtained both halves of the service secret from the same twenty-four-hour period, can derive that one user's keys and read that one user's cases. Other users are unaffected because each user's keys come from their own password. CARE-Y answers this by requiring a password of at least 16 characters and by requiring a second factor before any encrypted data is served. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers what an attacker learns without any password at all. [[#failure-states #keys]]
**Derivation chain.** [[#keys #encryption]]
1. Argon2id stretches the password at 64 MiB of memory and 4 iterations with a single lane, over the 16-byte salt stored per user in `user_keys`, and the client enforces that floor even if the server suggests weaker parameters. [[#keys]]
2. The stretched output is blinded per RFC 9497 and sent for evaluation. [[#keys]]
3. The returned evaluation is finalized into a 64-byte OPRF output. [[#keys]]
4. HKDF-SHA512 expands that output under the label `care-y-master-v2` into the master key. [[#keys]]
5. One expansion of the master key produces the user's ristretto255 private scalar under an ECIES label, whose public point is published to the server and used to wrap per-case keys. [[#keys #encryption]]
6. The other expansion produces an unwrap key for the organization private key. [[#keys #encryption]]
The master key and the private scalar live in a Web Worker for the session and are transferred there by `postMessage` rather than held on the main thread. [[#keys #encryption]]
**Split evaluation and per-identity keys.** The evaluation secret is held as a 2-of-2 Shamir split across two evaluators in separate legal jurisdictions that never exchange shares. [Deployment](#deep-dive/deployment) covers where the evaluators run and who operates them. Each answers with a partial evaluation, and the application server combines the two by Lagrange interpolation into a single evaluated element, which is exactly the value one holder of the whole secret would have produced. The browser unblinds that element once and never sees either partial answer. Neither process uses its master share directly. Every request carries a server-constructed tag naming the identity it is for, whether a user id, a client account id, or an organization and channel pair, and each process derives its working share for that tag by HKDF over its master share. An evaluation under the wrong tag comes from an unrelated key and yields garbage, so identity claims bind mathematically rather than by bookkeeping, per-identity rate limits cannot be spread across claimed identities, and revoking a portal channel genuinely retires its key. [[#keys #server-holds]]
**What does the server store?** The `user_keys` table holds an Argon2id salt, a ristretto255 public point, an optional post-quantum public key, and a key version. [[#server-holds #privacy #keys]]
There is no private key, no encrypted shard, and no password hash used in derivation. The `users` table stores a separate Argon2id hash for authentication, which is not part of the key derivation chain. Login lookup uses `identifier_hash`, a keyed blind index computed from the identifier the browser sends over TLS, while the stored `encrypted_identifier` is a sealed box under the organization public key that no server flow reads back. A seized secrets file plus a seized database allows confirming a guessed username against the blind index, and does not allow recovering usernames. [[#server-holds #privacy #keys]]
**Rotation and recovery.** Because private keys derive rather than being stored wrapped, rotating a master share rotates every derived key at once, which makes rotation a coordinated re-enrollment window rather than a background task. [Password and key re-wrap](#settings/password) covers what happens when a user changes their password. Recovery from total loss of the key services runs from escrow, where the two master shares sit in one passphrase-encrypted file on hardware-encrypted offline drives. Recovery restores the same shares rather than re-splitting them, so all existing derivations stay valid. [[#keys #failure-states]]
**The derivation and evaluation code.** [[#keys]]
- `packages/crypto/src/oprf.ts` holds blinding, finalizing, tagged share derivation, Lagrange combination and proactive refresh, and `packages/crypto/src/derive.ts` holds the Argon2id floor, the master key, the organization unwrap key and the user keypair. [[#keys]]
- `packages/server/src/crypto/oprf-process.ts` performs evaluation, reached through `oprf-ipc.ts` over Unix sockets defined in `packages/server/src/env.ts`, with the share loaded into `sodium_malloc` memory and a canary beside it. [[#keys #server-holds]]
- `packages/client/src/lib/auth/login-crypto.ts` and the workers under `packages/client/src/lib/workers/` orchestrate the client side. [[#keys]]
- The `user_keys` table in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts` defines the storage shape. [[#keys #server-holds]]
demo_narrative_deepdive_org_key_lifecycl:
The organization key protects shared material that every signed-in user can read, and it also seals people-identifying fields such as display names and login identifiers. [How encryption works](#deep-dive/how-encryption-works) covers the full tier model. [[#keys #encryption]]
**How is the key created?** The first administrator's browser generates a Curve25519 keypair during setup, before any other account exists. The server stores only the public half at generation 1. The private half is wrapped to the administrator's own public key and stored on that account. No copy of the private half reaches the server in the clear. Setup requires an escrow export before it can finish. [Encryption keys and escrow](#admin-org/keys) covers the escrow file format and its derivation parameters. [[#keys #encryption]]
**How does each user receive a copy?** Each user's password derives an unwrap key for the organization private key through the key derivation protocol. [How keys are derived](#deep-dive/how-keys-are-derived) covers that derivation. The private key itself travels as a wrapped copy. A signed-in user with the Manage keys permission distributes wrapped copies automatically to enrolled accounts that do not yet have one. [Encryption keys and escrow](#admin-org/keys) covers what an account without a copy cannot read and how those accounts are found. [[#keys]]
**What happens when someone leaves?** Deactivating or removing a user revokes all key material for that account at once. The revocation covers per-ticket wrapped keys, the wrapped organization key copy, and the account's key enrollment. The server refuses when the account is the only one that can open a ticket, and a confirmation states how many tickets would become unreadable. An administrator who confirms proceeds, and those tickets cannot be read by anyone afterward. The server also refuses to deactivate or demote the last active administrator. Removing the last account that holds a wrapped copy of the organization key is refused unless the administrator forces it, and the confirmation names escrow as the recovery path. [[#keys #failure-states]]
**Why rotate?** An organization rotates when a copy of the key may have been compromised. A common reason is a departure on bad terms. Rotation replaces the keypair and reseals all people-identifying data to the new generation. Older ciphertext stays readable because each generation record seals the outgoing secret under the incoming one. [Encryption keys and escrow](#admin-org/keys) covers the rotation steps and the reseal sweep. [[#keys #encryption]]
**What if no remaining account holds the key?** When no active account holds a wrapped copy of the organization key, all data protected by that key is unreadable until the key is restored from escrow. [[#keys #failure-states]]
**The onboarding service and the offboarding transaction.** The keypair is generated in the browser by `generateOrgKeypair` from `packages/crypto/src/org-keypair.ts`, called in `SetupAccount.svelte` at `packages/client/src/lib/components/onboarding/SetupAccount.svelte`. The server-side bootstrap is `bootstrapAdmin` in `packages/server/src/onboarding/onboarding-service.ts`, which stores the public key in `org_config` and seals the first display name at generation 1. Offboarding runs through `revokeVolunteerKeys` in `packages/server/src/crypto/offboarding.ts`, which deletes `ticket_key_wraps`, `wrapped_org_keys`, and `user_keys` for the departing account in one transaction. The sole-holder guard is `SoleWrapHolderError`, which fires when the account is the only wrap holder for any ticket. The last-administrator guards are `CANNOT_DEACTIVATE_LAST_ADMIN` in `packages/server/src/auth/service.ts` and `CANNOT_DEMOTE_LAST_ADMIN` in `packages/server/src/routes/auth.ts`, which count active administrators. Removing, deactivating or revoking the last holder of the organization key is refused by a separate check unless forced. [[#keys]]
demo_narrative_deepdive_trust_boundary_b:
The trust boundary is the line between what the server can read and what only a browser can read, and knowing where it sits is how an organization decides whether CARE-Y is safe enough for the people it serves. [[#trust-boundary #encryption]]
The browser side of the line holds the content that identifies or quotes anyone. [[#trust-boundary #encryption #client-data]]
- A client's alias, which is the name the organization records for them. [[#trust-boundary #client-data]]
- Messages, case notes, and the files attached to a case. [[#trust-boundary #client-data]]
- Queue names, library articles and note types. [[#trust-boundary #encryption]]
- An intake form's questions and the answers a client submitted. [[#trust-boundary #client-data]]
The server side of the line holds the facts the server needs to do its job without a person present. [[#trust-boundary #server-holds #metadata]]
- It knows a case exists, when it was created, which queue it belongs to, what status and priority it carries, and which account is assigned to it. [[#trust-boundary #server-holds]]
- It knows how many messages a case has and when each arrived. [[#trust-boundary #metadata]]
- It knows which accounts exist, when they signed in, and which second-factor methods they enrolled. [[#trust-boundary #metadata]]
- It knows the credentials for the phone system and the mail server, because it has to use them. [[#trust-boundary #server-holds]]
- It has access to a client's phone number and email address, because it is what dials the number and addresses the mail, and those two values are sealed under the server's own operational key rather than under the organization's. [[#trust-boundary #server-holds #client-data]]
Metadata is the cost of that arrangement, and activity patterns are visible in it. A dump shows when the organization is busy, which queues carry the most work, how long cases stay open, how often a particular account is active, and when someone signed in. Relationship structure is visible too, because the assignment column names a real account and there is one read-marker row per user per case they opened. None of that identifies a client, and all of it describes the organization to anyone holding the database. An organization whose threat model includes an adversary interested in staffing patterns rather than case contents should weigh this exposure before adopting the system. [[#metadata #privacy #trust-boundary]]
The following sit outside the encryption boundary entirely by design. [[#trust-boundary #privacy]]
- Intake page branding is public, so a client can recognize who they are contacting. [[#trust-boundary #privacy]]
- A notification email address stored on an account is readable by the server under the operational key, because the server is what addresses the message. Removing email as a second factor clears the address unless the user has chosen to keep it for notifications. In-app and push notifications exist for users who would rather not store an address the server can read. [[#trust-boundary #privacy]]
Third parties hold their own copies of some things, and CARE-Y cannot encrypt what it never touched first. A text message existed in the carrier's network and at the telephony provider before it reached CARE-Y. An email existed in the sender's own mail system. [The telephony relay](#deep-dive/the-telephony-relay) covers what CARE-Y does about that, and [The portal channel lifecycle](#deep-dive/portal-channel-lifecycle) covers the channels that avoid third parties altogether. [[#telephony #portal #trust-boundary]]
**Plaintext columns, named.** The tables below carry the bulk of the plaintext metadata. [[#server-holds #metadata #client-data]]
- On `tickets`, the plaintext columns are `id`, `client_id`, `queue_id`, `status`, `priority`, `on_hold`, `assigned_to`, `key_generation` and `created_at`, while `encrypted_title` and `encrypted_description` are bytea. [[#server-holds #client-data]]
- On `clients`, `encrypted_alias` is bytea under the organization key with an `alias_hash` blind index beside it, `communication_tier` is plaintext and names which channel tier the client is on, `phone_id` and `email_id` are foreign keys to `phones` and `emails` respectively. On `phones`, `encrypted_number` is bytea under the server's operational key beside a `phone_hash` blind index, with `locale`, `location_city` and `location_region` in plaintext. On `emails`, `encrypted_address` is bytea under the operational key beside an `email_hash` blind index. [[#server-holds #client-data]]
- On `portal_channels`, the channel id, client id, auth hash, client public key, passphrase flag, status and activity timestamps are plaintext while every message body in `portal_messages` is ciphertext. [[#server-holds #portal]]
- On `ticket_read_cursors`, the case id and user id are the plaintext primary key with only the cursor value encrypted, so the row's existence discloses that the user opened that case while the position stays unreadable. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
Row counts, foreign key relationships and timestamp sequences are readable structurally throughout, which is what makes the activity inference above possible. Narrowing the case list is a SQL query the server runs over those same plaintext columns, so the queue, status, priority, hold state and assignment someone filtered to are visible to it, while a saved filter's name and stored state are sealed to the organization key and are not. [[#metadata #server-holds]]
**Audit and operational records.** The audit log is pseudonymous and largely plaintext by design, holding an event type, an actor id, an optional case id and a JSON metadata object, so an administrator's browser can query it without a decryption pass. It carries no case content, no phone numbers and no client aliases. A failed audit write does not block ordinary actions; failures are counted in an operational metric and the audit view shows a gap marker where entries are missing. An export that releases plaintext is refused when its audit write fails. Rate-limit counters, job queue rows, session tokens and the key-evaluation audit log are operational-tier data the server reads directly, while the IP address and user agent recorded on a session are sealed to the organization key and are not. [[#server-holds #metadata #privacy]]
**Where does enforcement live?** Every access decision is server-authoritative, and the client hiding a control is convenience only. [[#permissions #trust-boundary]]
- Case access runs through `packages/server/src/tickets/access.ts`. [[#permissions #trust-boundary]]
- Permission gates run through `packages/server/src/auth/roles.ts` and `role-middleware.ts`. [[#permissions]]
- Per-channel policy runs through service-layer assertions at every relay handler and tRPC procedure. [[#permissions #telephony]]
- Organization isolation runs through Kysely schema scoping in `packages/server/src/db/`. [[#permissions #server-holds]]
A contributor adding a query decides which side of the boundary its filter runs on, and a filter the server evaluates is a filter the server can read. [[#permissions #trust-boundary]]
demo_narrative_deepdive_deployment_body:
CARE-Y ships as one codebase and one Docker image that runs in two deployment types. A hosted multi-tenant deployment at care-y.app serves many organizations. A self-hosted single-tenant deployment serves one organization on its own infrastructure. Instances do not communicate with each other. [[#deep-dive #encryption #server-holds]]
**What differs between the two?** [[#deep-dive #trust-boundary]]
- On the hosted deployment, each organization gets its own PostgreSQL schema. The application server runs on a Hetzner VPS in Germany with full-disk encryption behind a Caddy reverse proxy. The key used during sign-in is split into two shares held by two separate servers joined by mutually authenticated TLS. One server is in the EU and one is in Iceland. Compelling both requires separate legal processes in separate jurisdictions. Both shares are re-randomized every twenty-four hours, and a share taken from one epoch is useless against the other server's share from a different epoch. When either server misses three consecutive heartbeats from the other (forty-five minutes), the surviving server destroys its own share and refuses all sign-in key evaluations until the operator restores from offline escrow. [[#trust-boundary #server-holds #keys]]
- On a self-hosted deployment, one organization runs one schema in the same schema-per-organization design. The sign-in key is split into the same two shares, held by two separate processes. By default both processes run on the operator's machine. The operator can move the second process to a separate server, ideally in a different jurisdiction, following the same procedure as the hosted deployment. Share refresh and the heartbeat monitor activate once the two shares are on separate machines. [[#trust-boundary #server-holds #keys]]
