- A self-hosted operator brings its own telephony provider account. The hosted deployment offers both managed and self-managed telephony. [Provider connection](#admin-comms/provider) covers the modes. [[#telephony]]
- The hosted deployment enables the version check by default. Self-hosted instances enable it through a configuration variable and can mirror the version file. The operator of the hosted deployment may publish a signed warrant canary. [[#privacy #server-holds]]
**What applies to both?** Each release carries a manifest of file hashes signed with an offline Ed25519 key. The browser's service worker checks the manifest on install, and a mismatch keeps the old version and shows a warning that cannot be dismissed. An organization can enable a Tor onion address that reaches the same backend. [[#privacy #server-holds]]
**What does choosing between them weigh?** One sign-in key serves every organization on the hosted deployment. Seizing both shares within one twenty-four-hour period would let an attacker attempt offline password guesses against every organization on it at once. Each password is still stretched through a deliberately slow, memory-intensive function that makes each guess expensive. A self-hosted deployment holds one organization's key material only, so a seizure on the hosted side cannot reach it, and a seizure of the self-hosted instance cannot reach anyone else. Organizations facing the strongest adversaries are expected to self-host. The tradeoff is the operational burden of running and patching the instance. [[#deep-dive #encryption #keys]]
[How keys are derived](#deep-dive/how-keys-are-derived) covers the split, the refresh, and the Lagrange combination. [The trust boundary](#deep-dive/the-trust-boundary) covers what any server can read regardless of deployment type. [What CARE-Y is](#deep-dive/what-is-care-y) covers the schema isolation and the contributor package map. [[#deep-dive]]
**The OPRF processes and socket configuration.** [[#keys #server-holds]]
- `packages/server/src/crypto/oprf-process.ts` runs evaluation, reached through `oprf-ipc.ts`. `dead-man-switch.ts` implements the heartbeat monitor and share destruction. [[#keys #server-holds]]
- `packages/server/src/env.ts` defines the two OPRF share-server socket settings, defaulting to Unix sockets on one machine. [[#keys #server-holds]]
demo_narrative_deepdive_verifying_the_co:
The server delivers the JavaScript that encrypts and decrypts data in the browser. A server that is seized or coerced could deliver modified code that sends keys or plaintext elsewhere. CARE-Y separates the code source (the application server, which an attacker could control) from the trust source (the project's GitHub Releases, which the server operator cannot control). The browser's service worker checks each update against a signed manifest before it runs. [[#deep-dive #encryption #trust-boundary]]
**What does the manifest contain?** Each release publishes a manifest listing the SHA-384 hash of every JavaScript and CSS file in the build. The manifest is signed with the project's Ed25519 release key. The maintainer holds that key and signs outside the CI pipeline, so a compromised pipeline can produce a build but cannot produce a signed one. [[#deep-dive #encryption #keys]]
**How does the browser check it?** The app installs as a PWA whose service worker prompts the user before accepting an update. When a new service worker installs, it fetches the signed manifest, verifies the signature against a public key built into the app, and compares hashes against the files it has precached. A mismatch causes the new service worker to be discarded. The previous verified service worker keeps serving. A warning that cannot be dismissed appears when verification fails, when the signature is invalid, or when no signed manifest exists for the running version. The warning is rendered by the known-good cached code. [[#deep-dive #encryption #failure-states]]
**Why are builds reproducible?** Anyone can rebuild a release from source and compare the file hashes against the published manifest. The build runs in a pinned Docker image with deterministic Vite settings. [[#deep-dive #trust-boundary]]
**Where does this protection stop?** [[#deep-dive #trust-boundary]]
- The first visit on any device runs code that nothing has checked, because no service worker exists until that visit installs one. Every end-to-end encrypted web application shares this limitation. [[#deep-dive #trust-boundary]]
- An attacker who controls both the CARE-Y server and the project's GitHub release infrastructure could serve a matching fake manifest. The design turns a single-target attack into one that requires compromising two independent systems. [[#deep-dive #trust-boundary]]
- A self-hosted instance running its own legitimate modifications triggers the warning unless it publishes its own signed manifest. [[#deep-dive #failure-states]]
[Deployment](#deep-dive/deployment) covers the version check defaults and the two deployment types. [How encryption works](#deep-dive/how-encryption-works) covers what the delivered code protects. [[#deep-dive]]
**The service worker and the precache.** `packages/client/src/service-worker.ts` precaches all build artifacts and static files on install, serves known assets cache-first, and clears caches from previous versions on activation. [[#deep-dive #server-holds]]
demo_narrative_deepdive_network_body:
All traffic between the browser and the server travels over TLS. Someone watching the connection cannot read the path, page content, request bodies, or API responses. What TLS does not hide is the hostname, and on the hosted deployment the hostname includes the organization's subdomain, so the DNS lookup and the TLS handshake both reveal which organization the user is connecting to. [Deployment](#deep-dive/deployment) covers the hosted and self-hosted models. [[#privacy #encryption]]
**What about portal and share links?** Portal links and share links carry their decryption key in the URL fragment. The fragment is the part after the # sign. Browsers never send the fragment to any server, so neither the network nor the CARE-Y server sees the key. [[#encryption #privacy]]
**What does the server store about a connection?** The server records the IP address and user agent of each staff session, sealed to the organization key, alongside keyed hashes used to detect a change. The server cannot read the sealed values during normal operation. A change of IP address clears the session's second-factor verification, and [Two factor authentication](#login/two-factor) covers what happens next. Rate limits count requests per IP address for sign-in, public intake, and portal reads. The key-evaluation service logs failed evaluations only, recording the requesting IP address as a keyed hash under a daily key. [[#server-holds #privacy]]
**What do notifications reveal?** Web push notifications carry no content. The server sends an empty body. Notification emails and text pings carry a fixed message with no content from the conversation. [[#privacy #metadata]]
**What about phone calls and texts?** The carrier and the telephony provider can read text messages and hear phone calls. [The telephony relay](#deep-dive/the-telephony-relay) covers what crosses that boundary and how the server handles plaintext. [[#telephony #privacy]]
**What does CARE-Y do about connection visibility?** Organizations can offer a Tor onion address alongside the regular hostname. When a user connects through Tor, the user's internet provider sees a connection to Tor but not to CARE-Y, and the CARE-Y server sees a Tor address instead of the user's real address. Sessions arriving over the onion address are not bound to an IP address, because Tor circuits change. The session token and user agent still bind the session. The server recognizes connections arriving through Tor exit nodes or the onion address and reports the connection type to the interface, so each user can see whether they are connected over Tor or the regular internet. [Security briefing](#settings/security) covers the onboarding walkthrough that explains what network surveillance can and cannot reveal. [[#privacy #trust-boundary]]
**Does the app contact any third party?** The content security policy restricts scripts, fonts, and connections to the application's own origin. Fonts are self-hosted. The client has no analytics service and no error-reporting service. In shipped code the browser contacts no third-party origin at runtime. The one exception is quick exit, which navigates to the organization's configured safe site on the user's action. API responses carry a no-store directive so the browser does not write them to its disk cache. [[#privacy #server-holds]]
**The response headers and the network-facing code.** Production responses carry HSTS with a two-year max-age, includeSubDomains, and preload. X-Frame-Options is DENY. Referrer-Policy is strict-origin-when-cross-origin. Cross-origin isolation headers are set. The CSP is defined in `packages/client/svelte.config.js`. Response headers are set in `packages/client/src/hooks.server.ts`. The no-store directive on API responses is in `packages/server/src/index.ts` and on blob downloads in `packages/server/src/routes/blob-download.ts`. The daily-rotating IP hash for key evaluations is derived in `packages/server/src/crypto/oprf-audit.ts`. Session IP and user-agent sealing is in `packages/server/src/auth/session-repository.ts`. The IP-change handler is in `packages/server/src/auth/service.ts`. Notification messages are in `packages/server/src/notifications/i18n.ts`, and the empty-body push sender is in `packages/server/src/notifications/push.ts`. [[#server-holds #privacy]]
demo_narrative_deepdive_on_the_device_bo:
Keys and decrypted case content live in the browser's memory. When the user signs out, closes the tab, or sits idle for fifteen minutes, the browser zeroes the keys and clears the decrypted caches. A small set of preferences and organization details stay in browser storage after the keys are gone. [[#privacy #keys #encryption]]
**What does memory hold?** Keys are held in a background process of the browser. Per-case ticket keys sit in a fifty-entry cache that zeroes each key it evicts. Decrypted text and organization material are held by the open page and registered together so they can be cleared in one step. The app writes nothing decrypted or key-bearing to the browser's database. [[#keys #encryption #client-data]]
**When are the keys zeroed?** Signing out clears the decrypted caches and zeroes the keys first, then asks the server to end the session. If the server does not confirm, the sign-in page shows a notice. The idle timeout after fifteen minutes does the same. Closing the tab clears the decrypted caches and zeroes the organization key, and the background process zeroes its own keys three seconds after the last tab disconnects. A thirty-minute backstop zeroes all keys if no request arrives, covering tabs that crash without sending a disconnect. [[#keys #privacy]]
**What stays after a staff user signs out?** The color scheme, the interface theme, and view-mode choices remain in local storage. The branding cache, the organization's terminology, saved-filter keys, and reply drafts are cleared on sign-out and on idle timeout. [Language selection](#settings/language) covers what the language preference stores. [[#client-data #privacy]]
**What stays on a client's device?** Client pages write no organization branding to the device's storage. The name and safe-exit address arrive in the page from the server. Portal and share links carry the decryption key in the URL fragment, which browsers do not include in requests. The page strips the fragment from the address bar once it has read it, but the path with the channel or share identifier stays in the browser history. The share view's decrypted text is a JavaScript string that cannot be zeroed; leaving the page drops the reference. Intake zeroes each key inside the call that created it, and its form fields turn browser autofill off. Client password fields discourage the browser from saving the password. A client's theme or language choice leaves the same local storage key as a staff user's. [Quick exit](#client-portal/quick-exit) covers what the exit control does and does not clear. The client account idle timeout revokes the server session and returns to the sign-in page. [Account sign in](#client-account/sign-in) covers that timeout. [[#client-data #portal #privacy]]
**The cleanup modules and the worker backstop.** Sign-out runs through `packages/client/src/routes/(auth)/logout/+page.svelte`. The idle timeout fires in `packages/client/src/routes/(app)/+layout.svelte`. Tab-close cleanup runs in `packages/client/src/lib/auth/cleanup.ts`. The cache registry that coordinates clearing is `packages/client/src/lib/crypto/cache-registry.ts`. The shared worker's idle self-zero backstop is `IDLE_SELF_ZERO_MS` in `packages/client/src/lib/workers/crypto-core.ts`. The per-case ticket key cache is `packages/client/src/lib/workers/tk-cache.ts`, with a fifty-entry cap and memzero on eviction. The service worker excludes all API paths from its cache in `packages/client/src/service-worker.ts`, and the server sets `no-store` on every tRPC response via `packages/server/src/http/response-headers.ts`. [[#keys #encryption]]
demo_narrative_deepdive_telephony_relay_:
Phone calls and text messages are the one part of CARE-Y where plaintext has to exist on the server, because a phone number and a message body have to be handed to a phone company in a form it can act on. The relay is where that happens, and it holds plaintext only long enough to forward it and then zeroes every buffer that carried it. [[#telephony #encryption]]
For an outbound text, the user's browser decrypts the reply and posts it with the ticket identifier to a single relay endpoint. The server looks up and decrypts the client's phone number from its own store, never from the request, then hands number and body to the telephony provider and wipes the memory it used. The relay writes nothing, logs no request body, and returns no content in an error response. The browser separately encrypts its own copy and stores that on the case thread, so the readable record of the conversation lives where only the ticket's members can open it. Outbound email follows the same shape through a relay endpoint of its own. An outbound call carries no message body, and the browser submits the user's own callback number, which the server refuses unless it hashes to the number the user verified, while the client's number is resolved server-side the same way. [[#telephony #server-holds]]
Inbound messages follow the same shape in reverse. A text arrives at the provider, the provider posts it to CARE-Y, and the server encrypts the body before writing anything to the database, then wipes the plaintext. CARE-Y then asks the provider to delete its own log of that message, and retries through a job queue if the request fails. [[#telephony #encryption]]
The message was already readable by other people before it arrived. The client's phone carrier saw it. The telephony provider saw it, and holds phone number and delivery metadata under its own retention rules and its own legal obligations regardless of what CARE-Y requests. A subpoena to the provider produces that metadata. It does not produce message content, because CARE-Y's stored copy is encrypted and CARE-Y asked the provider to delete its log. Clients who need the channel itself protected are better served by an encrypted channel in their browser, and [The portal channel lifecycle](#deep-dive/portal-channel-lifecycle) covers those. [What the network sees](#deep-dive/what-the-network-sees) covers the broader picture of what each observer along the path can read. [[#telephony #failure-states #privacy]]
**Why is the relay not part of the main API?** The relay endpoints are raw HTTP handlers rather than tRPC procedures, because the tRPC JSON parser produces JavaScript strings and a string cannot be zeroed. The handlers read the request body as a `Buffer`, use it, and call `.fill(0)` in `finally` blocks on every buffer that touched plaintext. That covers the raw body, the phone number buffer, the message buffer, and the ticket identifier buffer. Authentication uses the same session functions as the rest of the API, called directly, and the endpoints mount under a `/relay/` prefix with a maximum body size. [[#telephony #server-holds]]
**What does inbound handling do?** The webhook signature is validated before anything else, in development as well as in production, and a request with a missing or invalid signature is rejected. After validation, the request is deduplicated by provider message identifier. [[#telephony #encryption #failure-states]]
1. The client is resolved or created by blind index on the phone number. [[#telephony #client-data]]
2. The ticket is resolved or created. [[#telephony #client-data]]
3. The body is encrypted under a per-ticket key, and both plaintext and key are zeroed in `finally` blocks. [[#telephony #encryption]]
4. When the client has an active encrypted portal channel, a copy of the message is sealed to the channel's public key so that the client's view of the conversation matches the organization's. [[#telephony #portal]]
That portal copy is the one message class on the portal that the server rather than a browser seals. Voicemail audio is fetched from the provider, sealed to the ticket key, stored, and then deleted at the provider. A recording that cannot be routed to a ticket is sealed to the organization key and held in quarantine for an administrator to route by hand. [[#telephony #encryption #portal]]
**Provider boundary.** Provider-specific code sits behind one interface. The interface covers sending messages, placing calls, validating webhooks, and deleting call, message, and recording logs. Twilio is the implemented provider. SignalWire has a validated configuration shape and no provider module, so selecting it is not yet a working path. A mock provider stands in for development and for this handbook. Switching providers is configuration rather than code, and provider credentials live in the operational tier where the server can read them, which is the one tier the server has keys for. [[#telephony #server-holds]]
**The relay, webhook, and provider code.** Relay handlers are `packages/server/src/routes/relay.ts`, which mounts one endpoint each for a text, an email, a call, a WebRTC token, a phone lookup, and a consultant verification, with shared parsing and authentication in `relay-utils.ts`. [[#telephony #server-holds]]
- Webhook intake is `packages/server/src/routes/webhooks.ts`, dispatching to `packages/server/src/telephony/inbound-sms.ts`, `inbound-mms.ts`, `inbound-call.ts`, and `recording-handler.ts`. [[#telephony]]
- The provider interface is `packages/server/src/telephony/provider.ts` with `twilio.ts`, `provider-http.ts`, and `mock-provider.ts` behind it and `factory.ts` selecting one. [[#telephony]]
- Log deletion is `packages/server/src/jobs/log-deletion.ts` with helpers in `telephony/log-deletion-helpers.ts`. [[#telephony #retention]]
- The automatic reply is selected in `packages/server/src/telephony/sms-auto-reply.ts` and sent by `inbound-sms.ts` after the follow-up is written. [[#telephony]]
A new relay endpoint uses `Buffer` rather than string, logs no bodies, returns no plaintext in errors, and zeroes every buffer in a `finally` block. [[#telephony #server-holds]]
demo_narrative_deepdive_portal_channel_l:
A client's safest channel depends on their phone, their situation, and who else might see their screen. CARE-Y offers three tiers and lets the client move up without asking anyone's permission. The tiers differ in how much of the channel itself is protected. The help behind each tier is the same. [[#portal #privacy]]
Text and email is where every client starts. It works on any phone with no setup, and the organization's stored copy of the conversation is encrypted like everything else. The channel itself is not protected, because a text message is readable by the carrier and by the telephony provider on its way through. [The telephony relay](#deep-dive/the-telephony-relay) covers what that means in practice. [[#portal #telephony]]
A secure link is a private page for one client, reachable only by the exact link sent to them, with no account and no password to remember. Messages on that page are encrypted in the client's own browser, so neither the phone company nor the server can read them. The key material lives in the URL fragment, which browsers never send to a server. The server stores the conversation without ever being able to open it. The limitation follows directly from that design. Anyone who gets the whole link gets the conversation, which matters for a client whose phone might be looked through. A client can add a passphrase. The link alone then cannot open the conversation. The passphrase has an enforced minimum strength. [[#portal #encryption #failure-states]]
An encrypted account is the strongest of the three tiers. The client chooses a username and a password, and the password derives their keys through the same protocol a staff member's password uses. The credential is something the client knows rather than something in a message someone else could find. The client can add the account page to their home screen for repeat visits. A subpoena to the phone company or the mail provider produces a login page address and nothing else. Closing the tab clears the keys from the browser but does not revoke the server session; that session lapses within twenty minutes of the last renewal. [Account sign in](#client-account/sign-in) covers that session model. [[#portal #keys]]
Moving up a tier is the client's own decision, taken from inside their own session, and no member of staff has to enable it. The client is warned before submitting when messages on the device cannot be opened under the new key. [Security upgrades](#client-portal/account-upgrade) covers the upgrade paths and their limitations. [[#portal #privacy]]
- A client on a bare link is offered both the passphrase and the account. [[#portal]]
- A client on a passphrase link is offered the account. [[#portal]]
- A client already on an account is offered nothing further. [[#portal]]
Adding a passphrase or an account is the mitigation for a captured link, and gating a mitigation behind someone else's attention works against it, which is why the client controls the decision. [[#portal #privacy]]
One-time message links are a separate mechanism rather than a tier. A user sends a single encrypted message whose link stops working after its first read or after 72 hours, whichever comes first. That is how something sensitive travels over an insecure channel without living there. [[#portal #encryption]]
**Credential model per tier.** Each tier authenticates the client differently. [[#portal #keys #encryption]]
- Text and email has no portal credential, because the client's phone number is the address. [[#portal #telephony]]
- A secure link's credential is a 24-byte random seed carried in the URL fragment. From that seed the browser derives a 48-character channel id, a 32-byte auth token, and an Argon2id salt. The server stores only a BLAKE2b hash of the auth token for timing-safe comparison. [[#portal #keys]]
- An account's credential is a username and a password, which run the full staff pipeline and yield both a keypair and an independent auth token under separate HKDF labels. Neither reveals the other. [[#portal #keys]]
The channel keypair does not come from the seed directly. The seed, or the seed concatenated with the Argon2id stretch of a spoken passphrase, becomes the input to a key evaluation under a tag naming that organization and channel, and the evaluation's output is what derives the keypair. [[#portal #keys #encryption]]
**Why does the evaluation step matter?** Routing channel derivation through a tagged evaluation gives two properties a seed-only derivation cannot have. A passphrase guess costs a rate-limited round trip under that channel's tag rather than a local hash, which is what makes a short spoken phrase worth using. Revocation becomes cryptographic rather than procedural, because the evaluation path refuses tags whose channel is revoked or expired. No other credential is an oracle for that key, and a photographed link paired with a later database dump stops decrypting at revocation. An unknown channel id is allowed because a link is minted before its row exists. An active row requires the auth token. Revoked and expired rows are refused. [[#portal #keys #server-holds]]
**What does the server hold for a channel?** The portal_channels row is plaintext throughout. [[#server-holds #metadata #portal]]
- The channel id, the auth token hash, the client's public key and a passphrase flag. [[#server-holds #portal]]
- A key-check ciphertext with its ephemeral point and nonce. [[#server-holds #portal]]
- A status column, plus created, last-seen, last-notified and revoked timestamps. [[#server-holds #metadata]]
- Message rows for the channel carry direction, ephemeral point, nonce, ciphertext and timestamps. [[#server-holds #portal]]
A client has at most one active channel at a time, enforced by a partial unique index on client_id. The client row carries a plaintext tier column that the server updates when a channel is created or revoked. The server knows a channel exists, when it was opened, how often the client visited, and which tier the client moved to. It cannot read a word of the conversation. A wrong passphrase is detected in the client's browser against the stored key check. The server never learns whether a guess was right. [[#server-holds #metadata #portal]]
**Lifecycle and endings.** [[#portal #retention #failure-states]]
- It expires lazily after 30 days without the client reading it. The sweep runs on the next read request and deletes the client-side copies of messages, attachments and recordings. The organization's record of the case stays intact. Unseen replies from the organization are kept. [[#portal #retention]]
- Regenerating a link revokes the old channel and deletes the client's copies. The old link shows a dead-link state on the next open. [[#portal #failure-states]]
- A user revokes it outright. Revoked, unknown and badly authenticated channel ids all produce the same generic response, indistinguishable by design so a link cannot be probed. [[#portal #failure-states]]
- The organization disables the secure link channel at the policy level. New channel creation stops and replies are refused, but a client holding a working link can still open it and read, because a freeze can be lifted later while destroying a client's access to their own history cannot be undone. [[#portal #permissions]]
- Merging two clients revokes the losing client's channel. The revoked channel's content is kept until the merge is locked. [Merging clients](#admin-people/client-merge) covers that outcome. [[#portal #failure-states]]
**Client-side custody.** Portal crypto runs in a dedicated worker rather than on the page. The worker owns the seed after the main thread's one unavoidable touch of parsing the URL fragment, along with the passphrase stretch, the blind and finalize halves of the evaluation, the keypair, and message and attachment encryption. A zeroing operation fires on quick exit and page hide. A script injected mid-session can still read plaintext already rendered on the page, which nothing can prevent, but it cannot take the channel's private scalar out of the worker and decrypt the channel's future traffic offline. [[#portal #failure-states #encryption]]
**The derivation, worker, services and schema.** Channel derivation is `packages/crypto/src/portal.ts` and account derivation is `packages/crypto/src/client-account.ts`, both on the shared `keypairFromOprfOutput` helper. The portal worker and its bridge are under `packages/client/src/lib/workers/portal*`, and the client surfaces are under `packages/client/src/lib/portal/`. The server services are under `packages/server/src/portal/` with the tRPC surface in `packages/server/src/routes/client-portal.ts`. Schema is in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`, and the 30-day sweep is `packages/server/src/portal/portal-message-service.ts`. [[#portal #retention]]
demo_narrative_deepdive_permission_syste:
Every organization divides work differently, so CARE-Y ships three roles with sensible defaults and lets the organization move almost every individual ability between them. The three roles are Volunteer, Manager and Admin. Each role holds a set of fifty keys across eight capability groups. An administrator can add a key to any role or remove one. [[#permissions]]
The keys are grouped by the kind of work they govern rather than by seniority. [[#permissions]]
- Keys for the case record separate reading a case from acting on one. Viewing, opening, editing the summary, writing notes, changing status, linking, claiming, assigning, deleting someone else's note and downloading media each move independently. [[#permissions #client-data]]
- There is a separate key for texting, for email, for calling and for messaging in the portal. One key for sending files applies across all channels. [[#permissions #telephony]]
- Keys for the client's own access to their case cover share links, portal channels, login resets and revoking reply links. [[#permissions #portal]]
- Keys for client records cover viewing clients, viewing their personal information, editing contact details, editing aliases, merging and deleting. [[#permissions #client-data]]
- Keys for the knowledge base cover reading, writing, managing categories and deleting articles. [[#permissions]]
- Keys for queues separate queue management, queue membership and queue notifications. [[#permissions]]
- Keys for intake separate designing forms from viewing submitted responses. [[#permissions]]
- Keys for running the organization cover roles, users, identity, channel routing, retention, note types, encryption keys, infrastructure, greetings, automatic replies, voicemail quarantine, escalation, presets, reports and the audit log. [[#permissions]]
Defaults are chosen so that turning the system on changes nobody's day. Each key sits at the level that gated the same operation before the keys existed, which is why the client-contact keys start at Volunteer level even though an organization might prefer otherwise. Reaching a client used to require only a session, so starting those keys anywhere higher would have meant a fresh install where nobody can answer anyone. An organization that wants a back-office role withholds those keys deliberately. [[#permissions]]
Managing encryption keys, managing roles, and managing infrastructure stay with Admin regardless of overrides. That lock is enforced when an override is written and again when permissions are read, so a row inserted directly into the database granting one of the three to another role has no effect. [[#permissions #failure-states]]
Permissions govern actions, not visibility of already-released material. [Unreadable response](#admin-responses/key-not-held) covers what happens when a permission is revoked but key wraps from the grant period remain. [[#permissions #failure-states #encryption]]
**How is an effective set computed?** Each role has a default set in server-side configuration, and per-organization overrides live in `role_permission_overrides`, one sparse row per role and permission with an enabled flag. Setting a permission back to its default deletes the row rather than storing it. [[#permissions #server-holds]]
1. Start from the role's default set. [[#permissions]]
2. Apply each override row as an add or a remove. [[#permissions]]
3. Ignore override rows naming an unknown permission, so removed or future names do not break the merge. [[#permissions]]
4. Enforce the locks by force-adding all three locked keys to Admin and force-removing them from every other role. [[#permissions #failure-states]]
Role IDs in the database are deliberately opaque strings rather than readable names, so a database-only attacker cannot infer the organization's structure from them. The human-readable name lives server-side until encrypted admin configuration carries it. [[#permissions #server-holds]]
**Caching and its deployment constraint.** Effective sets are cached per organization in process memory. All three roles fill in one query on a cache miss. Every override mutation invalidates the cache, so a revoked permission stops working on the next request. That cache is process-local, which means a multi-instance deployment would let one instance keep serving a revoked set after another instance invalidated its own copy. The server refuses to boot with multiple instances enabled, and a shared-store cache is the prerequisite for lifting that restriction. [[#permissions #failure-states]]
**Queue membership is a separate grant.** Membership in a queue grants read access to every case in that queue, and it is governed by its own key rather than riding on queue management or on notification routing. Separating the three makes the access grant visible. Notification routing determines who gets pinged and grants no access on its own. [[#permissions #trust-boundary]]
**The Permission enum and the override surface.** [[#permissions]]
- `packages/shared/src/roles.ts` holds the `Permission` enum and its grouping. The enum is append-only after deployment because renaming a member orphans every override row that names it. [[#permissions]]
- `packages/server/src/auth/roles.ts` holds role defaults, the lock set, the merge function, the cache, the override repository and the permission-holder queries that intake and notification targeting use, with request-time gating in `role-middleware.ts`. [[#permissions]]
- The override table is `role_permission_overrides` in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`. [[#permissions #server-holds]]
- `packages/client/src/lib/components/admin/RolePermissionsSection.svelte` is the administrative surface, and `packages/client/src/lib/shell/section-registry.ts` maps sections to permissions for client-side gating. [[#permissions]]
demo_narrative_deepdive_data_retention_b:
Data an organization no longer needs can still be taken from it. For a population targeted by a state-level adversary, a case record from three years ago remains a live risk to a person who may have moved, changed names, or gone quiet. Encryption protects what is stored; retention decides whether it is stored at all. The two are different defenses and an organization needs both. [[#retention #privacy]]
The organization's retention policy is off until an administrator turns it on, and turning it on means choosing a window between 1 and 3,650 days. A daily job hard-deletes every closed case whose last activity is older than that window, removing its stored files before its rows and asking the telephony provider to delete its own call and recording logs for the case. A client record, together with its contact, portal channel and account rows, goes only when the last case for that client goes, so a client with an open or a recent case is untouched, and an organization that has never set a window is skipped. Enabling the policy and changing the window both ask for confirmation, and the confirmation states that deleted data cannot be recovered even from the escrow file, because escrow protects keys and not rows. With the policy off, everything is kept until someone deletes it by hand. [[#retention]]
The policy is one setting for the whole organization rather than a choice per queue or per case type. A per-queue window would be a decision someone has to get right on the day they create a queue. Configuring the policy requires the Manage retention permission, which sits with Admin by default and can be moved. [The permission system](#deep-dive/the-permission-system) covers how that moves. [[#retention #permissions]]
Retention cannot delete what a third party holds. It cannot delete a copy a client kept on their own phone either. For clients on a monitored device that copy is often the more dangerous one. Deletion is permanent; nothing the policy removes can be restored. [[#retention #failure-states]]
**Separate lifetimes.** Portal message copies, one-time share links, and telephony provider logs each follow their own schedule independent of the organization-wide window. [[#retention #portal #telephony]]
- Portal message copies on the client side are deleted after 30 days of channel inactivity, measured from the later of the last-seen and created timestamps. That sweep removes portal messages, portal attachments and portal recordings while leaving the organization's own record intact. [The portal channel lifecycle](#deep-dive/portal-channel-lifecycle) covers the channel model. [[#retention #portal]]
- One-time share links expire 72 hours after creation or on first read, whichever comes first. The ciphertext column is cleared at read time while the row survives as a tombstone until an expiry sweep removes it. [[#retention #portal]]
- CARE-Y asks the telephony provider to delete each call and recording log after processing, with retries when the request fails. [[#retention #telephony]]
**What survives a deletion?** [[#retention #metadata #server-holds]]
- Foreign key relationships and row counts remain readable in the tables that are left. [[#retention #metadata]]
- A deleted case removes its own ciphertext and its key wraps. A key wrap without its case cannot be recovered. [[#retention #encryption]]
- Escrow holds key material rather than data, so no escrow ceremony brings back a deleted row. [[#retention #keys]]
**The retention column and the purge jobs.** [[#retention]]
- The organization-wide window is `org_config.pii_retention_days`, an integer column defined in `packages/server/src/db/migrations/tenant/001_baseline.ts`, written through `setPiiRetentionDays` in `packages/server/src/auth/service.ts` behind a permission-gated tRPC procedure in `packages/server/src/routes/auth.ts`, and read back for display through the hub status query. [[#retention #permissions]]
- The purge itself is `packages/server/src/jobs/pii-retention.ts`, which exports `purgeTicket` and `purgeClient` so manual deletion runs the same cascade. [[#retention]]
- The independent sweeps live in `packages/server/src/jobs/`, where `portal-message-expiry.ts` handles the 30-day portal window across tenant schemas and `log-deletion.ts` dispatches provider log deletions with backoff. [[#retention #portal #telephony]]
- Share link expiry logic is in `packages/server/src/portal/share-service.ts`. [[#retention #portal]]

demo_entry_desc:
CARE-Y is a call intake and case management system for mutual aid organizations serving populations that are at risk. Both clients and volunteers face real danger if their identities or case details are exposed, and CARE-Y mitigates this by encrypting all personally identifiable information in the browser before it reaches the server, so the server itself cannot read it.
This handbook pairs live documentation with a working simulator of the CARE-Y application, running the real code against a real database entirely in your browser. Nothing leaves your device. The text alongside it explains what each screen does, how the system is built, and what protections are in place.
The handbook is both user documentation and a transparency tool. Organizations with this risk profile should be able to verify the claims CARE-Y makes, and the simulator is built to let them do that by watching the system run. The trust boundary is the same one that applies to any hosted software, because you cannot verify what a server you do not control actually runs. CARE-Y is open source and built for self hosting, so organizations that prefer to run it on their own infrastructure can remove that boundary entirely. The full open source codebase is available through the GitHub link in the header.
demo_entry_nav_body: The contents menu in the top bar lists every handbook section. The simulator follows where the handbook goes, and tapping around inside the simulator moves the handbook to match. Nothing you type in the simulator leaves your device.
demo_entry_controls_body: When the app simulator is open, a toolbar above the simulator lets you enter fullscreen mode, resize to phone or desktop presets, and switch the logged in user's role. The toolbar is also a drag handle, so you can grab it anywhere to reposition the simulator, and you can resize from any edge or corner by dragging.
demo_entry_flow_body: The Data flow button in the top bar opens the data flow panel, and every interaction in the simulator traces its path through screen, encryption, API, server, and database lanes, with each step showing direction, timing, and a payload preview. Some operations like incoming calls or scheduled events cannot be triggered on demand in a browser, so the handbook scripts those interactions to demonstrate the feature. A badge marks each scripted step so you can tell it apart from the real path.
demo_entry_roles_body: The user badge on the simulator toolbar opens a dropdown to switch between Admin, Manager, and Volunteer, and switching changes what every screen shows and what actions are available. The permission enforcement is real server middleware running in your browser, so each role sees exactly what it would in production.
demo_entry_search_body: The magnifying glass in the top bar searches across all handbook sections. Click a result to jump to that part of the handbook.
demo_entry_modes_body: Switch between the read-only handbook and the interactive simulator app from the top bar. Read shows the handbook as a document. The simulator is hidden but keeps running. Simulate places the simulator beside the text on wide screens. Fullscreen activates on narrow screens and whenever the simulator fills the window. In fullscreen the handbook moves into a resizable drawer, opened and repositioned from a book icon tab on the edge.

intake_protected_summary: The organization can open it until someone takes your case. After that, only your case volunteers can.
intake_protected_encrypted_what: Your information is encrypted in your browser before it is sent. The server receives only scrambled data it cannot read.
intake_protected_encrypted_why: Even if someone breaks into this server or seizes it, they cannot read what you wrote. Your information is locked and only unlocks for assigned volunteers.
intake_protected_volunteers_what: Until a volunteer first opens your case, the organization can unlock what you wrote. From then on, only the volunteers working on your case can read it.
intake_protected_volunteers_why: Your information is encrypted before it leaves your device. The people who run the servers can never read it, and nobody outside the organization can see it. The organization can open it until someone takes your case; after that, access narrows to the specific people helping you.
intake_protected_server_what: The server stores your information as scrambled data it cannot decode.
intake_protected_server_why: If someone gains access to this server, they see only encrypted text. Decrypting it requires a volunteer's password plus verification from two separate servers in different countries. No single server holds enough to read your information.
intake_privacy_who_body: Your data is collected by {orgName}, supported by the CARE-Y platform operator.
intake_privacy_what_title: What data we collect and why
intake_privacy_what_body: We collect the information you provide on this form (your name if given, contact details, and your message) to connect you with a volunteer who can help. All information is encrypted before it leaves your device.
intake_privacy_basis_body: We process your information to provide support you requested. Your organization should confirm the specific legal basis with legal counsel.
intake_privacy_sharing_title: Who we share your data with
intake_privacy_sharing_body: Volunteers decrypt your information on their own devices. Until someone first opens your case it can be unlocked with the organization's key; after that, only the volunteers working on your case can read it. If you call or text the hotline, your phone number passes through the phone service provider (currently Twilio, a US company) to connect the call or deliver the message.
intake_privacy_transfer_body: If you use the phone service, your phone number is processed by Twilio, which operates in the United States. This transfer is covered by Standard Contractual Clauses. Your encrypted web submissions stay on the European server and are never sent to a third party.
intake_privacy_retention_title: How long we keep your data
intake_privacy_retention_body: Your encrypted information is kept as long as your case is open, plus any retention period set by the organization. See the telephony data disclosure below for phone and text message retention by the phone provider. When your information is deleted, it leaves the live database at once and ages out of encrypted backups within the backup retention period.
intake_retention_disclosure: When you call or text this hotline, your phone number is used to connect the call or deliver the message. The hotline system encrypts your information immediately, but the phone service provider keeps a record of your phone number for up to 150 days. This is required by the provider's policies and cannot be changed by the hotline. Your messages are kept by the provider for up to 60 days. The hotline operator is evaluating alternatives that eliminate this third-party retention.
intake_privacy_rights_body: You can ask to see, correct, or delete your information. Contact the organization and provide your reference code (shown after you submit this form) so they can locate your records. You also have the right to restrict how your data is used or to receive a copy of the data you provided.
intake_privacy_complaint_body: If you believe your data has been handled incorrectly, you have the right to lodge a complaint with a data protection supervisory authority in your country.

intake_privacy_cookies_body: This site uses only session and security cookies that are needed for the form to work. These cookies do not track you and do not require your consent.

intake_continuation_expanded_warning: If you lose this link, there is no way to recover it. Save it somewhere safe.
intake_continuation_copy_error: Could not copy the link. Select it manually and copy.
intake_continuation_warning: This link is the only way back to your conversation. CARE-Y cannot recover it if lost. Anyone who has the link can read and add to this thread.
intake_continuation_hint: The link above carries the key that unlocks your conversation. Save it before leaving this page.

merge_channel_choice_heading: Both callers have a portal link
merge_channel_choice_explain: Only one link can stay active after the merge. The other link will stop working.
intake_forms_closes_at_hint_with_message: After this date, the form shows the closed message instead of accepting submissions.

form_content_editor_image_no_key: Image upload requires the organization key to be loaded

ticket_email_error_send: Email failed to send. Tap to retry.
ticket_email_error_record: Email was delivered, but saving it to the thread failed. Tap to retry saving.
ticket_email_rate_limited: Too many messages. Try again in {seconds} seconds.
ticket_email_error_no_email: No email address on file for this {client}.
ticket_email_too_long: Message is too long to send.
ticket_email_inbound_caution: This message arrived by email. Email is the easiest channel to fake. Check anything important in it before acting on it.
portal_upgrade_body: Your messages are encrypted, and the key travels inside your secure link. That also means anyone who gets your link can read them. You can protect them further in two ways.
portal_upgrade_passphrase_paragraph: Add a password to your link, so the link alone is not enough to open your messages.
portal_upgrade_account_paragraph: Or create an account and sign in at {url} instead, so you no longer depend on the link at all. With an account, losing the link no longer means losing access to your messages and support.
portal_upgrade_add_passphrase: Add a password to this link
portal_contact_footer: This is what {org} has on file to reach you.
portal_contact_footer_generic: This is the contact info on file to reach you.
portal_contact_error: Could not load your contact info. Try again later.
portal_passphrase_suggestion_label: Here is a suggested password you can copy:
portal_passphrase_paste_hint: Paste is allowed. Pick something you can remember.
portal_passphrase_success_body: Your link now also needs the password you just set. Anyone who only has the link will not be able to read your messages.
portal_passphrase_success_note: If you lose the password, ask your support contact for a new link.
portal_reseal_skipped_note: Some earlier messages could not be opened on this device, so they were left out of this change. Everything you can read here is unaffected.
portal_passphrase_error_already_set: A password has already been added to this link.

admin_channel_policy_subtitle: Control which communication channels are available to volunteers.
admin_channel_sms_off_hint: Volunteers cannot send text messages to clients.
admin_channel_email_off_hint: Volunteers cannot send emails to clients.
admin_channel_secure_link_off_hint: Portal setup and secure link messaging are unavailable.
admin_channel_voice_off_hint: Volunteers cannot place calls to clients.
admin_channel_share_link_off_hint: Volunteers cannot send one-time share links.
portal_messaging_disabled: Messaging is currently unavailable for this support line.
portal_messaging_disabled_aria: The organization has disabled messaging on this channel. You cannot send messages at this time.
revoke_reply_token_confirm_body: The client will no longer be able to reply to emails for this ticket. A new token will be created on the next outbound email.
demo_search_results_desc: Entries that match, shown as they read in the handbook.
reseal_banner_progress: Finishing key update: {done} of {total} items. You can keep working; leave the app open if you can.
admin_keys_reseal_ok: All records are on the current key.
admin_queue_watchers_hint: Watchers are notified about new activity in this {queue} but do not receive read access to its {tickets}. Members, by contrast, can read every {ticket} in the {queue}.
admin_presets_description: Saved replies appear in the compose bar when {volunteers} write to {clients}. Titles and content are encrypted with the organization key.
admin_presets_empty_hint: Tap Add reply to create one.
admin_presets_title_placeholder: A short name for this reply
admin_presets_delete_confirm: Are you sure you want to remove this saved reply? {Volunteers} will no longer see it in the compose bar.
hub_presets_subtitle: Reusable reply templates for composing messages
permission_not_yet_built_hint: View own shifts has nothing behind it yet. It is listed so its name stays settled, but granting it changes nothing until shift scheduling is built.
client_delete_confirm_body_one: Permanently deletes the {client}, their {count} {ticket}, and all associated messages, notes, recordings, and attachments. Deleted data leaves the live database at once and ages out of encrypted backups within the backup retention period.
client_delete_confirm_body_other: Permanently deletes the {client}, their {count} {tickets}, and all associated messages, notes, recordings, and attachments. Deleted data leaves the live database at once and ages out of encrypted backups within the backup retention period.
client_delete_confirm_body_zero: Deleting removes the {client} record, contact information, and portal access (no {tickets} on file). Deleted data leaves the live database at once and ages out of encrypted backups within the backup retention period.
